knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structured minimax complexity advantage and fixed-horizon limitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-model comparison and a limitation of the fixed-horizon structured nonsmooth scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the structured nonsmooth minimax problems covered by the scheme and any target accuracy \epsilon>0, the cited gradient-type method uses O(\epsilon^{-1}) iterations, compared with the O(\epsilon^{-2}) black-box benchmark; the improvement relies on explicit simple minimax structure rather than the standard black-box assumption. In the fixed-horizon version, the number of iterations must be selected in advance from \epsilon and the worst-case complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the structured nonsmooth minimax class addressed by the scheme, the cited gradient-type method has order 1/epsilon iteration complexity rather than the order 1/epsilon squared black-box benchmark. This improvement uses additional minimax structure, but the fixed-horizon version requires the iteration count to be chosen in advance from the desired accuracy and worst-case analysis.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
\text{The problem belongs to the explicit, simple structured nonsmooth minimax class assumed by the scheme}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-1})\text{ versus the }O(\epsilon^{-2})\text{ black-box benchmark, and the fixed-horizon scheme requires }N\text{ to be chosen in advance from }\epsilon\text{ and the worst-case bound}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate optimality certified by an aggregated lower model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of the objective is unnecessary once the global affine-minorant assumptions are imposed. The displayed hypothesis uses an attained minimum of the aggregate model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\ne\varnothing\), let \(f:P\to\mathbb R\), and let affine functions \(\ell_k:P\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\ell_k(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in P\). For \(\alpha_k>0\) with \(\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k=1\), define \(\ell_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k\ell_k(x)\). If \(x_N\in P\), \(r_N\ge0\), and \(f(x_N)\le\min_{x\in P}\ell_N(x)+r_N\), then \(f(x_N)\le\inf_{x\in P}f(x)+r_N\). If \(f\) attains its minimum on \(P\), then \(f(x_N)\le\min_{x\in P}f(x)+r_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a candidate value is within r_N of the attained minimum of a convex combination of global affine lower bounds, it is within r_N of the objective infimum. If the objective minimum is attained, this yields the corresponding additive approximate-optimality bound.
assumptions_latex: P\ne\varnothing,\quad f:P\to\mathbb R
\ell_k:P\to\mathbb R\text{ is affine and }\ell_k(x)\le f(x)\quad\forall x\in P
\alpha_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k=1
x_N\in P,\quad r_N\ge0,\quad f(x_N)\le\min_{x\in P}\ell_N(x)+r_N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_N)\le\inf_{x\in P}f(x)+r_N;\qquad \text{if }f\text{ attains its minimum, }f(x_N)\le\min_{x\in P}f(x)+r_N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted oracle gap function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted definition imposes no positivity or normalization requirement on the scaling coefficients and does not itself assert that the resulting quantity is nonnegative or an optimality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given test points \(y_0,\ldots,y_N\), scaling coefficients \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_N\), and a mapping \(g\) defined at each \(y_k\), define \(\delta_N:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) by \(\delta_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k\langle g(y_k),y_k-x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted oracle gap at a comparison point x is the weighted sum of the pairings between each oracle output and the displacement from x to its test point.
assumptions_latex: y_k\text{ and }g(y_k)\text{ are defined for }k=0,\ldots,N
\alpha_k\text{ are scaling coefficients}
x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and all displayed inner products are defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_N(x):=\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k\langle g(y_k),y_k-x\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accuracy Certificate from a Linear Estimating Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the estimating function and its normalized minimum for nonnegative weights with zero initial weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and set \(\bar f=f+\psi\). Let \(\{x_k\}_{k\ge0}\subseteq Q\), let \(a_0=0\) and \(a_k\ge0\) for \(k\ge1\), and suppose \(A_t:=\sum_{k=0}^t a_k>0\) for \(t\ge1\). Define \[\phi_t(x):=\sum_{k=1}^t a_k\left[f(x_{k-1})+\langle\nabla f(x_{k-1}),x-x_{k-1}\rangle+\psi(x)\right],\qquad \hat\ell_t:=\frac1{A_t}\min_{x\in Q}\phi_t(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative weights with zero initial weight, the linear estimating function is the weighted sum of composite first-order models based at the preceding iterates, and its normalized minimum over Q defines the certificate hat ell_t.
assumptions_latex: Q\text{ is convex}
f:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable}
\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is convex}
\{x_k\}_{k\ge0}\subseteq Q
a_k\ge0\quad(k\ge1)
A_t=\sum_{k=0}^t a_k>0\quad(t\ge1)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_t(x)=\sum_{k=1}^t a_k\left[f(x_{k-1})+\langle\nabla f(x_{k-1}),x-x_{k-1}\rangle+\psi(x)\right],\qquad \hat\ell_t=\frac1{A_t}\min_{x\in Q}\phi_t(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For t\ge 0,\qquad \widehat B_{v,t}:=a_0V_0+\left(\sum_{k=1}^{t}\frac{a_k^{1+2v}}{A_k^{2v}}\right)\frac{G_v^2D^{2v}}{2\sigma_{\Psi}}.

a_0\ge 0,\quad V_0\ge 0
a_k>0,\quad A_k>0\quad(k\ge 1)
v\in\mathbb R
G_v>0,\quad D>0,\quad \sigma_{\Psi}>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness of a strongly regularized max representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional max-representation theorem with an explicit gradient and Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2$ be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, let $A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2$ be linear with adjoint $A^*$ and operator norm $\|A\|_{1,2}$, and let $Q\subseteq\mathbb E_2$ be nonempty, closed, and convex. Let $\hat\phi:Q\to\mathbb R$ be proper, closed, and convex, and let $d_2:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and $1$-strongly convex with respect to $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_2}$. Fix $\mu>0$ and define $f_\mu(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\}$. If every $x\in\mathbb E_1$ has a unique maximizer $u_\mu(x)$, then $f_\mu$ is well defined, convex, and continuously differentiable on $\mathbb E_1$, with $\nabla f_\mu(x)=A^*u_\mu(x)$ for all $x$, and $\nabla f_\mu$ is Lipschitz continuous with constant $L_\mu=\|A\|_{1,2}^2/\mu$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A max-represented convex function regularized in its maximization variable by a positive multiple of a 1-strongly convex prox function is convex and continuously differentiable when each maximizer is unique. Its gradient is the adjoint image of the maximizer and has Lipschitz constant equal to the squared operator norm divided by the smoothing parameter.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2\text{ are finite-dimensional real normed spaces}
A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2\text{ is linear with adjoint }A^*
Q\subseteq\mathbb E_2\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
\hat\phi:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is proper, closed, and convex}
d_2\in C^1(Q)\text{ is }1\text{-strongly convex with respect to }\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_2}
\mu>0
\forall x\in\mathbb E_1,\ \arg\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\}=\{u_\mu(x)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_\mu\in C^1(\mathbb E_1),\quad f_\mu\text{ is convex},\quad \nabla f_\mu(x)=A^*u_\mu(x),\quad \operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f_\mu)\le\frac{\|A\|_{1,2}^2}{\mu}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegativity of an Objective-Gap Upper-Bound Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general objective-accuracy certificate property requiring neither convexity nor differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\neq\varnothing\), let \(f,\Psi:Q\to\mathbb R\), and set \(\bar f=f+\Psi\). If \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in Q}\bar f(u)\) and \(\delta:Q\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(\delta(x)\ge \bar f(x)-\bar f(x_*)\) for every \(x\in Q\), then, for every \(x\in Q\), \[\delta(x)\ge \bar f(x)-\bar f(x_*)\ge 0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a scalar certificate delta upper-bounds the objective gap from a global minimizer at every point, then delta upper-bounds a nonnegative quantity and is itself nonnegative everywhere.
assumptions_latex: Q\neq\varnothing
f,\Psi:Q\to\mathbb R
\bar f(x)=f(x)+\Psi(x)
x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in Q}\bar f(u)
\forall x\in Q,\quad \delta(x)\ge \bar f(x)-\bar f(x_*)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in Q,\quad \delta(x)\ge \bar f(x)-\bar f(x_*)\ge 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Linear-Model Upper Bound for Composite Conditional Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded estimate inequality; the method, regularity constant, and diameter constant retain their source-context definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated composite conditional-gradient iteration, the weighted objective value at every iterate is bounded by the corresponding weighted sum of affine models evaluated at any feasible comparison point, plus the accumulated regularity error.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty}
f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is differentiable on }Q
\Psi:Q\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is proper}
a_t>0,\quad A_t=\sum_{k=0}^t a_k
x_t\in Q\text{ is generated by method (6.4.12)}
\nu\in(0,1],\quad G_\nu<+\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Bound for Relative Accuracy under an Inverse-Quadratic Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bound applies to positive optimal value and to iterates satisfying the specified estimate for every positive iteration index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta>0\), \(r>1\), and \(p\in\mathbb N\) satisfy \(\frac{1+\delta}{\delta}\ln r\le p\le2\frac{1+\delta}{\delta}\ln r\). Let \(\varnothing\ne Q\), let \(f_p^*=\min_{y\in Q}f_p(y)>0\), let \(G\succ0\), and set \(d(x)=\tfrac12\|x-x_0\|_G^2\) with \(x_0\in\arg\min_{y\in Q}\|y\|_G\). If iterates \(x_k\in Q\) satisfy \(f_p(x_k)-f_p^*\le\frac{16(1+\delta)r\ln r}{\delta k(k+1)}f_p^*\) for every integer \(k\ge1\), then \(f_p(x_k)\le(1+\delta)f_p^*\) for every integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(k\ge\frac4\delta\sqrt{(1+\delta)r\ln r}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated inverse-quadratic relative suboptimality estimate, every positive iteration index at least four over delta times the square root of (1+delta) r log r achieves (1+delta)-relative objective accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \delta>0,\quad r>1
p\in\mathbb N,\quad \frac{1+\delta}{\delta}\ln r\le p\le2\frac{1+\delta}{\delta}\ln r
\varnothing\ne Q,\quad f_p^*=\min_{y\in Q}f_p(y)>0
G\succ0,\quad x_0\in\arg\min_{y\in Q}\|y\|_G,\quad d(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_G^2
x_k\in Q,\quad f_p(x_k)-f_p^*\le\frac{16(1+\delta)r\ln r}{\delta k(k+1)}f_p^*\quad\forall k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_p(x_k)\le(1+\delta)f_p^*\quad\text{for every integer }k\ge1\text{ with }k\ge\frac4\delta\sqrt{(1+\delta)r\ln r}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregated subgradient lower bound and feasibility of the aggregated dual point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The global lower-model conclusion uses convexity and selected subgradients. The additional dual-feasibility conclusion requires maximizing oracle outputs in a convex dual set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a real vector space with an inner product, let \(f:P\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and choose \(g(y_k)\in\partial f(y_k)\) for \(k=0,\ldots,N\). If \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k=1\), and \(\ell_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k\bigl[f(y_k)+\langle g(y_k),x-y_k\rangle\bigr]\), then \(\ell_N(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in P\). Moreover, if \(f(x)=\max_{u\in S}\Psi(x,u)\), each \(u(y_k)\in\operatorname{Argmax}_{u\in S}\Psi(y_k,u)\), and \(S\) is convex, then \(\widehat u_N=\sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k u(y_k)\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex combination of supporting affine models of a convex function is still a global lower model. If maximizing dual oracle outputs belong to a convex dual set, their convex combination remains in that set.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a real vector space with an inner product}
f:P\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is convex}
y_k\in P,\quad \partial f(y_k)\ne\varnothing,\quad g(y_k)\in\partial f(y_k),\quad k=0,\ldots,N
\alpha_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=0}^N\alpha_k=1
\text{For the additional conclusion: }f(x)=\max_{u\in S}\Psi(x,u),\quad u(y_k)\in\operatorname{Argmax}_{u\in S}\Psi(y_k,u),\quad S\text{ is convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_N(x)\le f(x)\quad\forall x\in P;\qquad \text{under the additional assumptions, }\widehat u_N\in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed epsilon-delta approximate solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value approximation criterion for a problem with an attained optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\ne\varnothing\), let \(\hat f:Q\to\mathbb R\), and suppose \(x^*\in Q\) attains \(\min_{x\in Q}\hat f(x)\). Given \(\epsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), a point \(\bar x\in Q\) is a mixed \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-approximate solution if \[(1-\delta)\hat f(\bar x)\le\hat f(x^*)+\epsilon.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Oracle-Based Iterative Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A method-independent adaptive query, information-update, decision, and termination protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\), \(\epsilon>0\), and \(\mathcal I_{-1}=\varnothing\), for \(k=0,1,\ldots\): query \(\mathcal O\) at \(x_k\); set \(\mathcal I_k=\mathcal I_{k-1}\cup\{(x_k,\mathcal O(x_k))\}\); use the method rule \(\mathcal M\) applied to \(\mathcal I_k\) to generate \(x_{k+1}\); and, if \(\mathcal T_\epsilon\) holds, form and return an output \(\bar x\), otherwise continue with \(k+1\).

\epsilon>0

\mathcal M\text{ maps accumulated information to a next query point}
\mathcal T_\epsilon\text{ is the stopping criterion}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output definitions for a finite prefix of an arbitrary optimization sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset\mathbb R^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint-model tractability need not follow from primal tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A modeling caveat about the computational operations implicitly required by a structured primal-dual representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closed-form solvability of the auxiliary optimization problem defined by the primal representation data $(\hat\phi,Q_2)$ does not by itself imply comparable tractability for the objects defining the corresponding adjoint representation; the latter auxiliary problem may fail to admit the same simple solution mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured representation may assume that its primal-side auxiliary problem is easy or closed form, but this assumption need not remain valid for the corresponding adjoint-side objects, so the two formulations can have different computational complexity.
assumptions_latex: \text{The primal representation treats }\hat\phi\text{ and }Q_2\text{ as simple enough for closed-form auxiliary optimization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Comparable closed-form solvability or computational complexity for the adjoint auxiliary problem does not necessarily follow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of an attained prox-regularized maximizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness is conditional on attainment; the proposition does not assert existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q_2$ be a nonempty convex set, let $d_2:Q_2\to\mathbb R$ be $1$-strongly convex, let $\mu>0$, let $\hat\phi:Q_2\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be convex, and let $A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2^*$ be linear. For fixed $x\in Q_1$, if the problem $\max_{u\in Q_2}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\}$ has an optimal solution, then that solution is unique; hence the attained maximizer $u_\mu(x)$ is uniquely defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positive multiple of a 1-strongly convex prox function makes the max objective strictly concave in the maximization variable. Consequently, any attained maximizer is unique, although existence is not guaranteed by this statement.
assumptions_latex: Q_2\ne\varnothing\text{ is convex}
d_2:Q_2\to\mathbb R\text{ is }1\text{-strongly convex}
\mu>0
\hat\phi:Q_2\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is convex}
A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2^*\text{ is linear}
x\in Q_1\text{ is fixed}
\arg\max_{u\in Q_2}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\}\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\arg\max_{u\in Q_2}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\}\right|=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic lower bound at a normalized prox-center
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A basic geometric consequence of differentiable strong convexity and minimization at the prox-center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q_2\subseteq\mathbb E_2$ be convex, and let $d_2:Q_2\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable and $1$-strongly convex with respect to $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_2}$, so that $d_2(v)\ge d_2(u)+\langle\nabla d_2(u),v-u\rangle+\tfrac12\|v-u\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2$ for all $u,v\in Q_2$. If $u_0\in\arg\min_{u\in Q_2}d_2(u)$ and $d_2(u_0)=0$, then $d_2(u)\ge\tfrac12\|u-u_0\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2$ for every $u\in Q_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable 1-strongly convex prox function normalized to zero at a minimizing prox-center dominates one half of the squared distance to that center throughout its convex domain.
assumptions_latex: Q_2\subseteq\mathbb E_2\text{ is convex}
d_2:Q_2\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable and }1\text{-strongly convex with respect to }\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_2}
u_0\in\arg\min_{u\in Q_2}d_2(u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u\in Q_2,\qquad d_2(u)\ge\frac12\|u-u_0\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform error of prox smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The uniform bound follows from the stated pointwise sandwich and is meaningful when the displayed maximum $D_2$ is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D_2:=\max_{u\in Q_2}d_2(u)$ and $f_0(x):=\max_{u\in Q_2}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\hat\phi(u)\}$. If, for every $x\in\mathbb E_1$, $f_0(x)\ge f_\mu(x)\ge f_0(x)-\mu D_2$, then $f_\mu$ uniformly approximates $f_0$ with $\sup_{x\in\mathbb E_1}|f_\mu(x)-f_0(x)|\le\mu D_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the smoothed max function lies pointwise between the original max function and that function minus the smoothing parameter times the maximum prox value, then its uniform approximation error is at most that same quantity.
assumptions_latex: D_2=\max_{u\in Q_2}d_2(u)\in\mathbb R
f_0(x)=\max_{u\in Q_2}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\hat\phi(u)\}
\forall x\in\mathbb E_1,\quad f_0(x)\ge f_\mu(x)\ge f_0(x)-\mu D_2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in\mathbb E_1}|f_\mu(x)-f_0(x)|\le\mu D_2.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Class Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a family of optimization instances independently of their oracle encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be an index set and let \(\mathfrak I\) be an ambient instance space. A problem-class family is a collection \(\{\mathcal P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}\) with \(\mathcal P_\theta\subseteq\mathfrak I\). Each instance \(I\in\mathcal P_\theta\) specifies an optimization task, including its feasible objects, objective or acceptance relation, and accuracy convention. The index \(\theta\) records uniform restrictions—such as dimension, convexity, smoothness, or Lipschitz parameters—under which oracle complexity is compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem-class family groups optimization instances by uniform structural and numerical restrictions while keeping the ambient instance space explicit.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\neq\varnothing\).
Every \(I\in\mathfrak I\) determines a well-defined optimization task.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_\theta\subseteq\mathfrak I\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).

notation.meaning: problem class indexed by parameter θ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports this oracle-model formulation.

children.title: Instance-Space Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations used to identify individual optimization instances within a modeled family.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Space Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes how abstract instances are encoded for access by an oracle algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak I\) be an abstract instance space and \(E\) an encoding space. An instance-space representation is a map \(\rho:\mathfrak I\to E\), together with an access rule specifying which features of \(\rho(I)\) an algorithm may query. Two instances are representation-equivalent when \(I\sim_\rho J\) if and only if \(\rho(I)=\rho(J)\). Any acceptance rule posed on encoded instances must be constant on each equivalence class of \(\sim_\rho\), unless the representation is refined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation maps abstract instances into encodings and identifies instances that an oracle algorithm cannot distinguish through that encoding.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak I\) and \(E\) are nonempty sets.
The algorithm accesses \(I\) only through the prescribed interface for \(\rho(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\sim_\rho J\iff \rho(I)=\rho(J)\), and representation-compatible acceptance is constant on \(\sim_\rho\)-classes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf and the same-encoding implication is plausible, but no source supports the formalization or the asserted compatibility requirement for acceptance rules.

children.title: Class–Instance Membership Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries determining which represented instances belong to the declared problem family.

knowledge_statements.title: Class–Instance Membership Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the predicate separating admissible class members from excluded instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak I\) be an instance space and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m:\mathfrak I\to\{0,1\}\) be declared structural predicates. The membership boundary of the class \(\mathcal P\) is fixed by \[I\in\mathcal P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C_j(I)=1\text{ for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.\] An instance for which at least one predicate vanishes lies outside \(\mathcal P\); boundary conventions for non-strict inequalities must be included in the corresponding predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Class membership is determined exactly by declared structural predicates, including explicit conventions for equality and other boundary cases.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\) is positive.
Each predicate \(C_j\) is defined on all of \(\mathfrak I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\{I\in\mathfrak I:C_j(I)=1\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predicate-based condition fits the membership-boundary leaf and is internally consistent, but it has no supporting citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle and Local Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an optimization oracle and the invariance property that makes it local.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a class \(\mathcal P\) of optimization problems, an oracle \(\mathcal O\) is a mechanism that, given a query point \(x\) for an instance \(P\in\mathcal P\), returns an answer \(\mathcal O_P(x)\) associated with \(P\) and \(x\). The oracle is local if every modification producing \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal P\) and supported sufficiently far from \(x\) leaves the answer at \(x\) unchanged: \(\mathcal O_{\widetilde P}(x)=\mathcal O_P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle returns problem information associated with a queried point. It is local when sufficiently distant changes to the problem data leave its answer at that point unchanged, provided the modified problem remains in the specified class.
assumptions_latex: P,\widetilde P\in\mathcal P
x\text{ is a query point}
\widetilde P\text{ is obtained from }P\text{ by modifications supported sufficiently far from }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal O_{\widetilde P}(x)=\mathcal O_P(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-, First-, and Second-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies objective-function oracles by the derivative information included in their responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a query point \(x\), a zero-order oracle returns \(f(x)\); a first-order oracle returns \((f(x),
abla f(x))\); and a second-order oracle returns \((f(x),
abla f(x),
abla^2 f(x))\), with the indicated derivatives defined at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-order oracle returns the objective value, a first-order oracle returns the value and gradient, and a second-order oracle returns the value, gradient, and Hessian at the query point.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a query point for }f
\nabla f(x)\text{ is defined for first- and second-order responses}
\nabla^2 f(x)\text{ is defined for a second-order response}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\mathcal O_0(x)=f(x),\quad \mathcal O_1(x)=(f(x),
abla f(x)),\quad \mathcal O_2(x)=(f(x),

children.title: Admissible Query Spaces
children.top_down_role: Objects that a procedure may submit to the oracle under the access model.

knowledge_statements.title: Admissible Query Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines history-dependent queries permitted by an oracle interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For round \(t\geq1\), let \(H_{t-1}\) be the set of valid transcripts through round \(t-1\). An admissible query space is a correspondence \(Q_t:H_{t-1}\rightrightarrows\mathcal Q\) with nonempty values. After observing history \(h_{t-1}\in H_{t-1}\), an algorithm may issue only \(q_t\in Q_t(h_{t-1})\). Restrictions on points, directions, batches, precision, measurability, or dependence on past responses are part of \(Q_t\), not implicit algorithmic freedoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each round, the admissible-query correspondence lists exactly which queries may be chosen from the current transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(H_{t-1}\neq\varnothing\).
\(Q_t(h)\neq\varnothing\) for every valid history \(h\in H_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_t\) is interface-admissible after \(h_{t-1}\) exactly when \(q_t\in Q_t(h_{t-1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The history-dependent correspondence is a suitable definition of admissible query spaces, but no oracle-interface source is cited.

children.title: Oracle Response Spaces
children.top_down_role: Possible information objects returned by the oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Response Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the typed set of responses available for each instance, history, and query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak I\) be an instance space, \(H_{t-1}\) a history space, and \(Q_t\) an admissible-query correspondence. An oracle response space is a correspondence \(R_t\) assigning a nonempty set \(R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\subseteq\mathcal R\) to every admissible triple \((I,h_{t-1},q_t)\) with \(q_t\in Q_t(h_{t-1})\). Deterministic oracles select one response from this set; stochastic oracles use a probability kernel supported on it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The response-space correspondence specifies all answers an oracle may legally return to each admissible query and history.
assumptions_latex: \(R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\neq\varnothing\) for every admissible triple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_t\) is a valid response exactly when \(r_t\in R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\).

notation.meaning: oracle response correspondence at round t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The response correspondence and deterministic/stochastic distinction fit the leaf, but the record lacks an inspectable supporting source.

children.title: Query–Response Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Restrictions linking each admissible query type to its permitted response types.

knowledge_statements.title: Query–Response Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when a response law is compatible with an admissible query and instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\), valid history \(h_{t-1}\), and admissible query \(q_t\in Q_t(h_{t-1})\), a deterministic response rule \(O_t\) is compatible when \[O_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\in R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t).\] A stochastic response kernel \(K_t(\cdot\mid I,h_{t-1},q_t)\) is compatible when \[K_t\bigl(R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\mid I,h_{t-1},q_t\bigr)=1.\] Compatibility is required at every round and every history reachable under the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic answer must belong to the allowed response set; a stochastic answer law must assign that set probability one.
assumptions_latex: \(R_t(I,h_{t-1},q_t)\) is measurable when a stochastic kernel is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The response rule is compatible precisely when every reachable response is supported on the prescribed response correspondence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic membership and stochastic support-one conditions correctly express query–response compatibility, subject to the stated measurability condition, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Information Transcripts
children.top_down_role: Histories of queries, responses, randomness, and revealed auxiliary information.

knowledge_statements.title: Information Transcripts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents all information revealed during an adaptive oracle interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T\in\mathbb N_0\), define the zero-round transcript by \(H_0=(\xi_0)\). For \(T\geq 1\), an information transcript is \[H_T=(\xi_0,q_1,r_1,a_1,\xi_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T,a_T,\xi_T),\] where \(q_t\) is the round-\(t\) query, \(r_t\) is its oracle response, \(a_t\) is auxiliary information revealed at that round, and \(\xi_t\) records algorithmic or oracle randomness made observable by the end of round \(t\). Validity requires each query to be admissible from the preceding transcript and each response to be compatible with that query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transcript records, in order, the queries, answers, revealed auxiliary data, and observable randomness generated by an oracle interaction; before any query, it consists only of the initially observable random data.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N_0\).
For every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), the query \(q_t\) and response \(r_t\) satisfy the prescribed query–response interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The valid transcript \(H_T\) records the interaction information available for constructing the next query or the terminal output.

notation.meaning: auxiliary information revealed at round t
random data observable by the end of round t

children.title: Solution Acceptance Interface
children.top_down_role: Required solution objects, certificates, error criteria, and probabilistic success modes.

children.title: Required Output Objects
children.top_down_role: Solution objects that a procedure must return.

knowledge_statements.title: Required Output Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the codomain and type constraints of acceptable algorithmic outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance \(I\in\mathfrak I\), let \(Y(I)\) be the nonempty set of correctly typed candidate outputs, such as feasible points, objective values, dual variables, or structured tuples. A required output specification is the correspondence \(Y:\mathfrak I\rightrightarrows\mathcal Y\). After a finite transcript \(H_T\), an algorithm must return \(y_T=A_T(H_T)\in Y(I)\); membership in \(Y(I)\) enforces output type but does not by itself assert accuracy or success.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The output specification determines what kind of object an algorithm must return, separately from whether that object solves the instance accurately.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(I)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(I\in\mathfrak I\).
The terminal map \(A_T\) is defined on every valid terminal transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A well-typed terminal output satisfies \(A_T(H_T)\in Y(I)\).

notation.meaning: required output-object set for instance I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The output-typing definition fits the required-output leaf and properly separates type correctness from success, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Certificate Requirements
children.top_down_role: Evidence accompanying an output to support its claimed quality or status.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a verifier-based certificate attached to a candidate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(I)\) be the candidate-output set for instance \(I\), let \(\mathcal C(I)\) be a certificate space, and let \(V_I:Y(I)\times\mathcal C(I)\to\{0,1\}\) be a verifier. A pair \((y,c)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-certificate when \(V_I(y,c)=1\), verification uses only the information permitted by the acceptance interface, and verifier soundness guarantees \[V_I(y,c)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\in S_\varepsilon(I),\] where \(S_\varepsilon(I)\) is the declared set of \(\varepsilon\)-acceptable outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate is auxiliary data accepted by a permitted verifier whose soundness guarantees that the accompanying output meets the declared accuracy requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(S_\varepsilon(I)\subseteq Y(I)\).
The verifier \(V_I\) is sound for the declared acceptance criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_I(y,c)=1\Longrightarrow y\in S_\varepsilon(I)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The verifier-soundness formulation and certificate content kind fit the exact leaf, but the definition lacks cited support for this acceptance-interface model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Estimate certificate and rate for the fast composite-gradient method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the sequences generated by method (6.1.19) for problem (6.1.18), using the notation of that method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{x_k\}_{k\ge0}\), \(\{y_k\}_{k\ge0}\), and \(\{v_k\}_{k\ge0}\) be generated by method (6.1.19). For every \(k\ge0\) and \(x\in Q\),
\[
\frac{k(k+1)}4\widetilde f(x_k)+\frac L2\lVert v_k-x\rVert^2\le \phi_k(x),
\]
where
\[
\phi_k(x)=Ld(x)+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{i+1}{2}\bigl(f(y_i)+\langle\nabla f(y_i),x-y_i\rangle\bigr)+\frac{k(k+1)}4\Psi(x).
\]
Consequently, if \(x^*\) is an optimal solution of (6.1.18), then for every \(k\ge1\),
\[
\widetilde f(x_k)-\widetilde f(x^*)+\frac{2L}{k(k+1)}\lVert v_k-x^*\rVert^2\le\frac{4Ld(x^*)}{k(k+1)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fast composite method's estimate function bounds a weighted objective value and the distance from v_k to every comparison point. At an optimal solution this yields an objective-and-distance error bound proportional to 1/[k(k+1)].
assumptions_latex: \(\{x_k\},\{y_k\},\{v_k\}\) are generated by method (6.1.19).
\(k\ge0\) and \(x\in Q\) for the estimate inequality.
\(x^*\) is an optimal solution of problem (6.1.18), and \(k\ge1\), for the convergence bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{k(k+1)}4\widetilde f(x_k)+\frac L2\lVert v_k-x\rVert^2\le\phi_k(x)\), and \(\widetilde f(x_k)-\widetilde f(x^*)+\frac{2L}{k(k+1)}\lVert v_k-x^*\rVert^2\le\frac{4Ld(x^*)}{k(k+1)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual gap and iteration bound for accelerated smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the objects and notation of problems (6.1.10), (6.1.12), (6.1.26), and method (6.1.19).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Apply method (6.1.19) to problem (6.1.26) for \(N\ge1\) iterations with
\[
\mu=\frac{2\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}\sqrt{\frac{D_1}{D_2}}.
\]
Define
\[
\widehat x=x_N\in Q_1,
\qquad
\widehat u=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{2(i+1)}{(N+1)(N+2)}u_\mu(y_i)\in Q_2.
\]
Then
\[
0\le f(\widehat x)-\phi(\widehat u)
\le\frac{4\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}\sqrt{D_1D_2}}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}+
\frac{4MD_1}{N(N+1)}.
\]
Consequently, for \(\epsilon>0\), an iteration count sufficient to obtain an \(\epsilon\)-solution of the primal and dual problems is at most
\[
\frac{4\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}\sqrt{D_1D_2}}{\epsilon}
+2\sqrt{\frac{MD_1}{\epsilon}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the prescribed smoothing parameter and weighted primal and dual outputs, accelerated smoothing produces a nonnegative primal–dual gap bounded by a term of order 1/N plus a term of order 1/N². The displayed expression gives a sufficient iteration bound for an ε-solution.
assumptions_latex: \(N\ge1\), and method (6.1.19) is applied to problem (6.1.26).
\(\mu=2\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}\sqrt{D_1/D_2}/\sqrt{N(N+1)}\).
\(\widehat x=x_N\) and \(\widehat u=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{2(i+1)}{(N+1)(N+2)}u_\mu(y_i)\).
\(\epsilon>0\) for the iteration-complexity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f(\widehat x)-\phi(\widehat u)\le\frac{4\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}\sqrt{D_1D_2}}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}+\frac{4MD_1}{N(N+1)}\), with sufficient iteration count \(\frac{4\lVert A\rVert_{1,2}\sqrt{D_1D_2}}{\epsilon}+2\sqrt{MD_1/\epsilon}\).

children.title: Deterministic Success Criteria
children.top_down_role: Nonprobabilistic standards used to judge an output.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Success Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses worst-case acceptance over instances and all oracle behavior allowed by the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal P\), an accuracy level \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and acceptable-output sets \(S_\varepsilon(I)\). A deterministic algorithm \(A\) succeeds within \(T\) queries if, for every \(I\in\mathcal P\) and every response sequence compatible with the oracle interface, its terminal transcript \(H_T\) satisfies \[A_T(H_T)\in S_\varepsilon(I).\] If the oracle response is uniquely determined by \(I\) and each query, the universal quantifier over compatible response sequences reduces to that unique interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic success requires every allowed instance and every compatible oracle interaction to produce an acceptable output within the query budget.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
\(S_\varepsilon(I)\subseteq Y(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(I\in\mathcal P\), every compatible terminal transcript \(H_T\) satisfies \(A_T(H_T)\in S_\varepsilon(I)\).

notation.meaning: algorithm output after the terminal transcript

children.title: Probabilistic Success Criteria
children.top_down_role: Confidence-based or risk-based standards used to judge an output.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Success Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines high-probability acceptance uniformly over the specified problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\), \(\delta\in[0,1)\), and a query budget \(T\). A randomized algorithm with a possibly stochastic oracle is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-successful on \(\mathcal P\) if, for every \(I\in\mathcal P\), \[\Pr_I\!\left(A_T(H_T)\in S_\varepsilon(I)\right)\geq1-\delta.\] The probability is taken jointly over all algorithmic and oracle randomness prescribed by the model. If adversarial oracle choices remain outside that probability law, the inequality must hold for every compatible adversarial choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probabilistic success means each allowed instance yields an acceptable output with probability at least one minus the declared failure level.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon\geq0\), \(\delta\in[0,1)\), and \(T\in\mathbb N_0\).
The joint law of algorithmic and oracle randomness is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{I\in\mathcal P}\Pr_I\!\left(A_T(H_T)\in S_\varepsilon(I)\right)\geq1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: joint interaction law for instance I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The high-probability condition is mathematically coherent, explicitly handles joint randomness and residual adversarial choices, and fits the leaf, but it lacks a supporting source and locator.

children.title: Information Locality Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: The extent of the problem representation exposed by one interaction.

children.title: Pointwise Local Information
children.top_down_role: Information attached to a queried point, direction, or local neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Local Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines oracle information invariant under changes away from the queried point or neighborhood germ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let instances \(I,J\) define local mathematical data on a common domain \(X\). For \(x\in X\), write \(I\equiv_x J\) when the data specified by the oracle model agree at \(x\), or on some neighborhood of \(x\) when germ information is allowed. An oracle supplies pointwise local information at query \(x\) if \[I\equiv_x J\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal L(I,x)=\mathcal L(J,x).\] Thus modifying an instance outside the prescribed local equivalence class cannot change the response at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise local information depends only on the instance data attached to the queried point or its permitted neighborhood germ.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are defined on a common query domain \(X\).
The local-equivalence relation \(\equiv_x\) is fixed by the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\equiv_x J\Longrightarrow\mathcal L(I,x)=\mathcal L(J,x)\).

notation.meaning: instances agree in the prescribed local sense at x
local oracle information returned at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariance formulation fits the pointwise-local-information topic and keeps the permitted point-versus-germ convention model-dependent, but no source supports this locality definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Black-Box Information Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the oracle-only access restriction and the locality invariance assumption of the local black-box concept.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method operates under the local black-box concept when (i) the only problem information available to it is supplied by oracle answers and (ii) the oracle is local: if \(P\) is replaced by \(\widetilde P\) in the same problem class through modifications supported sufficiently far from a query point \(x\), then \(\mathcal O_{\widetilde P}(x)=\mathcal O_P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the local black-box model, a method may use only oracle answers, and an answer at a query point cannot change when problem data sufficiently far from that point are modified without leaving the problem class.
assumptions_latex: P,\widetilde P\text{ belong to the same specified problem class}
x\text{ is a query point}
\widetilde P\text{ differs from }P\text{ only through modifications supported sufficiently far from }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{available problem information consists only of oracle answers},\qquad \mathcal O_{\widetilde P}(x)=\mathcal O_P(x)

children.title: Regional-Setwise Information Granularity
children.top_down_role: Information about a region, level set, feasible body, or family of constraints.

children.title: Regional Information
children.top_down_role: Information attached to neighborhoods, level regions, or other localized portions of the domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines access to a point-indexed information field throughout a queried region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a query domain, let \(R\subseteq X\), and let \(f\) belong to a function class \(\mathcal F\). A regional-information oracle accepts \(R\) and returns an indexed family \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}(f,R)=(I_f(x))_{x\in R}\), where each \(I_f(x)\) is prescribed local information, such as a value or subgradient. The response is regional if it depends only on the restriction \(f|_R\): whenever \(f,h\in\mathcal F\) satisfy \(f|_R=h|_R\), one has \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}(f,R)=\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}(h,R)\). Thus a single query exposes consistently indexed information at every point of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regional access returns a point-indexed information field over a queried region and cannot distinguish functions that agree throughout that region.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is an admissible subset of the query domain \(X\).
The local-information map \(I_f(x)\) is defined for every \(f\in\mathcal F\) and \(x\in R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f|_R=h|_R\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}(f,R)=\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}(h,R).\]

notation.meaning: local information about the objective at a point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes regional access as simultaneous point-indexed local information depending only on the objective restricted to the region

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits the Regional Information leaf, but no inspectable source supports the proposed terminology, the simultaneous field response at every point of a region, or its distinction from setwise access. The standard-field rationale is insufficient to establish this taxonomy-specific model.

children.title: Setwise Information
children.top_down_role: Information attached to feasible bodies, constraint families, or other represented sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Setwise Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines access to a joint functional of an entire queried set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a query domain, let \(S\subseteq X\), and let \(f\in\mathcal F\). A setwise-information oracle returns a joint object \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}(f,S)=J(f|_S,S)\), where \(J\) may be an aggregate value, an optimizer set, a separating object, or another functional defined from all of \(S\). Setwise locality requires that \(f|_S=h|_S\) imply \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}(f,S)=\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}(h,S)\). Unlike a regional point-indexed field, the response need not determine separate information \(I_f(x)\) for each \(x\in S\); it may encode only a collective property of the restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Setwise access returns a joint functional of the objective on a queried set, possibly without revealing separate information at individual points.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) belongs to the oracle's admissible family of query sets.
The functional \(J\) is well-defined on restrictions \(f|_S\) for \(f\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f|_S=h|_S\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}(f,S)=\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}(h,S).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes setwise access through a functional of the objective restricted to the complete query set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the intended setwise container and is mathematically intelligible, but the broad class of joint objects and the claimed contrast with regional point-indexed information have no cited, inspectable support. A taxonomy or oracle-model source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Regional–Setwise Granularity
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between localized regional exposure and information about a represented set as a whole.

knowledge_statements.title: Regional–Setwise Granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares regional fields and joint set functionals through oracle simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For oracle models \(\mathcal O_1\) and \(\mathcal O_2\), write \(\mathcal O_1\preceq\mathcal O_2\) when a fixed deterministic decoder \(D\) satisfies \(\mathcal O_1(f,Q)=D(Q,\mathcal O_2(f,Q))\) for every admissible \(f\) and query set \(Q\). Regional and setwise access are not universally ordered by \(\preceq\). A regional response may reveal the complete field \((I_f(x))_{x\in Q}\) while omitting a noncomputable joint functional \(J(f|_Q,Q)\); conversely, a setwise response may reveal \(J(f|_Q,Q)\) without identifying any individual \(I_f(x)\). Comparability requires an explicit reconstruction rule connecting the field and the joint functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regional and setwise information are generally incomparable; one simulates the other only when a uniform reconstruction rule connects their responses.
assumptions_latex: Both oracle models use the same objective class and admissible query sets.
Simulation permits only a fixed decoder and no additional oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}\preceq\mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}\ \text{or}\ \mathcal O_{\mathrm{set}}\preceq\mathcal O_{\mathrm{reg}}\quad\text{only when the corresponding uniform decoder exists}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: information granularity is compared by uniform simulation between oracle responses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simulation-preorder comparison is suitable as a property of regional–setwise granularity, but the universal incomparability claim is unsupported. In particular, “noncomputable” depends on an unstated computational model, and no source or explicit counterexample establishes failure of either simulation direction.

children.title: Global Statistical Information
children.top_down_role: Access to reusable samples, datasets, or population-level subproblems exceeding local stochastic responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Statistical Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reusable dataset or population-functional access beyond fresh local samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a probability law on a sample space \(\mathcal Z\), and let \(\ell(x;z)\) be a loss. A global-statistical-information oracle exposes either a reusable sample \(D=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)\) with \(Z_i\sim P\), or a population-level functional \(T(P)\), and permits subsequent adaptive queries to use that same object. For example, the response may evaluate \(F_D(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(x;Z_i)\) or solve a subproblem formed from all of \(D\). This access is stronger than a local stochastic oracle that returns only a newly sampled response at the current query and does not reveal or preserve the underlying sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global statistical access exposes reusable data or population functionals, allowing multiple adaptive operations on information shared across queries.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) are sampled according to the specified statistical model.
The revealed dataset or population functional remains available across adaptive queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D\ \text{or}\ T(P)\ \text{is shared across queries, rather than resampled independently at each query}.\]

notation.meaning: empirical objective induced by the dataset

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reusable samples and population functionals constitute global statistical access in stochastic optimization

children.title: Global Structured-Subproblem Information
children.top_down_role: Responses obtained through optimization or inversion over a globally represented structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Structured-Subproblem Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines oracle responses obtained by globally optimizing or inverting represented structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a feasible domain and let \(G\) denote globally represented structure, such as a constraint set, regularizer, or monotone operator. A global structured-subproblem oracle accepts a parameter \(q\) and returns an element of a solution mapping \(S_G(q)\) defined by optimization or inversion over the full structure. Canonical forms include \(S_G(q)=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{x\in X}\{\langle q,x\rangle+G(x)\}\) and \(S_G(q)=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}(q)\). The response therefore uses global information about \(G\) or \(A\), rather than only values or first-order data at the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This oracle solves or inverts a parameterized subproblem using the full represented constraint, regularizer, or operator structure.
assumptions_latex: The solution mapping \(S_G(q)\) is nonempty for every admissible query \(q\).
Any scale parameter satisfies \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal O_G(q)\in S_G(q),\quad S_G(q)\ \text{being defined through the full represented structure}.\]

notation.meaning: represented operator in an inversion query

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear minimization, proximal, and resolvent calls are standard globally structured oracle responses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this leaf, and optimization or inversion over globally represented structure matches its role. Nevertheless, the combined linear-minimization and resolvent formulation lacks a cited taxonomy source, and the spaces, identity map, operator domain/codomain, and conditions making the resolvent expression meaningful are not fully specified.

children.title: Oracle Fidelity Axes
children.top_down_role: Independent exactness, approximation, and randomness qualifications applicable across oracle types.

children.title: Response Fidelity Pair
children.top_down_role: Access distinguished by whether response fidelity is exact or tolerance-dependent.

children.title: Exact Responses
children.top_down_role: Oracle responses delivered without a modeled approximation allowance.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convex first-order value-and-subgradient oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). An exact first-order response at \(x\) is a pair \((v,g)\) satisfying \(v=f(x)\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\), equivalently \(f(y)\ge v+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in X\). Exactness means that no deterministic error tolerance, stochastic perturbation, or residual relaxation is admitted in these relations. When \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the subgradient component is uniquely fixed as \(g=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact convex first-order response gives the true function value and a genuine subgradient at the queried point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on a real vector space with a compatible dual pairing.
\(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v=f(x),\qquad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for all }y\in X.\]

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the objective at the query

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact value-subgradient responses are standard in convex first-order oracle models
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex value-and-subgradient definition is standard, precise, and appropriate for Exact Responses, but the record supplies no source reference. An authoritative convex-analysis or oracle-model citation with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is required.

children.title: Approximate Responses
children.top_down_role: Oracle responses qualified by a tolerance or permitted error level.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses value error and the convex approximate-subgradient model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and choose tolerances \(\delta,\varepsilon\ge0\). A \((\delta,\varepsilon)\)-approximate first-order response is a pair \((v,g)\) such that \(|v-f(x)|\le\delta\) and \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\), where \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) means \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\) for every \(y\in X\). The tolerances are part of the fidelity specification and must be distinguished from randomness in the returned pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate response permits bounded value error and an epsilon-subgradient inequality valid over the entire domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex, and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
The fidelity tolerances satisfy \(\delta,\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|v-f(x)|\le\delta,\qquad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\quad\text{for all }y\in X.\]

children.title: Exactness–Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Modeling distinctions that determine when response error changes the access class.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness–Approximation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies exact first-order responses as the zero-tolerance endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\) and a query \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), every exact first-order response is \((\delta,\varepsilon)\)-approximate for all tolerances \(\delta,\varepsilon\ge0\). Conversely, a response satisfying the approximate conditions with \(\delta=0\) and \(\varepsilon=0\) is exact, because \(\partial_0 f(x)=\partial f(x)\) and the value-error inequality forces \(v=f(x)\). Hence the exact oracle is the zero-tolerance member of this approximation family; positive tolerances alone do not certify that the returned response differs from an exact one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact first-order responses are precisely zero-tolerance approximate responses, while a positive tolerance permits but does not require error.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex, with \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
Approximation is measured by value error \(\delta\) and approximate-subgradient error \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(v,g)\ \text{is exact}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |v-f(x)|\le0\ \text{and}\ g\in\partial_0 f(x).\]

The cited section supports approximate subdifferentials but does not clearly support the added value-error model or the resulting two-parameter exactness boundary, so the complete claim still needs a source.

children.title: Response Randomness Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Access distinguished by repeatability and the source of response randomness.

children.title: Deterministic Responses
children.top_down_role: Repeatable oracle behavior for a fixed instance and query.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines determinism conditionally on the complete observable query history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_{t-1}\) denote the query-response history before query \(q_t\), and let \(Y_t\) be the oracle response. The oracle has deterministic responses if there exists a fixed mapping \(\Phi\) such that \(Y_t=\Phi(q_t,H_{t-1})\) almost surely for every admissible history and query. Equivalently, the conditional response law is the Dirac measure \(\mathcal L(Y_t\mid q_t,H_{t-1})=\delta_{\Phi(q_t,H_{t-1})}\). Dependence on prior responses, stored state, or deterministic approximation error does not itself make the response random, provided identical histories and queries always produce identical outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A response is deterministic when the current query and complete history uniquely determine it, even if the oracle is stateful or inexact.
assumptions_latex: The history \(H_{t-1}\) includes every oracle state component exposed to the access model.
Conditional response laws are defined for admissible histories and queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal L(Y_t\mid q_t,H_{t-1})=\delta_{\Phi(q_t,H_{t-1})}.\]

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the point y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a deterministic oracle is characterized by a point-mass conditional response kernel
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Dirac-kernel characterization is a reasonable definition of deterministic responses and fits the leaf. No cited source supports the history-dependent formulation, however, and the phrase “every oracle state component exposed to the access model” does not ensure that hidden deterministic state is included, which affects whether identical displayed histories determine identical outputs.

children.title: Random Responses
children.top_down_role: Response behavior carrying modeled randomness for a fixed instance and query.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines random oracle responses through a non-Dirac conditional kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_{t-1}\) be the history, \(q_t\) the current query, and \(Y_t\) the response. A random-response oracle is specified by a probability kernel \(K(\cdot\mid q_t,H_{t-1})\) and samples \(Y_t\sim K(\cdot\mid q_t,H_{t-1})\). The response is genuinely random at \((q_t,H_{t-1})\) when this kernel is not a Dirac measure. Properties such as unbiasedness, \(\mathbb E[Y_t\mid q_t,H_{t-1}]=T(q_t,H_{t-1})\), or bounded conditional variance are additional fidelity conditions and are not implied by randomness alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random response is drawn from a non-point-mass conditional distribution; unbiasedness and variance bounds require separate assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a probability kernel on the response space.
The conditioning history contains the information available before the new random draw.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Y_t\sim K(\cdot\mid q_t,H_{t-1}),\qquad K(\cdot\mid q_t,H_{t-1})\ne\delta_y\ \text{for every response }y.\]

notation.meaning: optional target response used in an unbiasedness condition

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stochastic oracles are naturally formalized as conditional probability kernels
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probability-kernel definition correctly separates randomness from unbiasedness and variance assumptions and fits the Random Responses leaf. It nevertheless lacks an inspectable source for the conditional-history oracle formulation and for the non-Dirac criterion used as the defining boundary.

children.title: Response Randomness Sources
children.top_down_role: Origins of randomness in sampling, observation, oracle state, or interface implementation.

knowledge_statements.title: Response Randomness Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates common exogenous and endogenous seeds generating an oracle response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random oracle response can be represented as \(Y_t=\Phi(q_t,H_{t-1},\xi_t^{\mathrm{data}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{alg}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{noise}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{sched}})\). Here the seeds respectively encode data or coordinate sampling, randomized internal computation, measurement or communication noise, and random scheduling or asynchronous execution. The seeds need not be mutually independent unless the oracle model states that assumption, and their conditional laws may depend on \(H_{t-1}\). Conditional on all seeds and the history, \(Y_t\) is deterministic. A source affects response randomness precisely when varying that seed while holding the other arguments fixed can change \(\Phi\) with positive conditional probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomness may enter through sampling, internal randomization, noise, or scheduling; conditioning on all such seeds makes the response deterministic.
assumptions_latex: All unobserved random inputs relevant to the response are included among the displayed seeds.
The response admits a measurable functional representation \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal L(Y_t\mid q_t,H_{t-1},\xi_t^{\mathrm{data}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{alg}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{noise}},\xi_t^{\mathrm{sched}})\ \text{is a Dirac measure}.\]

children.title: Fidelity Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Access distinguished by whether the querying procedure can request a response accuracy.

children.title: Fixed-Fidelity Access
children.top_down_role: Interfaces whose response quality is predetermined by the oracle model.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Fidelity Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an oracle whose accuracy regime cannot be selected per query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(q)\) denote an ideal response and let \(Y(q)\) be the returned response. An oracle provides fixed-fidelity access when its admissible error or noise envelope is chosen before interaction and the query contains no fidelity-control parameter. For example, fixed constants \(\bar\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(\bar\sigma\ge0\) may satisfy \(d(Y(q),T(q))\le\bar\varepsilon\) deterministically or \(\mathbb E[d(Y(q),T(q))^2\mid q]\le\bar\sigma^2\) stochastically for every admissible \(q\). The algorithm may choose \(q\), but it cannot request a smaller tolerance or variance by modifying that query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-fidelity access supplies every query under one predetermined accuracy or noise envelope, with no query-level control over fidelity.
assumptions_latex: The response space carries a discrepancy measure \(d\).
The constants defining the fidelity envelope are fixed before oracle interaction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q\ \text{is selectable, but}\ (\bar\varepsilon,\bar\sigma)\ \text{is not a query-controlled argument}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-fidelity models hold accuracy and noise specifications constant across algorithmic queries
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Fixed-Fidelity Access leaf and clearly distinguishes fidelity from the selectable query. No source supports this terminology or the proposed deterministic-error and conditional-mean-square envelopes as representative forms of the same access regime. A specific oracle-model citation is required.

children.title: Query-Controlled Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Interfaces permitting the querying procedure to request a response quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Query-Controlled Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic oracle access whose accuracy is selected separately at each query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a query domain, let \(Y\) be a response space with metric \(d_Y\), and let \(T:X\to Y\) be the exact information map. A query-controlled-fidelity oracle is a map \(\mathcal O:X\times E\to Y\), where \(E\subset(0,\infty)\) is a set of admissible tolerances, such that every query \((x,\varepsilon)\) satisfies \[d_Y\bigl(\mathcal O(x,\varepsilon),T(x)\bigr)\leq \varepsilon.\] The algorithm may choose \(\varepsilon\) adaptively from previous responses; consequently, two queries at the same point may request different fidelity levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm supplies both a point and an accuracy tolerance, and the oracle returns information within that requested tolerance of the exact response.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\), and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
\(E\subset(0,\infty)\) is the set of supported tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_Y(\mathcal O(x,\varepsilon),T(x))\leq\varepsilon\) for every \((x,\varepsilon)\in X\times E\).
review_flags: Exact taxonomy-specific formulation lacks a supporting source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric-error formulation is mathematically coherent and the definition fits the leaf, but query-controlled fidelity need not universally mean an absolute metric tolerance. No source locator supports this taxonomy-specific convention.

children.title: Fidelity–Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Resource consequences associated with selecting stronger response fidelity.

knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity–Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the resource price attached to increasingly accurate oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O(x,\varepsilon)\) approximate an exact response \(T(x)\) with error at most \(\varepsilon\), and let \(c:E\to[0,\infty]\) denote the worst-case cost of requesting tolerance \(\varepsilon\). A fidelity–cost tradeoff is present when \(c\) is nonincreasing in tolerance: \[0<\varepsilon_1\leq\varepsilon_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c(\varepsilon_1)\geq c(\varepsilon_2).\] For an adaptive algorithm making queries \((x_t,\varepsilon_t)\) for \(t=1,\ldots,N\), its oracle expenditure is measured by \(C_N=\sum_{t=1}^N c(\varepsilon_t)\), rather than by query count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-fidelity queries cost at least as much as lower-fidelity ones, so complexity is the sum of requested-fidelity costs, not merely the number of calls.
assumptions_latex: \(E\subset(0,\infty)\) is ordered by the usual tolerance order.
\(c(\varepsilon)\) bounds the resource cost of a tolerance-\(\varepsilon\) response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_N=\sum_{t=1}^N c(\varepsilon_t)\), with \(c(\varepsilon_1)\geq c(\varepsilon_2)\) whenever \(\varepsilon_1\leq\varepsilon_2\).

notation.meaning: total cost of N oracle calls

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this variable-fidelity cost model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the fidelity–cost leaf, but monotone tolerance cost and additive expenditure are modeling choices rather than universal consequences of variable fidelity. A source specifying this cost model is required.

children.top_down_role: The boundary between opaque information and interfaces exposing reusable structure.

children.title: Opaque Black-Box Access
children.top_down_role: Responses that conceal the internal encoding and decomposition of the instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Opaque Black-Box Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines access that exposes aggregate responses but no latent instance decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance \(I\) induce an aggregate response map \(T_I:X\to Y\). An oracle \(\mathcal O_I\) provides opaque black-box access when, for every query \(x\in X\), its response is determined solely by \(x\) and \(T_I(x)\), and carries no identifier or separately addressable data for components, samples, blocks, agents, or subproblems of \(I\). Equivalently, if \(T_I=T_J\), then no adaptive algorithm interacting only with the oracle can distinguish \(I\) from \(J\) through their response transcripts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An opaque oracle reports only aggregate information; instances with identical aggregate response maps are indistinguishable even if their internal decompositions differ.
assumptions_latex: Each instance \(I\) determines a response map \(T_I:X\to Y\).
Algorithms observe only query–response transcripts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_I=T_J\) implies identical admissible oracle transcripts for \(I\) and \(J\).

notation.meaning: aggregate response map of instance I

review_flags: The indistinguishability formulation is taxonomy-specific and lacks a supplied source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate-access idea matches the leaf, but the asserted transcript indistinguishability requires a common deterministic response rule or an explicitly identical conditional response distribution. The current assumptions and absent source do not establish the claimed equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural Information Can Overcome Black-Box Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between opaque oracle models and algorithms that exploit known objective structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complexity limitations proved for a pure black-box model need not persist when the objective's representation or decomposition is available: known structure can be used to construct more efficient algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound for an opaque black-box model does not automatically apply when the objective's internal structure is known, because algorithms may exploit that structure to improve efficiency.
assumptions_latex: \text{the optimization model exposes exploitable structural information beyond opaque oracle responses}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{black-box complexity limitations need not govern structure-exploiting algorithms}

children.title: Decomposition-Revealing Access
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing samples, components, blocks, agents, or separable terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Revealing Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines oracle interfaces that permit separately addressed access to constituent terms or blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an instance has an indexed decomposition \(T_I=\mathcal A(T_{I,1},\ldots,T_{I,m})\), where \(m\geq2\) and \(\mathcal A\) is an aggregation rule. A decomposition-revealing oracle accepts a component label \(i\in\{1,\\ldots,m\}\) together with a local query \(x\in X_i\) and returns \(\mathcal O_I(i,x)=T_{I,i}(x)\), or a declared approximation thereof. Because the label is exposed and selectable, an algorithm may sample, prioritize, or update individual components without evaluating the full aggregate map \(T_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface exposes component labels and allows separate queries to samples, blocks, agents, or separable terms instead of only aggregate evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq2\) constituent response maps are explicitly indexed.
The aggregation rule \(\mathcal A\) defines the full response from the constituents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query interface contains an address \(i\), and \(\mathcal O_I(i,x)\) reveals information about \(T_{I,i}(x)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly defines this oracle-transparency class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The component-addressable interface matches the leaf, but no source supports the proposed unified definition. In addition, the component-index set contains the malformed TeX sequence `\\ldots`, which must be corrected if a sourced record is submitted.

children.title: Subproblem-Revealing Access
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing tractable projection, proximal, linear-optimization, or response problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem-Revealing Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines access through exact solutions of structured auxiliary optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a feasible domain and let \(\mathscr P\) be a declared family of parameterized auxiliary problems associated with an instance \(I\). A subproblem-revealing oracle accepts parameters \(q\in Q\) and returns a solution \[\mathcal O_I(q)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in Z_I(q)}\Phi_I(z;q),\] or a declared approximation satisfying a specified residual or objective-gap tolerance. The sets \(Z_I(q)\) and objectives \(\Phi_I(\cdot;q)\) may encode projection, proximal, linear-minimization, or best-response operations; thus the response exposes structured computational access beyond local values or derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle solves a declared structured auxiliary problem, such as a projection, proximal step, linear minimization, or best response.
assumptions_latex: For each admissible \(q\in Q\), the solution set is nonempty.
The auxiliary family \(\mathscr P\) and any approximation criterion are fixed by the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_I(q)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in Z_I(q)}\Phi_I(z;q)\), or satisfies the model's declared approximation criterion.

notation.meaning: subproblem parameters supplied by the query

review_flags: The unified subproblem-oracle definition is not supported by the supplied locators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and structured-subproblem interpretation fit the leaf, but the unified treatment of projection, proximal, linear-minimization, and best-response access is taxonomy-specific. The alternative approximate response is also not mathematically fixed without a declared criterion and supporting source.

children.title: Function-Value Oracles

knowledge_statements.title: Function-Value Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the exact deterministic zeroth-order oracle convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be an objective function. The exact function-value oracle for \(f\) is the map \(\mathcal O_f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) defined by \[\mathcal O_f(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] A query reveals the calibrated numerical value of the objective at the requested point but, by itself, supplies no derivative, subgradient, comparison-only encoding, or decomposition label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any queried point, the oracle returns the objective's calibrated numerical value and no derivative or decomposition information.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is pointwise defined on the query domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f(x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).

children.title: Ordinal Feedback Oracle Family
