knowledge_statements.title: Weak Membership Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-sensitive membership with an indeterminate boundary band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed subset of a normed space \(X\), and define \(C^{+\delta}:=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\delta\}\) and \(C^{-\delta}:=\{x\in C:B(x,\delta)\subseteq C\}\). For \(\delta>0\), a weak membership oracle returns \(M_{C,\delta}(x)\in\{0,1\}\) with the guarantees \[x\in C^{-\delta}\Rightarrow M_{C,\delta}(x)=1,\qquad x\notin C^{+\delta}\Rightarrow M_{C,\delta}(x)=0.\] Either answer is allowed in \(C^{+\delta}\setminus C^{-\delta}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak membership oracle must answer correctly away from the boundary but may return either answer within a prescribed tolerance band.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is closed
\(X\) is normed
\(\delta>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle is exact on \(C^{-\delta}\) and on \(X\setminus C^{+\delta}\), with ambiguity only between them.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar access to Euclidean distance from a query point to a nonempty closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\) be a closed subset of a Euclidean space \(X\). A distance oracle for \(C\) returns, for each query \(x\in X\), the scalar \[d_C(x):=\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\inf_{y\in C}\lVert x-y\rVert.\] Consequently, exact membership is represented by \(x\in C\Longleftrightarrow d_C(x)=0\), while proximity at radius \(\delta\ge 0\) is represented by \(d_C(x)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance access returns the infimal Euclidean distance to the set; for a closed set, zero distance characterizes membership, and thresholding the distance characterizes proximity.

\(X\) is a Euclidean space
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_C(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\lVert x-y\rVert\), and \(x\in C\Longleftrightarrow d_C(x)=0\)

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Membership Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean access to membership in a prescribed outer neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\) be a closed subset of a normed space \(X\), and let \(\delta\ge0\). A near-membership oracle at radius \(\delta\) returns the exact Boolean value \[N_{C,\delta}(x)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\delta.\] Equivalently, it is a strong membership oracle for the outer neighborhood \(C^{+\delta}:=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\delta\}\). \(X\) is normed
\(\delta\ge0\)

knowledge_statements.title: Membership-Tolerance Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity region of a proximity-membership query for a closed set in Euclidean space.

\(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Volume and side-length reduction under coordinate bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested axis-aligned boxes obtained by midpoint bisections, with an additional cyclic-coverage conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $B_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_k\le x\le b_k\}$, where $a_k\le b_k$ componentwise. Suppose that at each step $k$, the box $B_{k+1}$ is obtained from $B_k$ by replacing exactly one coordinate interval, indexed by $i_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with either its lower or upper half, while every other coordinate interval is unchanged. Then $\operatorname{vol}_n(B_{k+1})=\tfrac12\operatorname{vol}_n(B_k)$ for every $k\ge0$. If, moreover, for every $k\ge0$ and every coordinate $i$ there exists $t\in\{k,\ldots,k+n-1\}$ with $i_t=i$, then $b_{k+n}-a_{k+n}=\tfrac12(b_k-a_k)$ componentwise for every $k\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bisecting one coordinate interval of an axis-aligned box halves its volume. If every coordinate is bisected during each block of n successive steps, then after that block every side length is exactly half its initial value.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{N}
B_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_k\le x\le b_k\},\quad a_k\le b_k\text{ componentwise}
\forall k\ge0\ \exists i_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}: B_{k+1}\text{ is one midpoint half of }B_k\text{ in coordinate }i_k\text{, with all other coordinate intervals unchanged}
\forall k\ge0\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\ \exists t\in\{k,\ldots,k+n-1\}:i_t=i\quad\text{for the side-length conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\ge0:\ \operatorname{vol}_n(B_{k+1})=\tfrac12\operatorname{vol}_n(B_k),\qquad \text{and under coordinate coverage, }b_{k+n}-a_{k+n}=\tfrac12(b_k-a_k)\text{ componentwise}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclic box-bisection resisting oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stateful resisting oracle based on nested axis-aligned boxes and cyclic coordinate bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $R>0$, let $\bar e_n$ be the all-ones vector, and initialize $a_0=-R\bar e_n$, $b_0=R\bar e_n$, $m=0$, and $i=1$. Write $B_k=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_k\le z\le b_k\}$ componentwise and $c_k=(a_k+b_k)/2$. On a query $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$: (1) if $x\notin B_0$, return any vector separating $x$ from $B_0$; (2) otherwise choose the largest $k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$ with $x\in B_k$; (3) if $k<m$, return $g_k$; (4) if $k=m$ and $x^{(i)}\ge c_m^{(i)}$, set $a_{m+1}=a_m$, $b_{m+1}=b_m+(c_m^{(i)}-b_m^{(i)})e_i$, and $g_m=e_i$; otherwise set $a_{m+1}=a_m+(c_m^{(i)}-a_m^{(i)})e_i$, $b_{m+1}=b_m$, and $g_m=-e_i$. Then increment $m$ and $i$, reset $i$ to $1$ if $i>n$, and return the separator constructed in the new-box step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the box [-R,R]^n, the resisting oracle either separates a query outside the initial box, reuses the separator attached to the deepest previously generated box containing the query, or bisects that box in the current cyclic coordinate and returns the corresponding signed coordinate vector.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb{R}^n
a_0=-R\bar e_n,\quad b_0=R\bar e_n,\quad m=0,\quad i=1
B_k=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_k\le z\le b_k\},\quad c_k=\tfrac12(a_k+b_k)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns either a separator of }x\text{ from }B_0\text{ or a stored/new vector }g_k\in\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_n\}\text{ while updating the nested-box state as specified.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid cuts whose retained halfspace extends beyond the localization center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) have designated center \(z\), and let \(K\subseteq L\) satisfy \(K\subseteq\{x:a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\}\). children.title: Validity Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access testing proposed inequalities over a represented set.

knowledge_statements.title: Validity Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact testing of a proposed linear inequality over a represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A validity oracle accepts \((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\), representing the inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\), and returns VALID exactly when \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) for every \(x\in K\). Equivalently, when the support value is defined in the extended reals, validity means \(\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\). A negative answer need not include a violating point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validity oracle decides whether a proposed linear inequality holds throughout the represented set, without necessarily returning a counterexample.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VALID}(a,b)=1\) if and only if \(\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\).

notation.meaning: Normal and offset of the proposed inequality.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the validity-oracle container, and the Boolean and support-function formulations agree, including for unbounded sets when the supremum is extended-real-valued. No inspectable source is supplied for this exact oracle interface.

children.title: Violation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access returning witnesses against proposed inequalities or conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Violation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity testing augmented with a point witnessing failure of the proposed inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A violation oracle queried with \((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\) either certifies \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) for every \(x\in K\), or returns a witness \(x^{v}\in K\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x^{v}>b\). Thus every negative validity response is accompanied by a directly checkable counterexample, assuming membership in \(K\) is independently verifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle either certifies a proposed inequality over the set or returns a represented-set point that violates it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) for all \(x\in K\), or \(x^{v}\in K\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x^{v}>b\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard witness-producing refinement of validity access
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The witness-producing definition matches the violation-oracle role, and its alternatives are mathematically consistent. No inspectable source is supplied for the exact interface or its distinction from decision-only validity access.

children.title: Constraint-Generation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Access exposing violated constraints from an implicit family.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Generation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation access to an implicit family of convex inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for every }i\in I\}\), where the index set \(I\) may be too large to enumerate. A constraint-generation oracle queried at \(y\in D\) either certifies \(g_i(y)\leq0\) for all \(i\in I\), or returns an index \(i_y\in I\) with \(g_{i_y}(y)>0\), together with a representation of that violated constraint. For convex \(g_{i_y}\), a subgradient may additionally generate a separating cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a candidate point, the oracle confirms all implicit constraints or exposes one violated constraint that can be added to a working model.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(K=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for all }i\in I\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(y\in K\), or the oracle returns \(i_y\in I\) such that \(g_{i_y}(y)>0\).

notation.meaning: Index of a constraint violated by y.

children.title: Set-Existence Certificate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Set-level access resolving whether admissible points exist.

children.title: Feasibility Oracles
children.top_down_role: Set-level access addressing the existence of admissible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision access for nonemptiness of a parameterized feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(u)=\{x\in D:F(u,x)\leq0\}\) denote the feasible set encoded by input \(u\), with componentwise interpretation for vector-valued \(F\). A feasibility oracle returns FEASIBLE exactly when \(K(u)\neq\varnothing\), and INFEASIBLE exactly when \(K(u)=\varnothing\). In the decision-only interface, neither response is required to include a feasible point or an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility oracle decides whether the constraints encoded by an input admit at least one point, without necessarily producing a witness or certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the prescribed decision domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{FEAS}(u)=1\) if and only if \(K(u)\neq\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard decision-oracle formulation of feasibility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly isolates a decision-only feasibility oracle from witness and certificate interfaces, and it fits the terminal container. No inspectable source is supplied for this parameterized oracle formulation.

children.title: Emptiness Oracles
children.top_down_role: Set-level access addressing the absence of admissible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Emptiness Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision access testing whether a represented or parameterized set contains no point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(u)\subseteq D\) be the set represented by input \(u\). An emptiness oracle returns EMPTY exactly when \(K(u)=\varnothing\), and NONEMPTY exactly when \(K(u)\neq\varnothing\). This interface is the logical complement of a decision-only feasibility oracle; by itself it need not return a point in the nonempty case or a certificate in the empty case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An emptiness oracle decides whether the represented set has no elements; witnesses and certificates belong to stronger interfaces.
assumptions_latex: \(K(u)\subseteq D\) is well-defined for every admissible input \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{EMPTY}(u)=1\) if and only if \(K(u)=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: emptiness is the Boolean complement of decision feasibility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition accurately presents emptiness as the Boolean complement of decision feasibility and keeps witnesses and certificates separate. No inspectable source is supplied for the interface.

children.title: Existence-Witness Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Response formats exposing an admissible point or other evidence of nonemptiness.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence-Witness Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive nonemptiness output for a represented feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(u)=\{x\in D:F(u,x)\leq0\}\). On an instance declared nonempty, an existence-witness interface returns \(x^{w}\in D\) satisfying \(F(u,x^{w})\leq0\), hence \(x^{w}\in K(u)\). The witness certifies nonemptiness whenever membership in \(D\) and the displayed inequalities can be checked from the encoding. If \(K(u)=\varnothing\), the interface may return EMPTY without an emptiness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty feasible set, the interface returns a point whose directly checkable constraints certify existence.
assumptions_latex: Membership in \(D\) and evaluation of \(F(u,\cdot)\) are verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(x^{w}\) certifies \(K(u)\neq\varnothing\) because \(x^{w}\in D\) and \(F(u,x^{w})\leq0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a feasible point is the canonical constructive certificate of nonemptiness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind is appropriate for this witness-producing terminal container, and the returned feasible point is a checkable nonemptiness certificate under the stated verification assumptions. No inspectable source is supplied for the interface and its one-sided EMPTY behavior.

children.title: Emptiness-Certificate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Response formats exposing verifiable evidence that no admissible point exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Emptiness-Certificate Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound and complete certificates for emptiness of a represented feasibility set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(\theta)\subseteq X\) be the feasibility set encoded by an instance \(\theta\), and let \(V(\theta,c)\in\{\mathsf{accept},\mathsf{reject}\}\) be a deterministic verifier. A string \(c\) is an emptiness certificate for \(\theta\) when \(V(\theta,c)=\mathsf{accept}\). The interface is sound if \[V(\theta,c)=\mathsf{accept}\;\Longrightarrow\;S(\theta)=\varnothing.\] It is complete if \[S(\theta)=\varnothing\;\Longrightarrow\;\exists c\;V(\theta,c)=\mathsf{accept}.\] An emptiness-certificate interface may return such a certificate or \(\mathsf{UNKNOWN}\); it must never return an accepted certificate for a nonempty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verifier accepts only valid proofs that the represented feasibility set is empty; completeness additionally requires an accepted proof for every empty instance.
assumptions_latex: \(S(\theta)\) is well defined for every admissible encoding \(\theta\).
The verifier \(V\) has access to the instance encoding and proposed certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\theta,c)=\mathsf{accept}\) certifies \(S(\theta)=\varnothing\), with existence of such \(c\) required under completeness.

notation.meaning: feasibility set represented by instance theta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind fits the leaf, and the soundness condition is mathematically coherent. An authoritative locator is required for this particular interface convention. The statement should also distinguish completeness of the certificate system (an accepted certificate exists) from completeness of a certificate-producing procedure (the interface returns one rather than UNKNOWN).

children.title: Geometric Optimization Access
children.top_down_role: Optimization and support interfaces associated with implicitly represented convex sets.

children.title: Strong Optimization Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact linear optimization over rational or explicitly encoded structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Optimization Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear maximization over a nonempty compact, exactly encoded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact, with an encoding under which membership and returned points have exact meaning. A strong optimization oracle receives an exactly represented direction \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and returns a point \(x_u\in K\) satisfying \[\langle u,x_u\rangle=\max_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle.\] Thus both feasibility of the returned point and optimality of its objective value are exact; no tolerance, outer approximation, or additive objective error is permitted. For rational oracle models, \(K\), \(u\), and \(x_u\) are supplied in the stipulated exact rational or algebraic encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a direction, the oracle returns an exactly feasible point attaining the exact maximum linear objective over the represented compact set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and compact.
The direction and admissible output points have exact finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x_u\) satisfies \(x_u\in K\) and \(\langle u,x_u\rangle=h_K(u)\) exactly.

notation.meaning: exact maximizing point returned by the oracle

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the strong-optimization-oracle container and is internally coherent for a nonempty compact set, but the exact encoding and output convention is model-specific and lacks an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Weak Optimization Oracles
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-sensitive optimization over approximate convex bodies.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Optimization Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard inner–outer tolerance formulation for weak linear optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact and convex, let \(B_2\) be the closed Euclidean unit ball, and define \(K^{+\varepsilon}=K+\varepsilon B_2\) and \(K^{-\varepsilon}=\{x\in K:x+\varepsilon B_2\subseteq K\}\). Given \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), a weak optimization oracle either correctly reports \(K^{-\varepsilon}=\varnothing\), or returns \(y\in K^{+\varepsilon}\) such that \[\langle u,y\rangle\geq \langle u,x\rangle-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }x\in K^{-\varepsilon}.\] If \(K^{-\varepsilon}\neq\varnothing\), the oracle must return such a point rather than an emptiness report.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At tolerance epsilon, the oracle approximately maximizes over the eroded body while returning a point in the expanded body.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and convex.
\(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The response is either a valid declaration \(K^{-\varepsilon}=\varnothing\) or a point \(y\in K^{+\varepsilon}\) with the stated additive guarantee.

notation.meaning: Euclidean outer parallel body of K
Euclidean inner parallel body of K

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the weak-optimization-oracle container, but this inner–outer formulation is convention-sensitive. A source must confirm the precise erosion, expansion, emptiness alternative, additive error, and whether the direction must be normalized or the error scaled by its norm.

children.title: Support-Function Oracles
children.top_down_role: Directional extremal-value information for a represented set.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact directional support values, optionally accompanied by exposed maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its support function is \[h_K(u)=\sup_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}.\] A support-function oracle receives a direction \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and returns \(h_K(u)\), or a declared unbounded value when the supremum is \(+\infty\). A value-and-witness variant also returns \(x_u\in K\) satisfying \(\langle u,x_u\rangle=h_K(u)\) whenever the supremum is finite and attained. If \(K\) is nonempty and compact, the returned value is finite and an attaining witness exists for every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns the supremum of a linear functional over the set and may also return an attaining point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
The query direction satisfies \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle value equals \(h_K(u)=\sup_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle\).

children.title: Query Adaptivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of query selection on preceding oracle responses.

children.title: Fully Adaptive Queries
children.top_down_role: Queries may depend on the complete preceding transcript.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Adaptive Queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential protocols with unrestricted dependence on the complete observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an oracle protocol of length \(T\) with queries \(Q_t\), replies \(Y_t\), private algorithmic randomness \(U\), and transcript \(H_t=(Q_1,Y_1,\ldots,Q_t,Y_t)\). The protocol is fully adaptive when, for every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), the next query is generated by an arbitrary measurable rule \[Q_t=\phi_t(U,H_{t-1}),\] or equivalently by a probability kernel conditional on \((U,H_{t-1})\). Hence any part of the complete preceding transcript may influence the next query, subject only to measurability and the admissible query domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each query may depend measurably on all earlier queries and replies, together with the algorithm’s private randomness.
assumptions_latex: The query and response spaces are measurable spaces.
The transcript \(H_{t-1}\) is observed before query \(Q_t\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), \(Q_t\) may be measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U,H_{t-1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits fully adaptive queries and correctly permits dependence on the complete preceding transcript, but the measurable-protocol convention has no cited locator.

children.title: Precommitted Query Regimes
children.top_down_role: Queries or query distributions fixed independently of observed responses.

children.title: Nonadaptive Query Schedules
children.top_down_role: Query schedules fixed without using observed oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonadaptive Query Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic query sequences fixed before any oracle reply is observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a query budget \(T\) and public problem data \(d\). A deterministic oracle protocol has a nonadaptive query schedule if there exist maps \(q_t\) such that \[Q_t=q_t(d),\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,\] and no \(q_t\) depends on any oracle reply. Equivalently, the entire vector \((Q_1,\ldots,Q_T)\) is fixed before interaction begins. Replies may be processed jointly after collection to form the output, but they cannot alter, cancel, reorder, or introduce queries within the precommitted schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All queries are fixed from public problem data before interaction; observed replies affect only the final processing, not the schedule.
assumptions_latex: A finite query budget \(T\) is fixed before interaction.
Public problem data \(d\) excludes oracle replies from the current interaction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query vector \((Q_1,\ldots,Q_T)\) is determined before observing \((Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits deterministic nonadaptive schedules and consistently excludes response-dependent changes, but it lacks an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Oblivious Query Distributions
children.top_down_role: Randomized query distributions selected independently of the realized response transcript.

knowledge_statements.title: Oblivious Query Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random query schedules whose joint law is fixed independently of oracle replies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix public data \(d\), a query budget \(T\), and a probability kernel \(\Pi_d\) on the product query space. An oblivious query distribution samples the complete schedule according to \[(Q_1,\ldots,Q_T)\sim\Pi_d\] before any oracle reply is observed. Consequently, for every measurable set \(A\), \[\mathbb{P}((Q_1,\ldots,Q_T)\in A\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)=\Pi_d(A)\] whenever the conditional probability is defined. The sampled queries may be mutually dependent, but their joint distribution cannot be updated using responses from the current interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full random query schedule is drawn before interaction from a response-independent law; queries may still be mutually correlated.
assumptions_latex: The product query space is measurable.
Public data \(d\) and budget \(T\) are fixed before oracle replies are observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditionally on \(d\), the joint query law is \(\Pi_d\) and is independent of the current oracle replies.

notation.meaning: precommitted joint distribution of all queries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Sampling the schedule before replies does not imply that the schedule is independent of the replies: replies generally depend on the sampled queries, so conditioning on them can change the conditional query law. Obliviousness should instead be expressed by measurability of the schedule with respect to preinteraction data and randomness, or by conditional independence from prior replies at query-selection time. A source is needed to fix the intended convention reliably.

children.title: Query Precommitment Scope
children.top_down_role: The portion of a query protocol that must be fixed before interaction begins.

knowledge_statements.title: Query Precommitment Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability criterion specifying exactly which query decisions are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{G}_0\) denote the information available before oracle interaction, and let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}\) be the indices declared precommitted. The protocol satisfies precommitment on scope \(S\) precisely when \[Q_t\text{ is }\mathcal{G}_0\text{-measurable for every }t\in S.\] Equivalently, changing oracle replies while holding the preinteraction information fixed cannot change any query indexed by \(S\). Queries with indices outside \(S\) may depend on the permitted preceding transcript. Full precommitment corresponds to \(S=\{1,\ldots,T\}\); partial precommitment records a proper subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A declared subset of queries is precommitted exactly when those queries depend only on information available before interaction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{G}_0\) contains all permitted preinteraction information.
\(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}\) is fixed before interaction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Precommitment on \(S\) holds if and only if every \(Q_t\), for \(t\in S\), is \(\mathcal{G}_0\)-measurable.

notation.meaning: set of query indices covered by precommitment

children.title: Limited-Adaptivity Protocols
children.top_down_role: Interaction partitioned into a bounded number of adaptive rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited-Adaptivity Protocols
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle interaction divided into a bounded number of sequentially adaptive query batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the query indices into ordered batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_R\). An oracle protocol is \(R\)-round adaptive if every query in batch \(B_r\) is selected using only public data, private randomness, and replies from batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_{r-1}\). Formally, for \(t\in B_r\), \[Q_t=\phi_t(U,Y_{B_1},\ldots,Y_{B_{r-1}}),\] and no query in \(B_r\) may depend on a reply generated within the same batch. A family is limited-adaptive when \(R\) is bounded by the stipulated round budget, independently of the total number of queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queries are issued in a bounded number of batches; each batch may use earlier batches’ replies but not replies from its own batch.
assumptions_latex: The query indices are partitioned into \(R\) ordered batches.
All replies from batch \(B_{r-1}\) are available before batch \(B_r\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Queries in \(B_r\) are measurable with respect to information available before round \(r\), excluding replies from \(B_r\).

notation.meaning: query indices in adaptive round r
collection of replies from batch r

children.title: Randomization Ownership
children.top_down_role: Randomness originating in the querying procedure, the oracle, or their interaction.

children.title: Algorithmic Randomization
children.top_down_role: Random query selection with deterministic instance responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmic Randomization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Private algorithmic randomness with conditionally deterministic oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a private random seed sampled by the algorithm, and let the instance \(\theta\) determine a deterministic oracle map \(O_\theta\). A protocol has algorithmic randomization when queries satisfy \[Q_t=\phi_t(U,H_{t-1})\] while replies satisfy \[Y_t=O_\theta(Q_t).\] Thus, conditional on \(\theta\), \(U\), and the induced queries, the replies contain no additional randomness: \(\mathbb{P}(Y_t=O_\theta(Q_t)\mid Q_t,\theta)=1\). All randomness in the transcript is therefore inherited from the algorithm’s seed and its randomized query-selection rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm randomizes its queries using a private seed, while the oracle response is deterministic for each instance and query.
assumptions_latex: The instance \(\theta\) specifies a deterministic response map \(O_\theta\).
The algorithm samples a private seed \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditional on \((\theta,Q_t)\), the response \(Y_t=O_\theta(Q_t)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: deterministic oracle map for instance theta

children.title: Oracle Randomization
children.top_down_role: Random responses produced by sampling, observation, or internal randomized computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Randomization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random oracle responses generated conditionally on the instance, query, and transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the algorithm use no private random seed, so that each query has the form \(Q_t=\phi_t(H_{t-1})\). An oracle-randomized protocol specifies response kernels \(P_{\theta,t}(\cdot\mid Q_t,H_{t-1})\) and samples \[Y_t\sim P_{\theta,t}(\cdot\mid Q_t,H_{t-1}).\] The kernel may represent sampling noise, observational noise, or randomized internal computation. Randomness in later queries may arise indirectly through earlier random replies, but, conditional on the observed transcript, the algorithm’s next-query rule itself is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle samples its responses from specified kernels; the algorithm has no private seed, though past random replies may randomize later queries.
assumptions_latex: The query and response spaces are measurable.
Each \(P_{\theta,t}\) is a probability kernel on the response space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Given \((\theta,Q_t,H_{t-1})\), the reply law is \(P_{\theta,t}(\cdot\mid Q_t,H_{t-1})\).

notation.meaning: oracle response kernel at time t

children.title: Coupled Algorithm–Oracle Randomness
children.top_down_role: Protocols in which query randomization and response randomness are jointly dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Algorithm–Oracle Randomness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jointly distributed query and response randomness not separable into independent private seeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) and \(V\) denote latent random variables used respectively in query selection and oracle response generation. A protocol has coupled algorithm–oracle randomness when its joint law specifies \[Q_t=\phi_t(U,H_{t-1}),\qquad Y_t=\psi_t(V,Q_t,H_{t-1}),\] and \(U\) and \(V\) are not required to be independent; equivalently, the protocol may use shared randomness \(W\) influencing both maps. The coupling must be included in the oracle model because the marginal laws of randomized queries and randomized responses alone do not determine the transcript law or the performance guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query and response randomness may share or correlate latent variables, so their marginals alone do not determine the interaction law.
assumptions_latex: A joint probability law for the latent randomness and transcript is specified.
The query and response maps are measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transcript law is induced by the joint law of \((U,V)\), which may differ from the product of its marginals.

children.title: Concurrent Query Protocols
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous-query access and its distinction from sequential interaction.

children.title: Fixed-Width Query Batches
children.top_down_role: Parallel access with a prescribed number of queries per round.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Width Query Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic batch width in a round-based oracle protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\) be an oracle and let \(H_{r-1}\) denote the transcript available before round \(r\). A fixed-width \(b\)-batch protocol, where \(b\in\mathbb N\), selects a tuple \(Q_r=(q_{r,1},\ldots,q_{r,b})\) measurable with respect to \(H_{r-1}\) and the algorithm's internal randomness. It submits all \(b\) queries before observing any response from round \(r\), receives \(Y_r=(\mathcal O(q_{r,1}),\ldots,\mathcal O(q_{r,b}))\), and sets \(H_r=(H_{r-1},Q_r,Y_r)\). Thus queries within a batch may be jointly designed but cannot adapt to responses from that batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every round submits exactly b jointly chosen queries; all depend only on the earlier transcript, never on responses from the same batch.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb N\) is fixed before the protocol begins.
Oracle responses are indexed by their submitted queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|Q_r|=b\) for every round \(r\), and \(Q_r\) is chosen before \(Y_r\) is observed.

children.title: Adaptive Batch Width
children.top_down_role: Query width selected from the transcript or resource state.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Batch Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-dependent query width under an explicit resource constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_{r-1}\) be the transcript and \(S_r\) the resource state before round \(r\). An adaptive-width concurrent protocol first chooses a nonnegative integer \(B_r=\beta_r(H_{r-1},S_r)\), possibly using internal randomness, and then chooses \(Q_r=(q_{r,1},\ldots,q_{r,B_r})\) from the same available information. All queries in \(Q_r\) are submitted before any round-\(r\) response is observed. Admissibility requires a stated resource rule, such as \(B_r\leq b_{\max}\) or \(\sum_{r=1}^{R}B_r\leq N\); without such a rule, batch width does not define a meaningful access restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The protocol chooses each round’s batch size from the prior transcript and resource state, subject to a declared width or total-query budget.
assumptions_latex: The batch-size rule is measurable with respect to information available before round \(r\).
A width or cumulative-query resource constraint is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_r\) may vary with \((H_{r-1},S_r)\), but no response from round \(r\) influences \(B_r\) or \(Q_r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit adaptive batch width, and the mathematical conventions are internally coherent. No evidence is supplied for the transcript-dependent width model or for the assertion that a separate resource constraint is required for meaningful access restriction.

children.title: Parallel-Depth Protocols
children.top_down_role: Interaction organized by sequentially dependent parallel rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Depth Protocols
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential adaptivity measured by the number of parallel oracle rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-depth-\(R\) oracle protocol consists of batches \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_R\). For each \(r\), the entire batch \(Q_r\) is selected from the transcript \(H_{r-1}\) and internal randomness, submitted concurrently, and answered before \(Q_{r+1}\) is selected. Its parallel depth is the number \(R\) of sequentially dependent oracle rounds; its work is \(N=\sum_{r=1}^{R}|Q_r|\). A complexity claim in this model must state both the admissible batch-width rule and whether it bounds depth \(R\), work \(N\), or both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel depth counts sequentially dependent batches, while work counts all oracle queries; a model must specify which resource is bounded.
assumptions_latex: Queries within a round cannot depend on responses from that same round.
The protocol terminates after finitely many rounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The protocol has depth \(R\) and total oracle work \(N=\sum_{r=1}^{R}|Q_r|\).

children.title: Synchronous Response Models
children.top_down_role: Queries and responses proceed in coordinated global rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronous Response Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-round model with a response barrier after every query batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A synchronous oracle protocol is partitioned into global rounds \(r=1,2,\ldots\). At the start of round \(r\), the algorithm selects a finite batch \(Q_r\) using only the completed transcript \(H_{r-1}\). The oracle evaluates every query in \(Q_r\), and a barrier releases the complete response batch \(Y_r\) before the next round begins. The algorithm then forms \(H_r=(H_{r-1},Q_r,Y_r)\). Consequently, no query in \(Q_r\) uses a response generated in round \(r\), and every response in \(Y_r\) is available when \(Q_{r+1}\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each global round ends with a barrier: all current responses arrive before any query in the next round is chosen.
assumptions_latex: Every submitted query receives a response within its global round.
The algorithm updates its transcript only after the round barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_r\) depends only on \(H_{r-1}\), while \(Q_{r+1}\) may depend on the complete \(Y_r\).

notation.meaning: queries submitted in global round r
responses released at the round-r barrier

children.title: Bounded-Delay Models
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous access with controlled response age.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Delay Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asynchronous responses whose discrete-time age has a uniform bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Index algorithmic update events by \(t\in\mathbb N\). If a response used at event \(t\) was generated from a query issued at event \(s(t)\leq t\), its age is \(\tau_t=t-s(t)\). The access model has bounded delay when there exists a finite constant \(\tau_{\max}\) such that \(0\leq\tau_t\leq\tau_{\max}\) for every response incorporated by the algorithm. Equivalently, every incorporated response was generated from one of the most recent \(\tau_{\max}+1\) query states. The bound concerns response age, independently of whether updates occur synchronously or in wall-clock order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every response used by the algorithm was generated at most a fixed finite number of update events earlier.
assumptions_latex: Query issue and response-use events admit a common discrete ordering.
Each used response is associated with its generating query event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_t \tau_t\leq\tau_{\max}<\infty\).

notation.meaning: issue event for the response used at event t

children.title: Adversarial Delay Regimes
children.top_down_role: Protocols in which response age or ordering lacks a usable bound.

children.title: Unbounded Response Age
children.top_down_role: Access regimes lacking a usable upper bound on response age.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Response Age
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite individual delays with no uniform age bound over the execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s(t)\leq t\) be the issue event of the oracle response incorporated at update event \(t\), and define its age by \(\tau_t=t-s(t)\). The execution has unbounded response age when every incorporated response has finite age but no finite uniform bound exists: \[\forall T<\infty\;\exists t\in\mathbb N\quad \tau_t>T.\] This condition is distinct from permanent missingness: a response may eventually arrive while its age grows arbitrarily large. It is also an execution-level property rather than a claim that every permissible schedule necessarily has unbounded age.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All used responses may eventually arrive, yet their ages exceed every finite bound somewhere along the execution.
assumptions_latex: Response ages are measured in a common discrete event ordering.
Each incorporated response has a finite generating event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{t\in\mathbb N}\tau_t=\infty\).

notation.meaning: generating query event for the response used at t
response age at update event t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The execution-level condition is coherent and correctly distinguishes unbounded finite ages from permanent missingness, but no source supports this exact convention or distinction.

children.title: Adversarial Response Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Response timing or ordering controlled by a hostile scheduler.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Response Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent adversarial selection of which outstanding responses are released.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t\) be the transcript immediately before event \(t\), and let \(P_t\) be the set of outstanding query-response pairs. An adversarial response scheduler is a rule \(\sigma\) that selects a release set \(D_t=\sigma(H_t,P_t)\subseteq P_t\), possibly to maximize an algorithmic loss criterion. A nonanticipating scheduler may depend on the realized history, submitted queries, and already generated responses, but not on future private random bits of the algorithm. Unless an additional fairness condition is imposed, \(\sigma\) may postpone a pending response indefinitely; bounded-delay and eventual-delivery restrictions are separate assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive adversary chooses which pending responses arrive next using the realized history, subject only to explicitly imposed delay or fairness rules.
assumptions_latex: The scheduler releases only responses belonging to outstanding submitted queries.
The scheduler cannot condition on the algorithm's unrealized private randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_t\subseteq P_t\) is history-dependent, and delivery guarantees hold only when separately required.

notation.meaning: outstanding query-response pairs before event t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal container, but the scheduler's permissible information, nonanticipation rule, and ability to postpone responses indefinitely depend on model-specific adversarial and fairness conventions for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Stale-Response Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of usable protocol guarantees under arbitrarily stale information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Response Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded staleness can destroy convergence even for a smooth strongly convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and the delayed-gradient update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta\nabla f(x_{t-\tau_t})\), with \(\eta>0\), initial history \(x_s=1\) for \(s\leq0\), and delays \(\tau_t=t\). Then every update uses the stale response \(\nabla f(x_0)=1\), so \(x_t=1-\eta t\). Hence \(|x_t|\to\infty\) and \(f(x_t)\to\infty\), although \(f\) is differentiable, \(1\)-smooth, and \(1\)-strongly convex. Thus ordinary smoothness and strong convexity do not ensure convergence when response age is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic delayed-gradient iteration diverges when every update uses the initial gradient, showing that unbounded staleness invalidates standard convergence guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The response used at event \(t\) has age \(\tau_t=t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t=1-\eta t\), so \(f(x_t)\to\infty\) rather than \(x_t\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon and failure_boundary content kind fit the leaf, and the stated quadratic iteration is mathematically consistent. However, the record supplies no external source and includes a short derivational argument rather than only stating the counterexample and its consequence; source-backed reformulation is required.

children.title: Sequential Feedback Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sequential interaction classified by information revealed after an action.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Introduction to Online Convex Optimization

children.title: Full-Information Feedback
children.top_down_role: Revelation of the current loss function or complete current first-order information.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Information Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online feedback revealing the complete current loss after the action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an action set. At round \(t\), the learner chooses \(x_t\in X\), incurs loss \(\ell_t(x_t)\), and then receives full-information feedback if the revealed object determines \(\ell_t(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). In a differentiable first-order formulation, complete current first-order information instead reveals a representation sufficient to evaluate both \(\ell_t(x)\) and \(\nabla\ell_t(x)\) throughout \(X\). The defining distinction is informational: after feedback, losses of actions not selected at round \(t\) are also recoverable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After acting, the learner can determine the current loss of every action, not merely the loss of the chosen action.
assumptions_latex: The current loss \(\ell_t:X\to\mathbb R\) is fixed for round \(t\).
Feedback is revealed after \(x_t\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in X\), the value \(\ell_t(x)\) is determined by the round-\(t\) feedback.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordinary online full-information definition is standard and matches the leaf, but no source is supplied. The added differentiable first-order formulation is a distinct, stronger representation convention and requires evidence establishing that it belongs in the same local definition rather than blending feedback variants.

children.title: Semi-Bandit Feedback
children.top_down_role: Componentwise feedback restricted to the parts selected by the current action.

knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Bandit Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component losses are observed exactly on coordinates selected by a combinatorial action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subseteq\{0,1\}^d\) be a combinatorial action set. At round \(t\), the learner chooses \(a_t\in A\), a loss vector \(\ell_t\in\mathbb R^d\) is realized, and the incurred loss is \(\langle a_t,\ell_t\rangle\). Semi-bandit feedback reveals \(\ell_{t,i}\) for every selected coordinate \(i\) satisfying \(a_{t,i}=1\), and reveals no coordinate loss solely because \(a_{t,i}=0\). Thus the scalar incurred loss is computable, but the complete vector \(\ell_t\) need not be identifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The learner sees each loss component used by its combinatorial action, while unselected components remain hidden.
assumptions_latex: \(A\subseteq\{0,1\}^d\).
The round loss is additive across selected coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observed index set is \(I_t=\{i:a_{t,i}=1\}\), with observations \((\ell_{t,i})_{i\in I_t}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise combinatorial semi-bandit definition is precise, correctly quantified, and matches the definition container, but it has no cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Bandit Feedback
children.top_down_role: Scalar or action-local outcome information without complete loss revelation.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandit Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only the realized loss of the selected action is revealed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an action set and \(\ell_t:X\to\mathbb R\) the loss at round \(t\). The learner selects \(x_t\in X\), incurs \(\ell_t(x_t)\), and receives bandit feedback when the observation is only the scalar \(y_t=\ell_t(x_t)\), possibly with specified observation noise. Without further structure or additional queries, this feedback does not determine \(\ell_t(x)\) for unselected \(x\neq x_t\), nor does it directly reveal \(\nabla\ell_t(x_t)\). The oracle therefore supplies action-local zeroth-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The learner observes only the chosen action’s scalar loss, leaving other current losses and the gradient unrevealed.
assumptions_latex: The learner chooses \(x_t\) before observing round-\(t\) feedback.
Any observation noise is separately specified by the access model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The round-\(t\) observation is \(y_t=\ell_t(x_t)\), not the full function \(\ell_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar action-local observation model correctly describes bandit feedback and uses the proper content kind. No source is provided, and the optional noisy-observation variant requires explicit source and model alignment.

children.title: Latency-Missingness Feedback Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sequential responses affected by latency, missingness, or partial disclosure.

children.title: Delayed Feedback
children.top_down_role: Sequential feedback subject to response latency.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round feedback becomes observable only after a nonnegative latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At decision round \(t\), let \(Z_t\) denote the feedback generated by the chosen action and let \(d_t\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\) be its delay. Under delayed feedback, \(Z_t\) is first revealed at round \(t+d_t\) when \(d_t<\infty\), and it is never revealed when \(d_t=\infty\). Consequently, the decision at round \(s\) may depend on \(Z_t\) exactly when \(t+d_t<s\), under the convention that feedback arriving at round \(s\) becomes available only after that round's action. Bounded, stochastic, and adversarial delays are distinct subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feedback generated at one round is hidden until its scheduled arrival, so intervening decisions cannot use it.
assumptions_latex: Rounds are indexed by \(t\in\mathbb N\).
Feedback arriving during a round is incorporated after that round's action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Before choosing at round \(s\), the available feedback indices are \(\{t<s:t+d_t<s\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The delayed-feedback definition is internally consistent under its stated after-action arrival convention, but that convention needs a source because it controls the strict inequality in the available-index set. Allowing infinite delay also blends delayed feedback with permanent missingness unless the enclosing taxonomy or a source explicitly adopts that convention.

children.title: Censored Feedback
children.top_down_role: Sequential feedback affected by missing or suppressed disclosures.

knowledge_statements.title: Censored Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential oracle feedback that may be permanently suppressed rather than merely delayed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm issue a query \(q_t\) at each round \(t\in\mathbb N\), and let \(Y_t\) denote the response generated by the underlying oracle. A censored-feedback protocol associates with each query an observation indicator \(M_t\in\{0,1\}\). The algorithm observes \(Y_t\) only if \(M_t=1\); if \(M_t=0\), it receives a censoring symbol \(\bot\) and never subsequently receives \(Y_t\). The censoring mechanism is specified by the conditional law of \(M_t\) given the history, query, and response; censoring is noninformative when \(M_t\) is conditionally independent of \(Y_t\) given the observable history and \(q_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Censored feedback permanently hides selected oracle responses; noninformative censoring makes the hiding decision independent of the hidden response after conditioning on known history and the query.
assumptions_latex: \(q_t\) is measurable with respect to the information available before round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_t=M_tY_t+(1-M_t)\bot\), with \(M_t=0\) implying that \(Y_t\) is never revealed.

notation.meaning: indicator that the response to query t is observed
censoring symbol carrying no response value

review_flags: exact feedback convention lacks a supplied supporting locator
distinction between censoring and infinite delay should be source-checked

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal container, but no cited source fixes the distinction between permanent censoring and infinite delay or supports the stated conditional-independence convention. The displayed arithmetic expression involving the nonnumeric symbol \(\bot\) should eventually be written piecewise.

children.title: Joint Latency–Missingness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feedback settings where latency interacts with incomplete observation.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Latency–Missingness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential feedback with both random arrival times and permanently missing responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a query issued at round \(t\), let \(Y_t\) be its generated oracle response, \(M_t\in\{0,1\}\) its eventual-observation indicator, and \(D_t\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\) its latency. The response is revealed at round \(t+D_t\) exactly when \(M_t=1\) and \(D_t<\infty\); otherwise it is permanently missing. A joint latency–missingness regime is the conditional law of \((M_t,D_t)\) given the pre-query history, \(q_t\), and possibly \(Y_t\). It is noninformative when \((M_t,D_t)\) is conditionally independent of \(Y_t\) given the observable pre-query history and \(q_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each response has both an eventual-observation indicator and a delay; the joint law may depend on history, the query, and, under informative missingness, the response itself.
assumptions_latex: \(q_t\) is chosen from information revealed strictly before round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y_t\) enters the observed filtration at time \(t+D_t\) if and only if \(M_t=1\) and \(D_t<\infty\).

notation.meaning: latency of the response generated at round t

review_flags: no supplied locator supports the joint protocol
whether missingness is encoded separately from infinite delay is convention-dependent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the joint-regime container, but the separate use of \(M_t\) and \(D_t=\infty\), the timing filtration, and the noninformative condition are convention-dependent and unsupported by a cited locator.

children.title: Separation–Optimization Equivalences
children.top_down_role: Forward and reverse reductions between separation and optimization access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation–Optimization Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time weak-oracle equivalence for a bounded, well-rounded convex body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact convex set for which rational data \(a_0\in\mathbb Q^d\) and \(0<r\le R\) satisfy \(B(a_0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(a_0,R)\). In the rational bit model, a weak separation oracle for \(K\) and a weak linear-optimization oracle for \(K\) simulate one another with a number of oracle calls and arithmetic operations polynomial in \(d\), the input encoding length, \(\log(R/r)\), and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). The simulated answers have tolerance polynomially related to the requested accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a well-bounded convex body with known rounding data, weak separation and weak linear optimization are mutually reducible in polynomial time and polynomial precision.
assumptions_latex: \(B(a_0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(a_0,R)\) with known rational \(a_0,r,R\).
Oracle inputs and tolerances use rational binary encoding.
\(\varepsilon>0\) is the requested weak-oracle accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{WSEP}(K)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathrm{WOPT}(K)\), with polynomially controlled accuracy loss.

notation.meaning: closed Euclidean ball of center a and radius r

review_flags: classical equivalence requires an exact theorem locator
weak-oracle tolerance conventions must be aligned with the project taxonomy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the correct role and broadly matches the terminal topic, but weak separation and weak optimization have multiple nonequivalent tolerance conventions. An exact theorem locator is required to verify the mutual reductions, bit-complexity parameters, and polynomial accuracy relationship.

children.title: Membership–Separation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Recovery of separating information from membership under rounding and approximation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership–Separation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized weak separation from weak membership under quantitative rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body satisfying \(B(a_0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(a_0,R)\), with known \(a_0,r,R\). Given weak membership access that distinguishes points in the inner erosion \(K_{-\eta}\) from points outside the outer expansion \(K_{+\eta}\), weak separation at accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) can be implemented by a randomized algorithm with failure probability at most \(\delta\). Its membership-query count and arithmetic cost are polynomial in \(d\), \(\log(R/r)\), \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), and \(\log(1/\delta)\), provided \(\eta\) is chosen inverse-polynomially relative to these parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quantitatively well-rounded convex body, sufficiently accurate weak membership access yields weak separation through a randomized polynomial-time reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(B(a_0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(a_0,R)\) with known rounding data.
Weak membership uses erosion-expansion tolerance \(\eta>0\).
The permitted reduction failure probability satisfies \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{WMEM}_{\eta}(K)\) implements \(\mathrm{WSEP}_{\varepsilon}(K)\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\) at polynomial cost.

notation.meaning: points at Euclidean distance at most eta from K
points whose eta-ball is contained in K

review_flags: precise membership-to-separation theorem and tolerance polynomial need a source
randomization and geometric regularity conventions vary across references

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the reduction topic, but the precise randomized membership-to-separation result cannot be validated without a source. In particular, the required relationship among \(\eta\), \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), and the rounding parameters is stated only qualitatively.

children.title: Validity–Optimization Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual relationships between inequality validation and directional optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Validity–Optimization Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between support-function evaluation and validation of linear upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty compact convex set \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\), define its support function by \(h_K(c)=\max_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle\). A validity query \((c,\gamma)\) asks whether \(\langle c,x\rangle\le\gamma\) for every \(x\in K\). Therefore
\[\langle c,x\rangle\le\gamma\ \text{for all }x\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_K(c)\le\gamma.\]
Consequently, exact directional optimization evaluates the threshold governing validity, while exact validity access determines \(h_K(c)\) by threshold search when finite certified bounds on \(h_K(c)\) and an exact-real or prescribed-precision comparison model are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear inequality is valid on a compact convex set exactly when its right-hand side dominates the set’s support value in that direction.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and compact.
\(c\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in K,\ \langle c,x\rangle\le\gamma\) if and only if \(\max_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle\le\gamma\).

notation.meaning: candidate upper bound in a validity query

review_flags: standard identity is unambiguous but no supplied locator addresses geometric validity oracles
computational reverse reduction depends on the numerical comparison model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-function identity is mathematically correct and the duality kind fits the leaf. However, no cited locator supports the oracle interpretation, and the claim that validity access determines the support value depends materially on the numerical model, certified bounds, and stopping precision.

children.title: Equivalence-Strength Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation and precision conditions separating approximate convex-body equivalences from exact encoded results.

children.title: Weak Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximate equivalence classifications under limited representation or precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle equivalence allowing tolerances, failure probability, and controlled geometric ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two oracle classes \(\mathcal O_1\) and \(\mathcal O_2\) are weakly polynomially equivalent on an instance class \(\mathcal K\) if, for each requested tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), every valid \(\varepsilon\)-weak query to either oracle can be answered using the other oracle at tolerance \(\eta\), where both \(\eta^{-1}\) and the simulation cost are bounded polynomially in the instance encoding length and \(\varepsilon^{-1}\). Randomized simulations must additionally succeed with probability at least \(1-\delta\) at cost polynomial in \(\log(1/\delta)\). No answer is required inside the ambiguity region prescribed by the weak-oracle convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak equivalence permits approximate answers and controlled ambiguity, provided simulations work both ways with polynomial cost, polynomial precision loss, and controlled failure probability.
assumptions_latex: Instances belong to a fixed encoded class \(\mathcal K\).
Each weak oracle has an explicitly specified tolerance and ambiguity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_1\equiv_{\mathrm{wpoly}}\mathcal O_2\) when weak polynomial reductions exist in both directions.

notation.meaning: accuracy requested from the simulating oracle

review_flags: project-specific weak-equivalence convention lacks a supplied source
encoding dependence and ambiguity regions require normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the weak-equivalence container, but it introduces a project-specific equivalence convention without a source. The weak-query answer relation, ambiguity region, encoding size, precision transfer, and randomized success convention must be normalized against an inspectable reference.

children.title: Strong Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact equivalence classifications under sufficiently explicit encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, representation-preserving mutual simulation without tolerance ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two exact oracle classes \(\mathcal O_1\) and \(\mathcal O_2\) are strongly polynomially equivalent on an encoded instance class \(\mathcal K\) if deterministic reductions exist in both directions such that every admissible query receives an exact valid answer, each reduction uses polynomially many oracle calls and arithmetic or bit operations, and all generated queries and returned certificates have polynomial encoding length. Unlike weak equivalence, the definition permits neither an unresolved tolerance band nor a positive probability of an incorrect answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong equivalence requires deterministic, exact, polynomial-cost simulations in both directions, with polynomial-size queries and certificates and no ambiguity region.
assumptions_latex: Instances, queries, and oracle answers have fixed finite encodings.
The exact answer relation for each oracle is specified on every admissible query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_1\equiv_{\mathrm{spoly}}\mathcal O_2\) precisely when exact polynomial reductions exist in both directions.
review_flags: strong equivalence is taxonomy-dependent and lacks a supplied locator
exact-real versus rational bit-model conventions must be fixed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the strong-equivalence container, but the exact-answer and polynomial-cost requirements depend on whether the setting is a rational bit model, an arithmetic model, or exact-real computation. No cited locator establishes the selected convention.

children.title: Precision-Driven Equivalence Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in equivalence strength caused by representation or precision requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Driven Equivalence Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How accuracy requirements determine whether an oracle reduction remains polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a reduction answering an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate query to \(\mathcal O_2\) by querying \(\mathcal O_1\) at precision \(\eta(\varepsilon,L)\), where \(L\) is the instance encoding length. In the bit model, the reduction preserves polynomial equivalence when its query count, arithmetic cost, and required precision length \(\log(1/\eta(\varepsilon,L))\) are polynomial in \(L+\log(1/\varepsilon)\). If instead \(\log(1/\eta)\) grows superpolynomially in that input length, the same mathematical simulation does not establish polynomial oracle equivalence. Exact equivalence is obtained only when the limiting exact-answer relation is computable with finite, polynomially encoded information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate simulation is polynomial only when its required oracle precision has polynomial bit length; excessive precision demand can destroy computational equivalence.
assumptions_latex: Accuracy parameters are represented in binary.
Oracle cost includes the bit length of requested precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(1/\eta(\varepsilon,L))\le \operatorname{poly}(L+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) is necessary for the stated simulation to certify polynomial equivalence.

notation.meaning: precision required from the simulating oracle

review_flags: complexity-model boundary is standard but no supplied source supports this formulation
exact-transition clause depends on answer encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly highlights precision bit length as part of polynomial simulation cost and fits the terminal container. A source is still required because the exact-transition clause and the claimed computational boundary depend on the oracle-answer encoding and cost model.

children.title: Differential-Information Reductions
children.top_down_role: Simulation of derivative information from weaker local evaluations.

children.title: First-Order Information from Values
children.top_down_role: Derivative-surrogate access constructed from multiple function evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Information from Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate central differences as approximate gradient information for smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\), with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient there. For \(h>0\), define
\[g_h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i)}{2h}e_i.\]
Then \(g_h(x)\) is recoverable from \(2d\) value-oracle calls and satisfies the coordinatewise bound \(\lvert (g_h(x))_i-\partial_i f(x)\rvert\le Lh/2\). Consequently, \(\lVert g_h(x)-\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\le \sqrt d\,Lh/2\). Thus value access simulates approximate first-order access, with query and accuracy losses depending on dimension and the finite-difference radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function with Lipschitz gradient, two value evaluations per coordinate produce a central-difference gradient estimate whose Euclidean bias is at most square-root-d times Lh/2.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on every segment \([x-he_i,x+he_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert g_h(x)-\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\le \sqrt d\,Lh/2\) using \(2d\) function values.
review_flags: standard finite-difference estimate lacks a supplied supporting locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the terminal topic, and the central-difference bounds follow under the stated segmentwise \(L\)-Lipschitz-gradient assumption. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied for this nontrivial estimate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Difference Derivative Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative surrogates constructed from nearby function values, without an asserted finite-step accuracy rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function $f$ defined at $x$ and $x+\epsilon d$, define the finite-difference quotient $Q_\epsilon(x;d)=\bigl(f(x+\epsilon d)-f(x)\bigr)/\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\ne0$. This quotient is a value-based surrogate for the directional derivative. If $D f(x)[d]$ exists, then $\lim_{\epsilon\to0}Q_\epsilon(x;d)=D f(x)[d]$. Taking $d=e_i$ gives the corresponding coordinate finite-difference surrogate for $\partial f/\partial x_i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite difference perturbs the variables by a nonzero finite step and divides the resulting function-value change by the step. If the relevant directional derivative exists, these quotients converge to it as the step tends to zero; coordinate perturbations give partial-derivative surrogates.
assumptions_latex: f(x)\text{ and }f(x+\epsilon d)\text{ are defined}
\epsilon\ne0
D f(x)[d]\text{ exists for the stated limiting conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_\epsilon(x;d)=\frac{f(x+\epsilon d)-f(x)}{\epsilon},\qquad \lim_{\epsilon\to0}Q_\epsilon(x;d)=D f(x)[d]\ \text{when the derivative exists}
