children.title: Directional-to-Full Information Conversion
children.top_down_role: Reconstruction of richer local information from directional queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional-to-Full Information Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gradient reconstruction from directional derivatives along a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a point \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), a differentiable function \(f\), and linearly independent directions \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\). Query the directional-derivative oracle for \(y_i=f'(x;v_i)=\langle
abla f(x),v_iangle\), form the matrix \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_d]\), and output
\[g=V^{-\mathsf T}y,\qquad y=(y_1,\ldots,y_d)^{\mathsf T}.\]
Then \(V^{\mathsf T}g=y=V^{\mathsf T}
abla f(x)\), so \(g=
abla f(x)\). With noisy answers \(\widetilde y=y+e\), the reconstructed error obeys \(\lVert V^{-\mathsf T}eVert_2\le \lVert V^{-\mathsf T}Vert_2\lVert eVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional derivatives in d linearly independent directions determine the full gradient by solving a linear system; noise is amplified by the basis conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\).
\(V\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(d\) directional queries, the output is \(g=\nabla f(x)\); under additive error \(e\), its error is \(V^{-\mathsf T}e\).

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the queried directions

review_flags: elementary reconstruction is unambiguous but no supplied locator supports it

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is appropriate, and the reconstruction and noise-amplification formulas are internally correct for a nonsingular direction matrix. No supporting source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Limited-to-Full Feedback Reductions
children.top_down_role: Estimator-mediated simulation of richer feedback from action-local observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited-to-Full Feedback Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Importance weighting reconstructs a full loss vector from one sampled coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell_t\in\mathbb R^d\) be an arbitrary loss vector and let an action \(I_t\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\) be sampled conditionally on the history with probabilities \(p_{t,i}>0\). After observing only \(\ell_{t,I_t}\), define
\[\widehat\ell_{t,i}=\frac{\ell_{t,I_t}\mathbf 1\{I_t=i\}}{p_{t,i}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d.\]
Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat\ell_t\mid\ell_t,p_t]=\ell_t\), so the limited observation simulates unbiased full-vector feedback. Moreover, \(\mathbb E[\lVert\widehat\ell_t\rVert_2^2\mid\ell_t,p_t]=\sum_{i=1}^d\ell_{t,i}^2/p_{t,i}\), displaying the variance penalty caused by small sampling probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One observed coordinate yields an unbiased estimate of the full loss vector through inverse-probability weighting, but rare actions create large second moments.
assumptions_latex: \(p_{t,i}>0\) for every coordinate that may have nonzero loss.
Conditional on \(p_t\) and \(\ell_t\), \(I_t\) has distribution \(p_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat\ell_t\mid\ell_t,p_t]=\ell_t\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert\widehat\ell_t\rVert_2^2\mid\ell_t,p_t]=\sum_i\ell_{t,i}^2/p_{t,i}\).

notation.meaning: conditional probability of sampling coordinate i

review_flags: standard estimator identity lacks a supplied supporting locator
record selects finite-action loss feedback as the local limited-feedback model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the reduction topic, and both conditional-moment identities are correct under the stated sampling law. A cited locator is required, especially because the broad terminal container has been specialized to finite-action coordinate feedback.

children.title: Simulation-Loss Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Information penalties introduced when weaker access simulates stronger access.

children.title: Dimension-Induced Losses
children.top_down_role: Information penalties attributable to ambient or effective dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Induced Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension dependence of one-point value-to-gradient simulation for a sufficiently regular function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta\overline{B}(0,1)\), where \(\delta>0\), and suppose \(\lvert f(z)\rvert\le M\) for every \(z\in x+\delta\mathbb S^{d-1}\). Draw \(u\) uniformly from \(\mathbb S^{d-1}\) and define \(g=(d/\delta)f(x+\delta u)u\). For the ball-smoothed function \(f_\delta(x)=\mathbb E_{v\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B(0,1))}[f(x+\delta v)]\), the spherical smoothing identity gives \(\mathbb E[g]=\nabla f_\delta(x)\). Moreover, \[\mathbb E\lVert g\rVert_2^2=\frac{d^2}{\delta^2}\mathbb E[f(x+\delta u)^2]\le\frac{d^2M^2}{\delta^2}.\] Thus this one-query estimator has an explicit quadratic dimension factor in its second-moment bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable function, the standard one-point spherical estimator is unbiased for the gradient of the ball-smoothed function and has second moment at most d-squared times M-squared divided by the smoothing radius squared.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x+\delta\overline{B}(0,1)\).
\(u\) is uniformly distributed on \(\mathbb S^{d-1}\).
\(\lvert f(x+\delta u)\rvert\le M\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g]=\nabla f_\delta(x)\) and \(\mathbb E\lVert g\rVert_2^2\le d^2M^2/\delta^2\).

notation.meaning: uniform-ball smoothing of f at radius delta

review_flags: spherical smoothing identity requires a supporting source locator
regularity strengthened to justify the smoothing identity
dimension loss depends on the chosen estimator and feedback normalization

children.title: Noise-Induced Losses
children.top_down_role: Information penalties attributable to noisy oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Induced Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaging loss for simulating an accurate deterministic first-order oracle from unbiased noisy responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stochastic oracle return \(G(x,\xi)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]=g(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}\|G(x,\xi)-g(x)\|^2\leq \sigma^2\). For \(m\) conditionally independent calls at the same point, define \(\bar G_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^m G(x,\xi_j)\). Then \[\mathbb{E}\|\bar G_m(x)-g(x)\|^2\leq \frac{\sigma^2}{m}.\] Hence root-mean-square simulation error at most \(\delta>0\) is guaranteed by \(m\geq \lceil\sigma^2/\delta^2\rceil\) noisy calls per simulated deterministic-oracle call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent averaging reduces gradient mean-square error by a factor of the sample count, costing order σ²/δ² noisy calls for RMS accuracy δ.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]=g(x)\).
\(\mathbb{E}\|G(x,\xi)-g(x)\|^2\leq\sigma^2\).
The \(m\) samples are conditionally independent given \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\bar G_m(x)-g(x)\|^2\leq\sigma^2/m\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The averaging bound and resulting call count are mathematically standard and fit the complexity-bound container, but no inspectable source supports the variance-reduction claim.

children.title: Smoothing-Induced Losses
children.top_down_role: Information penalties introduced by smoothing-based simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothing-Induced Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias and scale loss under Gaussian smoothing of a Lipschitz convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\), and define \(f_\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu Z)]\) for \(\mu>0\). Then \(f_\mu\) is convex and differentiable, and \[0\leq f_\mu(x)-f(x)\leq L\mu\,\mathbb{E}\|Z\|\leq L\mu\sqrt d.\] Thus ensuring uniform smoothing bias at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\mu\leq\varepsilon/(L\sqrt d)\), exhibiting the dimension-dependent scale loss of this reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing makes a convex Lipschitz objective differentiable but introduces bias at most Lμ√d, forcing a dimension-dependent smoothing radius.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).
\(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) and \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq f_\mu(x)-f(x)\leq L\mu\sqrt d\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

notation.meaning: standard Gaussian vector in d dimensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian-smoothing bias statement is precise and fits the loss container, but its differentiability and uniform bias claims lack an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Compounded Simulation Penalties
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiple conversion losses accumulate.

knowledge_statements.title: Compounded Simulation Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting rule for sequential oracle reductions with per-call cost bounds and additive simulation-error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb{N}\) be an upper bound on the number of ideal-oracle calls made by an algorithm. For each simulated call \(t\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}\), suppose the implementation uses \(n_t\) primitive calls with \(0\leq n_t\leq m_t\), where \(m_t\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and suppose its contribution to a deterministic additive error bound is at most \(e_t\geq0\). Then the actual primitive-call count \(N_{\mathrm{act}}\) and accumulated simulation contribution \(E\) satisfy \[N_{\mathrm{act}}=\sum_{t=1}^{Q}n_t\leq\sum_{t=1}^{Q}m_t,\qquad E\leq\sum_{t=1}^{Q}e_t.\] In particular, uniform bounds \(m_t\leq m\) and \(e_t\leq e\) imply \(N_{\mathrm{act}}\leq Qm\) and \(E\leq Qe\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential oracle simulation adds primitive-query costs and, when the analysis supplies additive per-call error bounds, adds those error contributions. Uniform per-call bounds m and e therefore give total bounds Qm and Qe.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{N}\) bounds the number of ideal-oracle calls.
For every \(t\), the actual primitive-call count satisfies \(0\leq n_t\leq m_t\) with \(m_t\in\mathbb{N}_0\).
The deterministic analysis bounds the accumulated simulation contribution by the sum of nonnegative per-call bounds \(e_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{act}}\leq\sum_{t=1}^{Q}m_t\) and \(E\leq\sum_{t=1}^{Q}e_t\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the number of ideal-oracle calls
actual primitive-call count used for simulated call t
upper bound on the primitive-call count for simulated call t
additive error bound assigned to simulated call t
actual total number of primitive calls

children.title: Projection Access

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean projection oracle for a nonempty closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A Euclidean projection oracle accepts \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and returns the unique point \[P_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\|x-y\|_2^2.\] Exact projection access means that one oracle call returns this minimizer, rather than an approximate feasible point or merely a separating direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection oracle returns the unique feasible point nearest to a query point in Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The distance is induced by \(\|\cdot\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2\) is uniquely defined.

children.title: Proximal Access
children.top_down_role: Proximal access for composite problem structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaled proximal oracle for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. For \(\lambda>0\), a proximal oracle accepts \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and returns the unique point \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{h(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|_2^2\right\}.\] Proximal access permits queries in both \(y\) and the positive scale \(\lambda\); fixed-scale access is the restriction to one prescribed value of \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal oracle exactly minimizes the function plus a scaled quadratic centered at the query point.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(y)\) exists and is unique for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Optimization Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear minimization oracle over a compact convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and compact. A linear-optimization oracle accepts a direction \(c\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and returns some point \[s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.\] The returned minimizer need not be unique. Exact linear-optimization access requires an attaining minimizer; an oracle returning only the optimal value or an approximately minimizing point is a different interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-optimization oracle returns a feasible point minimizing a supplied linear objective; the answer may be nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and compact.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\) exists.

children.title: Interface Strength Comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Interface Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction from projection to proximal access and the resulting one-call interface dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\iota_C(x)=0\) when \(x\in C\) and \(\iota_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then, for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\lambda>0\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\iota_C}(y)=P_C(y).\] Consequently, a proximal oracle that accepts the indicator of \(C\) simulates one exact projection query with one proximal query. This comparison does not by itself give a one-call reduction between projection access and linear-optimization access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal access subsumes Euclidean projection through the set indicator; no analogous one-call equivalence with linear optimization follows.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\iota_C}=P_C\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled indicator

children.title: Full First-Order Access

knowledge_statements.title: Full First-Order Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle access returning the complete function value and full subgradient or gradient at each query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex on a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A full first-order oracle accepts \(x\in C\) and returns \((f(x),g(x))\), where \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the response is \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\). Thus one query exposes all \(d\) coordinates of a valid first-order vector at the same point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full first-order query returns the objective value and an entire subgradient, or the full gradient when differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\) at queried points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle response is \((f(x),g(x))\) with \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.title: Component First-Order Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed first-order access for a finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) on a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), with each \(f_i\) convex. A component first-order oracle accepts \((x,i)\in C\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and returns \((f_i(x),g_i(x))\), where \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\). When every component is differentiable, it returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\). A single component query need not reveal \(f(x)\) or a subgradient of the full average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component oracle returns value and first-order information for one indexed term of a finite-sum objective.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(\partial f_i(x)\neq\varnothing\) at queried points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The response to \((x,i)\) is \((f_i(x),g_i(x))\) with \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\).

children.title: Coordinate First-Order Access
children.top_down_role: First-order information restricted to selected variables or directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate First-Order Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order access restricted to one coordinate of a gradient or selected subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable on an open convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A coordinate first-order oracle accepts \((x,j)\in C\times\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and returns \((f(x),\partial_j f(x))\), or only \(\partial_j f(x)\) when values are excluded by convention. One call reveals a single coordinate of \(\nabla f(x)\); obtaining the full gradient by direct coordinate queries requires at most \(d\) calls at the same point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate oracle reveals one selected partial derivative; querying every coordinate reconstructs the full gradient in at most d calls.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is open and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The derivative response is \(\partial_j f(x)=\langle\nabla f(x),e_j\rangle\).

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Reuse Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic reconstruction and reuse relations among full, component, and coordinate first-order interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a fixed point \(x\), one deterministic full-gradient response \(g=
abla f(x)\) answers every subsequent coordinate query through \(g_j=\langle g,e_jangle\). Conversely, \(d\) deterministic coordinate responses at that same point reconstruct \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_d)\). For a differentiable finite sum \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), all \(n\) component-gradient responses at the same point reconstruct \[
abla f(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(x).\] These identities justify caching only when the queried point and deterministic oracle instance are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full gradients answer all coordinate queries, while all coordinates or all finite-sum components reconstruct full information at a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: All responses are deterministic and evaluated at the same point \(x\).
The relevant objectives are differentiable.
For components, \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
abla f(x)=(\partial_1f(x),\ldots,\partial_df(x))\) and \(
abla f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(x)\).

children.title: Sampling-Reuse Access Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction between population sampling and reusable indexed components.

children.title: Fresh-Sample Access
children.top_down_role: Population access through newly drawn observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Sample Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic first-order oracle model in which each adaptive query uses a new sample whose conditional law is independent of the pre-query history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex, let \(F(\cdot,\xi)\) be a random objective on \(C\), and define \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\). Let \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\) denote the history available before query \(t\), and require the query point \(x_t\in C\) to be \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\)-measurable. Under fresh-sample first-order access, the oracle draws \(\xi_t\) so that \[\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=\mathcal L(\xi)\] and returns \((F(x_t,\xi_t),G(x_t,\xi_t))\), where \[\mathbb{E}[G(x_t,\xi_t)\mid\mathcal H_{t-1}]=g(x_t)\in\partial f(x_t).\] The interface exposes neither a persistent sample index nor an operation for reevaluating the realized sample \(\xi_t\) at another point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Before each adaptive query, the oracle draws a new sample with the original distribution independently of the complete prior history and returns an unbiased first-order response. The realized sample has no persistent index and cannot be reevaluated later through this interface.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex and \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\) is well defined.
\(x_t\) is \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\)-measurable.
\(\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=\mathcal L(\xi)\).
\(\mathbb{E}[G(x_t,\xi_t)\mid\mathcal H_{t-1}]=g(x_t)\in\partial f(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi_t\) has the base sample law conditionally on \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\), and the returned first-order response has conditional mean \(g(x_t)\in\partial f(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: complete information available before query t
fresh random sample drawn for query t
sample first-order response at the adaptive query point
conditional mean first-order response and a subgradient of the population objective

children.title: Finite-Sum Access
children.top_down_role: Reusable access to indexed objective components.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent indexed access to components of a finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a query domain and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), where the labeled components \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\) remain fixed throughout the computation. A finite-sum oracle accepts a chosen pair \((i,x)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\times X\) and returns an allowed local response \(O_i(x)\), such as \(f_i(x)\), a subgradient in \(\partial f_i(x)\), or both. The algorithm may choose indices adaptively and may query the same label repeatedly, thereby reusing information about a persistent component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum access permits adaptive queries to fixed, labeled component functions, including repeated queries to the same component at different points.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is finite and known to the querying algorithm.
The component labels and functions remain persistent across oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O_{\mathrm{fs}}(i,x)=O_i(x)\) may be queried repeatedly for any chosen \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

notation.meaning: Allowed response from component i at x.

review_flags: A source specifically formalizing persistent indexed finite-sum oracle access is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Finite-Sum Access leaf and consistently distinguishes persistent indexed components from fresh sampling, but no source with an inspectable locator supports this particular oracle model, including adaptive index choice and repeated access to a fixed component.

children.title: Resampling–Reuse Boundary
children.top_down_role: Information distinctions between disposable samples and revisitable components.

knowledge_statements.title: Resampling–Reuse Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes independent fresh sampling from controlled reuse of persistent component identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stochastic response family \(O(x,\xi)\), fresh-sample access requires the oracle to draw \(\xi_t\) independently from a fixed distribution \(P\) at every call and return only \(O(x_t,\xi_t)\). Reuse access instead exposes a persistent label or retained realization and permits a later query to request \(O(x_s,\xi_t)\) for a previously observed \(\xi_t\). The resampling–reuse boundary is crossed exactly when the algorithm can force two or more responses to share the same latent realization; coincidental equality of independent samples does not constitute controlled reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse begins when an algorithm can deliberately query one retained latent component again; independent redraws remain fresh-sample access even if values coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is fixed during the interaction.
Under fresh sampling, \(\xi_t\) is independent of the preceding transcript conditional on \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Controlled reuse holds iff the algorithm can require \(\xi_s=\xi_t\) for selected distinct calls \(s\ne t\).

notation.meaning: Latent realization used at call t.
Oracle response at x under latent realization xi.

review_flags: The exact taxonomy boundary is mathematically explicit but lacks a supplied supporting oracle-model source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the boundary leaf, but the exact iff characterization of reuse by enforceable equality of latent realizations is source-dependent and currently uncited. A source must also confirm whether retained realizations, persistent labels, and repeated component queries are treated as equivalent forms of reuse.

children.title: Local-Global Statistical Access Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Comparative information strength of local random responses and reusable global statistical information.

children.title: Local Stochastic Access
children.top_down_role: Random responses tied to locally selected query points.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Stochastic Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fresh stochastic information evaluated only at the current query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb{R}\) be measurable and define \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\). A local stochastic first-order oracle, queried at \(x_t\in X\), draws a fresh \(\xi_t\sim P\) and returns \((F(x_t,\xi_t),G(x_t,\xi_t))\), or an allowed subset thereof, where \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]\in\partial f(x)\) whenever the expectation exists. The call reveals neither the sampled function away from \(x_t\) nor a reusable representation of \(\xi_t\); subsequent calls use conditionally independent fresh draws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local stochastic oracle supplies a fresh random value or first-order estimate only at the queried point, without revealing the sampled function globally.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\cdot,\xi)\) is measurable for \(P\)-almost every \(\xi\).
The displayed expectations exist at every admissible query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]\in\partial f(x)\), while one call exposes information only at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Sampling distribution of the latent variable.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

review_flags: Confirm that the cited section uses fresh local samples and the stated unbiasedness convention.

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Stochastic forward-backward method p. 162

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition fits Local Stochastic Access, but the cited stochastic forward-backward section has not been inspected sufficiently to confirm fresh conditional independence, point-local disclosure, or the stated subgradient-unbiasedness convention. The formulation also needs a declared measurable-space structure and conditions ensuring that the expected response belongs to the chosen subdifferential of f; mere existence of the expectation is insufficient.

children.title: Global Statistical Access
children.top_down_role: Reusable statistical information with global problem relevance.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Statistical Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sampled realization exposes a function or data object usable at multiple query points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\). A global statistical oracle call draws \(\xi\sim P\) and returns a representation \(R_\xi\) from which the algorithm can evaluate an allowed response \(O(x,\xi)\) at every \(x\in X\), without drawing a new latent realization for each evaluation. Thus one call exposes the cross-point coupling induced by the same \(\xi\); evaluations \(O(x,\xi)\) and \(O(y,\xi)\) may be jointly inspected for adaptively selected \(x,y\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global statistical access reveals a sampled function or reusable data realization, allowing multiple evaluations coupled through the same sample.
assumptions_latex: A representation \(R_\xi\) determines every permitted response \(O(x,\xi)\).
The access model charges drawing \(R_\xi\) separately from any declared evaluation costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\xi\) permits jointly coupled evaluations \(\{O(x,\xi):x\in X\}\) for one retained \(\xi\).

notation.meaning: Reusable representation of a sampled realization.
Permitted response derived from that realization.

review_flags: A source distinguishing reusable sampled-function access from pointwise stochastic-oracle access is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the Global Statistical Access leaf and clearly describes reusable cross-point coupling, but no cited source formalizes this sampled-function or reusable-realization oracle, its representation R_xi, or the separation between sampling and evaluation costs.

children.title: Local-to-Global Information Gaps
children.top_down_role: Comparative limits separating local random access from global statistical access.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Information Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two random-function laws with identical local marginals but distinguishable global coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{-1,1\}\) and let \(Z\) be uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\). Under model \(A\), set \(F_A(-1)=Z\) and \(F_A(1)=Z\); under model \(B\), set \(F_B(-1)=Z\) and \(F_B(1)=-Z\). At either fixed \(x\in X\), both models return the same uniform marginal distribution, so fresh local observations at one point per independent realization have identical laws. A global sample reveals both values and distinguishes the models with certainty because \(F_A(-1)F_A(1)=1\), whereas \(F_B(-1)F_B(1)=-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical pointwise marginals can conceal opposite cross-point correlations; a reusable global sample detects the difference while fresh local samples cannot.
assumptions_latex: Each fresh local call uses an independent copy of \(Z\).
A global call exposes both coordinates generated by the same copy of \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local marginals coincide, but \(F_A(-1)F_A(1)=1\ne-1=F_B(-1)F_B(1)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Random functions under the two statistical models.

review_flags: The counterexample is directly checkable, but a source for its use as an oracle-separation example is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically consistent and its content kind is appropriate for the information-gap leaf: the pointwise marginals agree while the within-realization products differ. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale supporting its use as an oracle-access separation example.

children.title: Heterogeneous Component Oracles
children.top_down_role: Composite instances whose terms expose different access types.

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Component Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite objectives whose components have distinct response types or query costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_j f_j(x)\) on a common domain \(X\), with \(w_j\ge0\). A heterogeneous component-oracle model assigns to each component \(j\) an oracle \(O_j\), response space \(Y_j\), and positive call cost \(c_j\), where \(O_j(x)\in Y_j\) may encode a value, derivative, proximal point, stochastic estimate, or another declared response. An algorithm may query the component oracles independently, and its resource usage is the vector \((N_1,\ldots,N_m)\) together with weighted cost \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_jN_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component of a composite objective may expose a different oracle response and cost, so resource use is recorded component by component.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(w_j\ge0\), and \(c_j>0\) for every \(j\).
All component functions share the query domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle usage is represented by \(N\in\mathbb{N}_0^m\) and total declared cost \(C(N)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_jN_j\).

notation.meaning: Number of calls to component oracle j.
Cost of one call to component oracle j.

source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods
source_refs.locator: 2.3 Sum of Two Functions p. 61

A source directly supporting those oracle-model claims is required.

children.title: Oracle Cost-Tier Splitting
children.top_down_role: Separate treatment of oracle families with materially different evaluation costs.

children.title: Expensive Oracle Families
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces with dominant evaluation or implementation cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Oracle Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost tier containing oracle families above a declared call-cost threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given oracle families \(O_1,\ldots,O_m\) with positive per-call costs \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) and a declared threshold \(\tau>0\), the expensive tier is \(E_\tau=\{j:c_j>\tau\}\). For a transcript containing \(N_j\) calls to family \(j\), expensive-tier usage is recorded both as the count vector \((N_j)_{j\in E_\tau}\) and as the cost \(C_E=\sum_{j\in E_\tau}c_jN_j\). The classification is relative to the specified cost model and threshold; it is not an intrinsic property of an oracle's mathematical response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expensive oracle family has per-call cost above a declared threshold, and its calls and weighted cost are accounted for separately.
assumptions_latex: \(c_j>0\) is fixed for every oracle family.
The threshold \(\tau>0\) and charging convention are declared before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_\tau=\{j:c_j>\tau\}\) and \(C_E=\sum_{j\in E_\tau}c_jN_j\).

notation.meaning: Index set of expensive oracle families.
Number of calls to family j.

review_flags: The threshold-based tier convention requires a supporting heterogeneous-cost oracle reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold-relative definition is internally coherent and fits the Expensive Oracle Families leaf, but the threshold convention and separate count-and-cost accounting are uncited. Because expensive versus cheap is not an intrinsic mathematical classification, the declared convention requires explicit source support or an admissible standard-field rationale.

children.title: Cheap Oracle Families
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces suitable for comparatively frequent use.

knowledge_statements.title: Cheap Oracle Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost tier containing oracle families at or below a declared call-cost threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given oracle families \(O_1,\ldots,O_m\) with positive per-call costs \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) and a declared threshold \(\tau>0\), the cheap tier is \(H_\tau=\{j:c_j\le\tau\}\). For a transcript containing \(N_j\) calls to family \(j\), cheap-tier usage is recorded as \((N_j)_{j\in H_\tau}\) and \(C_H=\sum_{j\in H_\tau}c_jN_j\). Together with the strict expensive tier, this convention partitions all oracle families without overlap; changing \(\tau\) may change the classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cheap oracle family has per-call cost no greater than a declared threshold, with its calls and weighted cost tracked separately.
assumptions_latex: \(c_j>0\) is fixed for every oracle family.
The same threshold \(\tau\) is used for the cheap and expensive tiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_\tau=\{j:c_j\le\tau\}\), \(H_\tau\cap E_\tau=\varnothing\), and \(H_\tau\cup E_\tau=\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

notation.meaning: Index set of cheap oracle families.
Total charged cost of cheap-tier calls.

review_flags: The threshold-based tier convention requires a supporting heterogeneous-cost oracle reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is consistent with the complementary expensive tier and correctly produces a partition at the declared threshold, but no source supports this particular cheap-tier convention or its resource accounting. The dependency on the uncited expensive-tier definition further prevents acceptance.

children.title: Cost-Aware Oracle Allocation
children.top_down_role: Query-budget organization across materially different oracle costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Aware Oracle Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allocates heterogeneous oracle calls by optimizing a declared error bound under a cost budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input positive costs \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\), budget \(B\ge0\), and a certified error bound \(U:\mathbb{N}_0^m\to[0,\infty]\) for call counts. Initialize \(N=0\). While some coordinate increment is affordable, choose \(j\) maximizing \((U(N)-U(N+e_j))/c_j\) among indices satisfying \(c_j\le B-\sum_k c_kN_k\), and replace \(N\) by \(N+e_j\). Stop when no increment is affordable and output \(N\) together with the remaining budget. Every chosen allocation is feasible, although this greedy rule need not globally minimize \(U\) without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly buy the affordable oracle call giving the largest certified error-bound decrease per unit cost, then return the feasible count allocation.
assumptions_latex: \(U(N)\) is finite and nonincreasing in every coordinate.
Each call has fixed cost \(c_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_jN_j\le B\).

notation.meaning: Certified upper error bound for allocation N.

review_flags: A source and structural conditions for performance guarantees of this greedy allocation rule are required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind is appropriate and the stated feasibility conclusion follows from its affordability rule, while the record properly disclaims global optimality. However, the greedy marginal-improvement-per-cost procedure is uncited, and no source or structural assumptions establish it as a recognized cost-aware oracle-allocation method for this taxonomy.

children.title: Componentwise Oracle Optimality
children.top_down_role: Optimality comparisons requiring each oracle count to be evaluated independently.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Oracle Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality measured separately for every oracle-family query count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance class \(\mathcal{F}\), accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(m\) oracle families, let \(N_j^A(\varepsilon)\) be the worst-case number of family-\(j\) calls made by algorithm \(A\). Suppose \(L_j(\varepsilon)\) is a lower bound on family-\(j\) calls that remains valid even when calls to all other families are free and unlimited. Algorithm \(A\) is componentwise oracle-optimal up to constants if, for each \(j\), there exists \(C_j<\infty\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), such that \(N_j^A(\varepsilon)\le C_jL_j(\varepsilon)\) throughout the stated accuracy regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm is componentwise optimal when every separate oracle count matches its own lower bound up to a constant, even against free access to other oracles.
assumptions_latex: The success criterion and worst-case instance class \(\mathcal{F}\) are fixed.
Each \(L_j\) is proved under free unlimited access to all families other than \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_j^A(\varepsilon)=O(L_j(\varepsilon))\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

notation.meaning: Worst-case family-j query complexity of algorithm A.
Lower bound for family-j calls with other families free.

review_flags: A source for the coordinatewise lower-bound convention in heterogeneous oracle complexity is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Componentwise Oracle Optimality topic and distinguishes coordinatewise oracle counts from aggregate cost. Its strong lower-bound convention—each family-j lower bound remaining valid under free unlimited access to all other families—is nontrivial and needs a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Value-Derivative Call Units

children.title: Value Call Units
children.top_down_role: Atomic accounting for objective-value responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic resource unit for obtaining one objective value at one query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). A value-oracle call selects \(x\in X\) and returns only \(f(x)\). Its atomic resource count increases by one for each queried point, including repeated queries, unless a declared caching convention states otherwise. Derivatives, subgradients, proximal points, and values of unqueried components are not included in this unit. If an implementation returns additional information in the same physical operation, that operation must instead be charged under a separately declared bundled-call convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One value-call unit pays for obtaining the objective value at one selected point and includes no derivative information unless bundling is declared.
assumptions_latex: The query domain \(X\) and objective \(f\) are fixed during the interaction.
No bundled-response convention is active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transcript \((x_t,f(x_t))_{t=1}^{T}\) consumes exactly \(T\) value-call units.

notation.meaning: Value returned at query point x.

children.title: First-Order Call Units
children.top_down_role: Atomic accounting for gradient or subgradient responses.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic resource unit for one gradient or subgradient response at one query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be differentiable or subdifferentiable on the admissible query set. A first-order call selects \(x\in X\) and returns \(\nabla f(x)\) in the differentiable model or one specified \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\) in the nonsmooth model. Each response consumes one first-order call unit. The objective value \(f(x)\) is excluded unless the access model explicitly declares a bundled value–derivative response; repeated calls are counted separately unless caching is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One first-order call unit obtains a gradient or permitted subgradient at one point; an objective value is separate unless the model bundles it.
assumptions_latex: Every admissible query point has the derivative or subgradient required by the declared model.
No bundled value–derivative convention is active.

children.title: Bundled Value–Derivative Calls
children.top_down_role: Accounting for queries returning both value and first-order information.

knowledge_statements.title: Bundled Value–Derivative Calls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint value and first-order information counted as one atomic oracle query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and let \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) be the declared query domain. A bundled value–derivative oracle accepts \(x\in D\) and returns \(\mathcal O_f^{0,1}(x)=(f(x),G(x))\), where \(G(x)=\nabla f(x)\) at points where the oracle contract uses differentiable access, and \(G(x)\in\partial f(x)\) at points where it uses a specified subgradient convention; in the latter case the contract requires \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\). One invocation counts as one bundled call, irrespective of the two returned fields. If either field is approximate or stochastic, its accuracy guarantee or sampling law is part of the oracle specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One admissible query returning both an objective value and a specified gradient or subgradient counts as one bundled call; the query domain, approximation guarantees, and sampling conventions must be declared.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is the declared query domain.
Whenever subgradient access is used at \(x\in D\), the selected subdifferential satisfies \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{0,1}\) equals the number of joint invocations of \(\mathcal O_f^{0,1}\), not the sum of its returned fields.

notation.meaning: declared domain of admissible bundled queries

knowledge_statements.title: Component Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic finite-sum access to one indexed summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), a component first-order oracle receives an admissible pair \((x,i)\) and returns information specified for the single summand \(f_i\), such as \(f_i(x)\), \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\), or their declared stochastic or approximate versions. Each invocation at one index counts as one component call. A simultaneous request involving a set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) counts as \(|S|\) component calls unless the cost model explicitly defines a separate minibatch unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accessing one indexed summand and its declared first-order information costs one component call; a batch costs its number of components unless separately normalized.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i\) with \(n<\infty\).
The returned information for each \(f_i\) is fixed by the oracle contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{comp}}\) is the total number of queried component indices, counted with multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Call Units

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\), with coordinate projections \(P_j:X\to X_j\). One invocation for one scalar coordinate counts as one coordinate call. If \(X_j\) is a block, the invocation counts as one block-coordinate call only when the block partition and its internal-cost convention are fixed in advance.

children.title: Partial-Access Normalization
children.top_down_role: Comparable work measures across component and coordinate granularities.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Access Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of partial-query counts into declared full-access equivalents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a reference full-access operation. In an equal-cost model, suppose one full access consists of exactly \(M\in\mathbb{N}\) atomic partial calls and a computation makes \(N\in\mathbb{N}_0\) such calls. Its normalized partial-access work is \(W=N/M\) full-access equivalents. Thus \(M=n\) when the reference operation comprises one call for each component of an \(n\)-term finite sum, and \(M=d\) when it comprises one call for each scalar coordinate in dimension \(d\). In a weighted model, if the computation makes \(N\) calls with positive costs \(c_1,\ldots,c_N\) and one reference full access has cost \(C_{\mathrm{full}}>0\), define \(W=(\sum_{q=1}^{N}c_q)/C_{\mathrm{full}}\). The unweighted quotient is valid only under the declared equal-cost decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-cost partial access, divide the number of partial calls by the number constituting one reference full access. For unequal costs, divide the total cost of all calls by the declared cost of one full access.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{N}\) and a reference full-access operation has a fixed decomposition into exactly \(M\) equal-cost atomic calls in the unweighted model.
\(N\in\mathbb{N}_0\).
In the weighted model, \(c_q>0\) for \(q=1,\ldots,N\) and \(C_{\mathrm{full}}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=N/M\) in the equal-cost model, while \(W=(\sum_{q=1}^{N}c_q)/C_{\mathrm{full}}\) in the weighted model.

notation.meaning: number of equal-cost atomic partial calls per reference full access
number of atomic partial calls made by the computation

children.title: Projection Call Units
children.top_down_role: Call accounting for projection-based subproblem access.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic evaluation of a metric projection onto a declared feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\). A projection-oracle query at \(v\in H\) returns the unique point \(\Pi_C(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\|x-v\|^2\). One exact evaluation counts as one projection call, independently of the internal algorithm used by the oracle. An approximate call must instead return \(z\in C\) satisfying a declared error criterion, such as \(\|z-\Pi_C(v)\|\leq\varepsilon\), and its tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is part of the resource transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One exact nearest-point evaluation onto a closed convex set is one projection call; approximate calls must record their error criterion and tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\Pi}\) equals the number of evaluations of \(v\mapsto\Pi_C(v)\) under the declared accuracy convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic evaluation of a proximal mapping for a declared function and parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:H\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(\lambda>0\). A proximal-oracle query at \(v\in H\) returns \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H}\{h(x)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|x-v\|^2\}\). One exact evaluation counts as one proximal call. For an inexact oracle, the residual, objective-gap, or distance criterion and requested tolerance must be declared; calls made at different tolerances remain distinct transcript entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One exact minimization defining a proximal point is one proximal call; an inexact call must include its chosen error criterion and tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(h\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{prox}}\) counts evaluations of \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}\) under the declared parameter and accuracy convention.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of h with parameter lambda

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic evaluation of the resolvent of a set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(\lambda>0\). A resolvent-oracle query at \(v\in H\) returns the unique point \(z=J_{\lambda A}(v)=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}(v)\), equivalently satisfying \(v-z\in\lambda A(z)\). One exact evaluation counts as one resolvent call. An approximate resolvent call must specify a verifiable residual or graph-enlargement condition and its tolerance as part of the oracle contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One solution of the resolvent inclusion is one resolvent call; approximate evaluations require an explicit residual or graph-enlargement tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_J\) equals the number of evaluations of \(J_{\lambda A}\) under the declared accuracy convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Interface Cost Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical equivalences do not alone imply equal oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq H\), its indicator \(\iota_C\), and normal-cone operator \(N_C=\partial\iota_C\), the implicit maps satisfy \[\Pi_C=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\iota_C}=J_{\lambda N_C}\qquad(\lambda>0).\] More generally, for proper lower semicontinuous convex \(h\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}=J_{\lambda\partial h}\). These identities permit call-count conversion only when the oracle model assigns the corresponding interfaces the same input domain, accuracy requirement, and unit cost; otherwise projection, proximal, and resolvent counts are separate resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection, indicator-proximal, and normal-cone resolvent maps coincide mathematically, but their call counts are interchangeable only under an explicitly equal cost and accuracy model.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(h\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Map equivalence implies oracle-count equivalence only under a declared equal-cost, equal-accuracy interface identification.

children.title: Linear-Optimization Call Units
children.top_down_role: Call counts for exact, approximate, weak, or restricted linear access.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Optimization Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic exact or approximate minimization of a linear functional over a declared feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let \(Q\) be the declared set of admissible query vectors. A linear-optimization oracle receives \(c\in Q\) and returns \(s\in C\). An exact call requires \(\langle c,s\rangle=\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\), with attainment assumed for every admissible exact query. For a declared \(\delta\geq0\), an additive-\(\delta\) call requires \(\langle c,s\rangle\leq\inf_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle+\delta\). One invocation counts as one linear-optimization call. Weak or restricted variants must separately specify their admissible queries, permissible outputs, and response guarantees; counts from different variants are not interchangeable without a stated reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One invocation of a fixed exact or additive-error linear-minimization interface counts as one call. Exact access requires an attained minimum, and weak or restricted interfaces require separate domains and guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty.
\(Q\) is the declared admissible query set.
For every \(c\in Q\) submitted to the exact interface, \(\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\) exists.
For additive approximation, \(\delta\geq0\) and the relevant infimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{LO}}\) counts invocations of one fixed linear-optimization interface, with \(\delta=0\) agreeing with exact access when the minimum is attained.

notation.meaning: set of admissible linear-oracle query vectors

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive-error linear minimization is a standard declared oracle interface

children.title: Geometric Oracle Call Units
children.top_down_role: Call counts for membership, separation, validity, and related geometric access.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Oracle Call Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type-specific accounting for membership, separation, and validity queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A membership query at \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) returns whether \(y\in C\). A separation query at \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus C\) returns \((a,\beta)\in(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta<\langle a,y\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\). A validity query at \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\) decides whether \(\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\). Each invocation counts as one call of its stated type. Exact, weak, and approximate variants require separately declared response guarantees and separate counters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership, strict-separation, and validity invocations each count in their own oracle class. Weak or approximate variants require distinct guarantees and counters.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each oracle's admissible inputs and response guarantee are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{mem}}\), \(N_{\mathrm{sep}}\), and \(N_{\mathrm{val}}\) count their respective invocations and are not combined without an explicit reduction.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: membership, strong separation, and validity are conventional geometric-oracle interfaces

children.title: Pass-Accounting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Pass-based accounting under batching, reuse, and nonuniform access.

children.title: Epoch Accounting
children.top_down_role: Dataset-scale work expressed through nominal epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Epoch Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting for completed prescribed sweeps through a finite dataset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a dataset of size \(n\) and an algorithmic epoch schedule. One epoch is completed when the schedule has issued its prescribed collection of exactly \(n\) unit-cost component accesses, normally one per index under a permutation. After \(E\) completed epochs and \(r\) additional component accesses with \(0\leq r<n\), the literal epoch count is \(E\), while the fractional work count is \(E+r/n\). If an epoch uses repeated sampling, variable batch sizes, or unequal costs, its meaning must be separately specified and must not be identified automatically with one complete data sweep.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A literal epoch is one prescribed dataset-sized sweep; partial work may be reported fractionally, while repeated or unequal access requires a separate convention.
assumptions_latex: The dataset size \(n\) and epoch schedule are fixed.
The prescribed epoch contains exactly \(n\) equal-cost component accesses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{comp}}=En+r\) gives \(E\) completed epochs and \(E+r/n\) dataset-normalized passes.

notation.meaning: component accesses after the last completed epoch

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an epoch is conventionally a prescribed dataset-scale sweep

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent prescribed-sweep definition and correctly distinguishes completed epochs from fractional dataset-normalized work. However, epoch usage is model-dependent, and no inspectable source is supplied for the exact-n-access convention or its relationship to passes.

children.title: Effective-Pass Accounting
children.top_down_role: Dataset-scale work adjusted for actual access coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Pass Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalizes component-oracle work by one complete traversal of a finite-sum dataset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the objective contain \(n\ge 1\) indexed components. If oracle call \(t\) accesses a batch \(I_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), counting multiplicity when a component is queried repeatedly, then the effective-pass count through time \(T\) is \[P_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{T}|I_t|.\] Thus one full-batch call, \(n\) singleton calls, or any collection totaling \(n\) component accesses costs one effective pass. Reuse of cached information contributes only when the accounting convention declares it a new component-oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Effective passes equal total component accesses, including repeated accesses, divided by dataset size; batching therefore changes calls but not normalized component work.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) finite indexed components.
Each charged call has a specified accessed batch \(I_t\).

notation.meaning: component batch accessed at call t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-sum workload normalization by total component accesses
No supplied locator directly defines effective-pass accounting.

children.title: Nonuniform-Access Pass Conversion
children.top_down_role: Pass normalization under unequal sampling, batching, or reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform-Access Pass Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts unequal per-component access frequencies into an equivalent number of full uniform passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\) components, let \(a_i(T)\in\mathbb N_0\) be the number of charged accesses to component \(i\) through time \(T\). The pass-equivalent of the nonuniform access pattern is \[P_{\mathrm{nonunif}}(T)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i(T).\] Equivalently, if \(A(T)=\sum_i a_i(T)>0\) and \(p_i(T)=a_i(T)/A(T)\), then \(P_{\mathrm{nonunif}}(T)=A(T)/n\). This scalar records total normalized work; it does not assert that nonuniform sampling has the same statistical or convergence effect as uniform traversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sum all per-component access multiplicities and divide by dataset size; this converts work, but does not equate nonuniform and uniform statistical behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) components share the same unit access cost.
\(a_i(T)\) counts every charged access with multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{nonunif}}(T)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i(T)\).

notation.meaning: charged accesses to component i through time T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct conversion of heterogeneous component multiplicities into dataset-normalized work
No supplied locator directly supports this conversion convention.

children.title: Fresh-Sample Budgets
children.top_down_role: Counts of newly acquired independent or conditionally sampled observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Sample Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts newly acquired stochastic observations rather than repeated computation on stored observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the information filtration of an algorithm. A response \(Z_t\) is charged as a fresh sample when it is newly acquired and, conditional on the query or design selected from \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), is drawn from the prescribed observation kernel rather than recovered from stored data. The fresh-sample budget through time \(T\) is \[B_{\mathrm{fresh}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf 1\{Z_t\text{ is newly sampled}\}.\] Re-evaluation, resampling-free transformation, or repeated oracle use of the same stored observation does not increase this budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fresh-sample budget counts newly drawn observations under the prescribed conditional sampling law, excluding repeated processing or reuse of stored data.
assumptions_latex: Queries or designs at time \(t\) are measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\).
Each acquisition is identifiable as new or reused.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{fresh}}(T)\) equals the number of newly sampled observations through time \(T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between sample acquisition and computational reuse
Supplied learning-theory locators do not directly define conditional fresh-sample accounting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent definition of acquisition rather than reuse, but the conditional fresh-sample convention is not supported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Empirical Acquisition Budgets

children.title: Simulator Replication Budgets
children.top_down_role: Budget accounting for repeated simulator evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Replication Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts newly executed stochastic simulator replications under adaptively chosen input designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_t\) be a simulator input chosen from prior information and let \(U_t\) be a newly generated random seed or innovation. A simulator response has the form \(Y_t=S(x_t,U_t)\). The replication budget through time \(T\) is \[B_{\mathrm{sim}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf 1\{S(x_t,U_t)\text{ is newly executed}\}.\] Replications may use different designs and need only be conditionally independent according to the declared simulator law. Replaying a stored trajectory or recomputing a statistic from stored simulator output does not constitute a new replication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator budget counts newly executed stochastic runs, including adaptively designed runs, but excludes replay and postprocessing of stored outputs.
assumptions_latex: Each charged run uses a newly generated simulator innovation \(U_t\).
The simulator law conditional on the selected input \(x_t\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{sim}}(T)\) is the number of newly executed simulator runs through time \(T\).

notation.meaning: design and new innovation for replication t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard simulation-experiment distinction between independent executions and replayed outputs

children.title: Experimental Trial Budgets
children.top_down_role: Budget accounting for controlled experimental trials.

knowledge_statements.title: Experimental Trial Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts executed experimental units or interventions under a declared trial protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_t\) denote the design or intervention assigned to experimental unit \(t\), possibly as a function of prior outcomes. A trial is charged when the protocol is physically or operationally executed on a new experimental unit or in a new trial instance. The experimental-trial budget is \[B_{\mathrm{trial}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf 1\{d_t\text{ is executed as a new trial}\}.\] Multiple measurements produced by one trial remain one trial unless the protocol explicitly declares measurement-level costing; reanalysis of recorded outcomes incurs no additional trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trial budget counts newly executed interventions or experimental units, not repeated analysis or multiple measurements from one trial unless explicitly declared.
assumptions_latex: Every charged execution has a declared experimental unit and design \(d_t\).
The protocol specifies whether cost is assessed per trial or per measurement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{trial}}(T)\) equals the number of newly executed trials under the declared protocol.

notation.meaning: design or intervention for trial t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: protocol-relative accounting separates intervention executions from measurements and analysis
No supplied source locator directly supports this trial-budget convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The protocol-relative trial count fits the leaf, but the distinction among trial instances, experimental units, and measurement-level costs needs an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Physical Observation Budgets
children.top_down_role: Budget accounting for observations collected from physical systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Physical Observation Budgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts newly acquired measurements from a physical system under a specified acquisition unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an acquisition unit, such as one sensor reading, sampled unit, or observation interval. If \(O_t\) is a measurement newly obtained from the physical system at acquisition event \(t\), define \[B_{\mathrm{phys}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf 1\{O_t\text{ is a new acquisition unit}\}.\] Calibration readings, repeated sensors, and simultaneous measurements are charged according to the declared unit before comparison. Storage, transmission, denoising, or repeated analysis of an already acquired measurement does not increase the physical-observation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Physical-observation cost counts newly acquired measurement units under a declared convention, excluding storage, transmission, and reanalysis of existing measurements.
assumptions_latex: A single physical acquisition unit is specified before accounting.
Each measurement event can be classified as new acquisition or reuse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{phys}}(T)\) is the number of declared physical acquisition units obtained through time \(T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: acquisition accounting requires an explicit physical measurement unit and excludes downstream processing
No supplied source locator directly defines physical-observation budgets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately requires a declared acquisition unit, but no inspectable source supports the precise inclusion and exclusion rules for physical-observation accounting.

children.title: Cross-Source Budget Comparability
children.top_down_role: Normalization across simulated, experimental, and observational resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Source Budget Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when simulator, trial, and physical-observation counts admit a defensible scalar comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(B_1,\ldots,B_m)\in\mathbb R_+^m\) collect acquisition counts from distinct sources. These budgets are scalar-comparable only after declaring positive conversion coefficients \(c_s\) with a common target unit and invariant operational meaning across the procedures compared. Under that convention, the converted budget is \[C_c(B)=\sum_{s=1}^{m}c_sB_s.\] If no such coefficients are justified, comparison must retain the vector \(B\); neither \(\sum_s B_s\) nor an unweighted ranking is intrinsically meaningful. Conclusions based on \(C_c\) are conditional on the declared coefficient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different acquisition sources are scalar-comparable only through justified conversion weights to a common unit; otherwise their budgets must remain a vector.
assumptions_latex: \(B_s\ge0\) counts source-specific acquisition units.
Each \(c_s>0\) converts source \(s\) into one common declared unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scalar comparison uses \(C_c(B)=\sum_{s=1}^{m}c_sB_s\); without justified \(c\), only vector comparison is valid.

notation.meaning: declared conversion cost for source s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: heterogeneous resources require declared exchange rates before scalar aggregation
No supplied source locator directly establishes cross-source acquisition comparability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition for scalarizing heterogeneous acquisition budgets is mathematically coherent and fits the container, but the claimed necessity of justified common-unit coefficients lacks cited support.

children.title: Heterogeneous Resource Accounting
children.top_down_role: Multidimensional accounting when a single call count does not represent total cost.

children.title: Separated Oracle-Count Vectors
children.top_down_role: Independent call counts for multiple interfaces used by one procedure.

knowledge_statements.title: Separated Oracle-Count Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains one coordinate for each oracle interface used by an optimization procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a procedure can query \(m\ge1\) distinct oracle interfaces \(\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_m\). If \(N_j(T)\in\mathbb N_0\) is the number of charged calls to \(\mathcal O_j\) through time \(T\), its separated oracle-count vector is \[N(T)=(N_1(T),\ldots,N_m(T))\in\mathbb N_0^m.\] Interfaces must be distinguished by the information returned or by their declared charging rules. This representation preserves heterogeneous access requirements and does not aggregate coordinates unless an additional cost model is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separated count vector records calls to each oracle interface independently, preserving heterogeneous access requirements until a cost model is chosen.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge1\) oracle interfaces have fixed identities and charging rules.
Every charged query is assigned to its corresponding interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(T)=(N_1(T),\ldots,N_m(T))\in\mathbb N_0^m\) records the procedure's oracle use.

notation.meaning: calls to interface j through time T

children.title: Weighted Query Costs
children.top_down_role: Scalar resource accounting based on declared relative oracle costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Query Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalarizes heterogeneous oracle counts using declared nonnegative per-query costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=(N_1,\ldots,N_m)\in\mathbb N_0^m\) be separated oracle counts and let \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_m)\in\mathbb R_+^m\) be declared per-call costs in a common resource unit. The weighted query cost is \[C_w(N)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_jN_j=\langle w,N\rangle.\] The weights are part of the computational model and must remain fixed across procedures being compared. A zero weight declares an interface free in this model; it does not imply that the interface requires no physical work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted query cost is the dot product of interface-specific call counts and declared per-call costs measured in one common unit.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N_0^m\) is a separated oracle-count vector.
\(w\in\mathbb R_+^m\) uses one common resource unit and is fixed across comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_w(N)=\langle w,N\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_jN_j\).

children.title: Pareto Resource Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Nonscalar comparisons among query, communication, arithmetic, memory, and sample resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Resource Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares algorithms componentwise when resource vectors should not be scalarized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(A),r(B)\in\mathbb R_+^m\) be resource vectors for two procedures under identical accuracy, success, instance-class, and accounting conventions. Procedure \(A\) weakly Pareto-dominates \(B\) when \[r_j(A)\le r_j(B)\quad\text{for every }j.\] It strictly Pareto-dominates \(B\) when weak dominance holds and the inequality is strict for at least one coordinate. If each procedure uses less of at least one resource and more of another, they are Pareto-incomparable. This relation is invariant under coordinatewise strictly increasing changes of resource units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At matched guarantees, one procedure Pareto-dominates another if it uses no more of every resource and strictly less of at least one.
assumptions_latex: Both vectors use identical resource coordinates and accounting conventions.
Procedures are compared at the same accuracy, success criterion, and instance class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict dominance means \(r(A)\le r(B)\) componentwise and \(r(A)\ne r(B)\); otherwise tradeoffs may be incomparable.

notation.meaning: coordinate j of A's resource use

children.title: Distributed Resource Accounting

children.title: Adaptive-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Sequentially dependent query rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures sequential dependence while allowing parallel queries within each adaptive batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an oracle model, an admissible instance class, and a declared \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) output guarantee, where \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in[0,1)\). An oracle procedure executes in \(R\) adaptive rounds if its queries can be partitioned into batches \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_R\) such that every query in \(Q_r\) is determined by the procedure's internal randomness and the responses from \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_{r-1}\), but not by responses to other queries in \(Q_r\). The adaptive-round complexity is the least \(R\) among procedures that satisfy the declared guarantee on every admissible instance. Batch sizes and total query counts are separate resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed oracle model, instance class, and target guarantee, adaptive-round complexity is the minimum number of sequential query batches among successful procedures; queries within a batch cannot depend on responses from that same batch.
assumptions_latex: An oracle model and admissible instance class are fixed.
An \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) output guarantee is fixed, with \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in[0,1)\).
Queries in round \(r\) depend only on internal randomness and responses from earlier rounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adaptive-round complexity is the minimum feasible number \(R\) of sequentially dependent query batches among procedures satisfying the declared guarantee.

notation.meaning: query batch in adaptive round r
