children.title: Communication-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Synchronization or message-exchange rounds required by distributed access.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts sequential synchronization or message-exchange phases in a declared distributed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a distributed model with a processor set, communication topology, admissible instance class, and within-round message rules. A communication round is one model-defined phase in which processors may form messages from their local states, exchange permitted messages, and update their local states after receiving that phase's messages. For a declared output guarantee with tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) and failure probability \(\delta\in[0,1)\), the communication-round complexity is the least \(R_{\mathrm{comm}}\) among distributed procedures that satisfy the guarantee on every admissible instance. Message length, local computation, and oracle calls are separate resources unless the model explicitly incorporates them into a round.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed distributed model, instance class, and target guarantee, communication-round complexity is the minimum number of model-defined message-exchange or synchronization phases among successful distributed procedures.
assumptions_latex: The processor set, communication topology, admissible instance class, and within-round message rules are fixed.
An \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) output guarantee is fixed, with \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathrm{comm}}\) is the minimum number of communication phases among distributed procedures satisfying the declared guarantee.

children.title: Communication Payload Resources
children.top_down_role: Communication accounting beyond round counts.

children.title: Message-Volume Accounting
children.top_down_role: Aggregate communication measured through transmitted message content.

knowledge_statements.title: Message-Volume Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts communicated payload, separately from message latency and local arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed execution with a finite processor set \(I\) and a finite set \(\mathcal M\) of directed messages, let \(\operatorname{src},\operatorname{dst}:\mathcal M\to I\) identify the endpoints and let \(s_m\ge 0\) be the encoded length of message \(m\) in bits. The total message volume is \[V=\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}s_m.\] For each \(i\in I\), define \(V_i^{\mathrm{out}}=\sum_{m:\,\operatorname{src}(m)=i}s_m\) and \(V_i^{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_{m:\,\operatorname{dst}(m)=i}s_m\). The peak endpoint volume is \(V_{\max}=\max_{i\in I}\max\{V_i^{\mathrm{out}},V_i^{\mathrm{in}}\}\). Message count alone does not determine \(V\), because payload lengths may vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication volume is the sum of encoded message lengths; endpoint volume records the largest amount sent or received by any processor in the specified finite processor set.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(\mathcal M\) are finite.
\(\operatorname{src},\operatorname{dst}:\mathcal M\to I\).
Each message has a specified nonnegative encoded bit length \(s_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}s_m\), with peak endpoint load \(V_{\max}=\max_{i\in I}\max\{V_i^{\mathrm{out}},V_i^{\mathrm{in}}\}\).

notation.meaning: Finite set of directed messages in the execution.
Encoded payload length of message m in bits.

children.title: Bandwidth Constraints
children.top_down_role: Communication limits imposed by transmission capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A link-capacity feasibility condition for scheduled distributed communication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite set of directed communication links, with bandwidth \(b_e>0\) bits per unit time for each \(e\in E\). Over an interval \([0,T]\) with \(T>0\), let \(x_e:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)\) be the measurable aggregate transmission rate assigned to link \(e\). The schedule is bandwidth-feasible when \[x_e(t)\le b_e\quad\text{for every }e\in E\text{ and almost every }t\in[0,T].\] Defining \(v_e=\int_0^T x_e(t)\,dt\), feasibility implies \(v_e\le b_eT\) for every \(e\in E\), and therefore \(T\ge\max_{e\in E}v_e/b_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule is bandwidth-feasible when every link's aggregate transmission rate stays within its capacity almost everywhere; the resulting link volumes impose a communication-time lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite set of directed communication links.
Each link \(e\in E\) has fixed bandwidth \(b_e>0\).
\(T>0\), and each rate function \(x_e:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)\) is measurable and integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bandwidth feasibility implies \(v_e=\int_0^T x_e(t)\,dt\le b_eT\) for every \(e\in E\), hence \(T\ge\max_{e\in E}v_e/b_e\).

notation.meaning: Aggregate rate scheduled on link e at time t.
Integral of the scheduled rate on link e over the interval.

children.title: Payload-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions based on per-message payload size.

knowledge_statements.title: Payload-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies distributed algorithms by asymptotic message payload length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a problem-size parameter \(n\), let \(s_m(n)\) denote the encoded bit length of message \(m\), and define the worst payload \(S(n)=\max_m s_m(n)\). A family of executions is in the constant-payload regime when \(S(n)=O(1)\), the logarithmic-payload regime when \(S(n)=O(\log n)\), and the polynomial-payload regime when \(S(n)=n^{O(1)}\). It is unbounded-payload relative to a stated resource model when no prescribed bound on \(S(n)\) is imposed. The chosen encoding and size parameter are part of the regime specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Payload regimes classify executions by how the largest encoded message grows with problem size, under an explicitly fixed encoding.
assumptions_latex: A problem-size parameter \(n\) and message encoding are fixed.
Every execution at size \(n\) has finitely many messages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is determined by the asymptotic growth of \(S(n)=\max_m s_m(n)\).

notation.meaning: Encoded bit length of message m at size n.
Worst message payload at size n.

children.title: Work-Depth Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Joint accounting for total work and critical-path length.

children.title: Total Work
children.top_down_role: Aggregate computational effort across all processing units.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work measure for a finite dependency graph of primitive operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent one execution by a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), whose vertices are primitive operations and whose edges encode precedence. If operation \(v\in V\) has nonnegative cost \(c(v)\), the total work is \[W(G)=\sum_{v\in V}c(v).\] Under unit-cost accounting, \(c(v)=1\) for every \(v\in V\), and \(W(G)=|V|\). This quantity is independent of how mutually independent vertices are assigned to processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total work is the sum of all primitive-operation costs in the execution DAG, independent of how those operations are scheduled in parallel.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic computation graph.
Each vertex \(v\in V\) has a specified cost \(c(v)\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(G)=\sum_{v\in V}c(v)\), and under unit costs \(W(G)=|V|\).

children.title: Critical-Path Depth
children.top_down_role: Sequential depth imposed by dependencies in parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Path Depth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted dependency depth of a parallel computation DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite nonempty computation DAG \(G=(V,E)\) with vertex costs \(c(v)\ge 0\), its critical-path depth is \[D(G)=\max_{P}\sum_{v\in P}c(v),\] where the maximum ranges over all directed paths \(P\) in \(G\). Under unit-cost accounting, \(D(G)\) is the maximum number of vertices on a directed path. If each vertex is an indivisible operation of duration \(c(v)\) and edges impose precedence constraints, every precedence-respecting execution requires time at least \(D(G)\), even with arbitrarily many processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Critical-path depth is the largest accumulated operation duration along a dependency path and lower-bounds execution time when vertices are indivisible operations subject to the DAG precedences.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite nonempty directed acyclic computation graph.
Each vertex \(v\in V\) is an indivisible, nonparallelizable operation of duration \(c(v)\ge 0\).
Every edge imposes a precedence constraint on its endpoint operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(G)=\max_P\sum_{v\in P}c(v)\), and every execution satisfying the stated model has running time at least \(D(G)\).

notation.meaning: A directed path in the computation graph.

children.title: Parallel Speedup
children.top_down_role: Performance improvement relative to a sequential work baseline.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Speedup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Speedup and efficiency relative to the same computation's sequential time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1>0\) be the running time of a fixed computation on one processor and \(T_p>0\) its running time on \(p\ge 1\) identical unit-speed processors under the same cost model. Its parallel speedup and efficiency are \[S_p=\frac{T_1}{T_p},\qquad E_p=\frac{S_p}{p}.\] Suppose the computation is represented by a DAG of indivisible operations with total work \(W\) and critical-path depth \(D\), and the parallel execution performs exactly those operations. Then \(T_p\ge\max\{W/p,D\}\), so \(S_p\le T_1/\max\{W/p,D\}\). If additionally \(T_1=W\), then \(S_p\le\min\{p,W/D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel speedup is one-processor time divided by p-processor time; for the same indivisible-operation DAG on identical unit-speed processors, total work and critical-path depth limit the attainable speedup.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge 1\), and \(T_1\) and \(T_p\) concern the same computation and cost model.
The computation is a DAG of indivisible operations with work \(W\) and depth \(D\).
The \(p\) processors are identical and unit-speed, and the parallel execution performs exactly the DAG operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_p=T_1/T_p\), and if \(T_1=W\), then \(S_p\le\min\{p,W/D\}\).

notation.meaning: Running time on p identical unit-speed processors.
Total work of the computation DAG.
Critical-path depth of the computation DAG.

children.title: Work–Depth Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Resource regimes balancing aggregate effort against critical-path length.

knowledge_statements.title: Work–Depth Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates processor-limited time to total work and dependency depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite computation DAG whose vertices are indivisible operations with nonnegative durations, total work \(W\), and critical-path depth \(D\). On \(p\ge 1\) identical unit-speed processors, every precedence-respecting schedule has running time \[T_p\ge\max\left\{\frac{W}{p},D\right\}.\] If communication and scheduling overhead are neglected and a work-conserving greedy list schedule assigns an available operation whenever a processor is idle, then \[T_p\le \frac{W}{p}+\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)D\le\frac{W}{p}+D.\] Thus reducing depth may expose more parallelism without reducing work, while reducing work need not shorten an unchanged critical path. When \(D>0\), the ratio \(W/D\) is the computation's average parallelism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time is constrained jointly by work per processor and critical-path depth; under an ideal work-conserving list schedule it is at most work per processor plus a depth term, so improving one measure need not improve the other.
assumptions_latex: The computation is a finite DAG of indivisible operations with nonnegative durations, work \(W\), and depth \(D\).
There are \(p\ge 1\) identical unit-speed processors, and all precedence constraints are respected.
For the upper bound, communication and scheduling overhead are neglected and the scheduler is a work-conserving greedy list scheduler.
For the ratio \(W/D\), assume \(D>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W/p,D\}\le T_p\le W/p+(1-1/p)D\le W/p+D\) under the stated scheduling model.

children.title: Per-Query Arithmetic Cost
children.top_down_role: Numerical work required to realize one nominal oracle call.

knowledge_statements.title: Per-Query Arithmetic Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic realization cost of one nominal oracle query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an oracle algorithm issue \(Q\ge 1\) queries \(q_1,\ldots,q_Q\). Fix a numerical representation and a set of unit-cost arithmetic primitives. For each \(j\in\{1,,Q\}\), let \(a_j\ge 0\) be the number of primitives assigned to constructing the input of query \(q_j\) and computing its returned value. The worst-case per-query arithmetic cost is \[A_Q=\max_{1\le j\le Q}a_j,\] and the total arithmetic cost assigned to oracle realization is \(A_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{j=1}^Q a_j\le QA_Q\). Oracle-query complexity \(Q\) alone does not determine these arithmetic costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-query arithmetic cost counts the numerical primitives assigned to forming one query and computing its oracle response under a fixed representation and implementation model.
assumptions_latex: The execution makes \(Q\ge 1\) oracle queries \(q_1,,q_Q\).
The numerical representation and unit-cost arithmetic primitives are fixed.
Each \(a_j\) counts the realization work assigned to query \(q_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_Q=\max_{1\le j\le Q}a_j\) and \(A_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{j=1}^Q a_j\le QA_Q\).

notation.meaning: Positive number of nominal oracle queries.
Arithmetic cost assigned to realizing query j.
Total arithmetic cost assigned to oracle realization.

children.title: Numerical Representation Cost
children.top_down_role: Dependence of query implementation on numerical representation and requested accuracy.

children.title: Numerical Precision Cost
children.top_down_role: Implementation cost associated with requested numerical precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Precision Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of representing and operating on finite-precision numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-precision arithmetic model. If operation \(k\) uses operands represented with \(b_k\) bits and has bit-operation cost \(C_k(b_k)\), then the numerical precision cost of an execution is \[C_{\mathrm{prec}}=\sum_k C_k(b_k).\] Its maximum working precision is \(b_{\max}=\max_k b_k\). A unit-cost real-arithmetic count corresponds to suppressing the dependence on \(b_k\); it need not bound \(C_{\mathrm{prec}}\) when the precision required for correctness grows with the input size or target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical precision cost sums bit-level operation costs at the precisions actually used, exposing work hidden by unit-cost real arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: A finite-precision number format and bit-operation cost model are fixed.
Every arithmetic operation has a specified working precision \(b_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{prec}}=\sum_k C_k(b_k)\), with maximum working precision \(b_{\max}=\max_k b_k\).

notation.meaning: Working precision in bits for operation k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for the exact bit-operation accounting model, the operation-dependent functions, or the comparison with unit-cost real arithmetic. Those choices materially determine the definition and require authoritative support.

children.title: Representation Encoding Cost
children.top_down_role: Storage and processing cost associated with encoded oracle inputs or outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Encoding Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates encoding and decoding work from nominal oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an abstract query or state space, let \(\mathcal B^*\) be the set of finite bit strings, and fix an injective encoding \(\operatorname{enc}:X\to\mathcal B^*\) with decoder \(\operatorname{dec}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dec}(\operatorname{enc}(x))=x\) on represented inputs. For objects \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\), the representation encoding cost is \[C_{\mathrm{enc}}=\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(C_{\\operatorname{enc}}(x_i)+C_{operatorname{dec}}(\operatorname{enc}(x_i))\bigr),\] measured in the fixed bit-operation model. Storage length \(|\operatorname{enc}(x_i)|\) and conversion cost are distinct resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representation encoding cost counts bit-level conversion between abstract objects and their finite encodings, separately from encoded length and oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an abstract object space with a fixed finite encoding.
The decoder recovers every represented input exactly.
Encoding and decoding costs use a fixed bit-operation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{enc}}\) is the sum of the encoding and decoding costs for all represented objects.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has no supporting source, and its displayed formula contains malformed commands (`C_{\\operatorname{enc}}` and `C_{operatorname{dec}}`). The proposed aggregation also counts both encoding and decoding for every object without specifying that both conversions actually occur. An authoritative source and a corrected accounting convention are required.

children.title: Accuracy-Driven Bit Complexity
children.top_down_role: Bit-level resource growth across requested-accuracy regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Driven Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts accuracy-dependent query and precision requirements into bit-operation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm returns an output \(x\) satisfying an error criterion \(\operatorname{err}(x)\le\varepsilon\) after at most \(Q(\varepsilon)\) oracle queries. Assume every query and local update uses at most \(A(\varepsilon)\) arithmetic operations on numbers of at most \(b(\varepsilon)\) bits, and one such operation costs at most \(M(b(\varepsilon))\) bit operations. Then its arithmetic bit complexity is bounded by \[C_{\mathrm{bit}}(\varepsilon)\le Q(\varepsilon)A(\varepsilon)M(b(\varepsilon))+C_{\mathrm{enc}}(\varepsilon).\] Thus query complexity becomes a bit-complexity statement only after precision, arithmetic, and encoding costs are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accuracy-dependent bit complexity multiplies query count by per-query arithmetic and finite-precision costs, then adds representation conversion cost.
assumptions_latex: The output must satisfy \(\operatorname{err}(x)\le\varepsilon\).
Query, arithmetic, precision, and encoding bounds hold uniformly over admissible inputs.
Arithmetic on \(b\)-bit values costs at most \(M(b)\) bit operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{bit}}(\varepsilon)\le Q(\varepsilon)A(\varepsilon)M(b(\varepsilon))+C_{\mathrm{enc}}(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Oracle-query bound at target accuracy ε.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound is not justified by the stated assumptions: saying every query and local update costs at most A operations does not bound the number of local updates by the query count. No source supports the proposed query-arithmetic-precision-encoding decomposition, so the mathematical bound cannot be reliably repaired without evidence.

children.title: State-Transfer Cost
children.top_down_role: Costs hidden by call counts when responses require large state or data transfers.

children.title: Memory Footprint Cost
children.top_down_role: Resident-state requirements hidden by oracle-call counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak simultaneously resident state under a fixed storage representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a storage representation and a nonempty set of observation times \(\mathcal T\). Let \(L(t)\) be the set of data objects simultaneously live at time \(t\in\mathcal T\), and let \(s(x)\ge 0\) be the stored size of object \(x\) in bits. The memory footprint cost is the peak live storage \[M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\sup_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{x\in L(t)}s(x).\] In a distributed execution with a finite processor set \(I\), let \(L_i(t)\) be the objects live on processor \(i\) at time \(t\), and define \(M_i=\sup_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{x\in L_i(t)}s(x)\). The quantities \(\sum_{i\in I}M_i\) and \(\max_{i\in I}M_i\) may both be reported, because the former sums local peak footprints while the latter records the largest local peak.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory footprint is the supremum of simultaneously live encoded storage over the observation times; distributed accounting can report both the sum of local peaks and the largest per-processor peak.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a nonempty set of observation times.
Object lifetimes and nonnegative encoded sizes \(s(x)\) are fixed by the implementation.
All relevant persistent and temporary objects are included.
For distributed accounting, \(I\) is a finite nonempty processor set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\sup_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{x\in L(t)}s(x)\), with local footprints \(M_i=\sup_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{x\in L_i(t)}s(x)\).

notation.meaning: Set of objects live at time t.
Stored size of object x in bits.
Peak live memory footprint expressed as a supremum.
Peak local footprint of processor i.

children.title: Data-Movement Cost
children.top_down_role: Resource costs from transferring oracle inputs, outputs, or stored data.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Movement Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts transferred data independently of arithmetic work and oracle-query count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution trace \(\tau\) on a machine with memory or communication interfaces \(E\), let \(b_e(t)\) be the number of bits transferred across interface \(e\in E\) by event \(t\). The data-movement cost is \[D(\tau)=\sum_{t\in\tau}\sum_{e\in E} b_e(t).\] If interfaces have nonnegative weights \(w_e\), the weighted cost is \(D_w(\tau)=\sum_{t,e}w_e b_e(t)\). Reads served entirely within the designated local memory do not cross an interface and contribute zero; cache misses, device transfers, and inter-worker messages contribute at the interface they cross.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-movement cost is the total, or interface-weighted total, number of bits transferred across designated memory or communication boundaries during an execution.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\) is a finite execution trace.
\(E\) is a fixed collection of designated transfer interfaces.
\(b_e(t)\ge 0\) and, for weighted cost, \(w_e\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\tau)\) and \(D_w(\tau)\) quantify transferred bits rather than arithmetic operations or oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Bits transferred across interface e at event t.

children.title: State-Transfer Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Regimes where movement of large state dominates query execution.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Transfer Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bandwidth and latency lower bounds induced by transfers on an execution’s critical path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an execution move \(D_e\) bits across each interface \(e\), whose sustained bandwidth is at most \(B_e>0\), and let its critical path contain \(m_e\) nonoverlapped transfers across that interface, each having latency at least \(\lambda_e\ge 0\). Its elapsed time \(T\) necessarily satisfies \[T\ge \max_{e}\frac{D_e}{B_e},\qquad T\ge \sum_e m_e\lambda_e.\] Consequently, whenever either bound asymptotically exceeds the available arithmetic-time lower bound, state transfer is a performance bottleneck even if the oracle-query count is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is bounded below by transferred bits divided by bandwidth and by unavoidable critical-path latencies; either can dominate arithmetic despite identical query counts.
assumptions_latex: Each interface \(e\) has sustained bandwidth no greater than \(B_e\).
The \(m_e\) counted transfers lie on the execution critical path and cannot overlap.
Latency and bandwidth accounting use the same interface boundaries as the transfer trace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\ge \max\{\max_e D_e/B_e,\sum_e m_e\lambda_e\}\).

notation.meaning: Transferred bits and bandwidth bound for interface e.
Critical-path transfer count and minimum latency.

children.title: Inner-Solver Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational effort hidden inside structured subproblem oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solver Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounts for computational work performed inside an inexact structured-subproblem oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose outer query \(k\) asks an inner oracle to approximately solve a subproblem \(\min_{z\in Z_k}\phi_k(z)\) to tolerance \(\eta_k\), producing \(z_k\). If the inner procedure uses \(q_k\) primitive inner-oracle calls and \(a_k\) arithmetic operations, then the cumulative inner-solver costs through \(K\) outer queries are \[Q_{\mathrm{in}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_k,\qquad A_{\mathrm{in}}(K)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k.\] These costs are recorded separately from \(K\); treating the structured oracle as unit cost suppresses them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner-solver cost sums primitive oracle calls and arithmetic work used to solve the structured subproblems requested by outer iterations.
assumptions_latex: Each outer query specifies a subproblem and an accuracy tolerance \(\eta_k\).
The inner solver terminates with an output satisfying the chosen tolerance criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource vector includes \((K,Q_{\mathrm{in}}(K),A_{\mathrm{in}}(K))\), not merely the outer-query count \(K\).

notation.meaning: Primitive inner-oracle calls for outer query k.
Inner arithmetic operations for outer query k.

standard_field_rationale: nested algorithms require outer and inner resources to be distinguished

children.title: Worst-Case Class Complexity
children.top_down_role: Uniform resource requirements over an entire problem class.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Class Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform query requirement of a fixed algorithm over a specified problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class, \(\mathcal O\) an oracle model, and \(A\) a fixed possibly randomized algorithm. For instance \(f\), define \(T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)\) as the least number of oracle calls after which \(A\) returns an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output with probability at least \(1-\delta\). The worst-case class complexity of \(A\) is \[C_A(\mathcal F,\varepsilon,\delta)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta),\] with value \(+\infty\) if no finite uniform bound exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case class complexity is the largest query requirement of one fixed algorithm over all instances in the declared class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\), the oracle model, and the admissible-output criterion are fixed.
Probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and any stochastic oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\mathcal F,\varepsilon,\delta)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: worst-case complexity uses a supremum over instances after fixing the algorithm and information model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytical Complexity Bound for Uniform-Grid Global Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded upper bound depending on the source-defined uniform-grid method and epsilon-accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\epsilon>0\), \(B_n=[0,1]^n\), and suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) satisfies
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\qquad\forall x,y\in B_n
\]
for some \(L\ge0\). For the source-defined uniform-grid method \(\mathcal G\) and its stated \(\epsilon\)-accuracy criterion,
\[
\mathcal A(\mathcal G)\le\left(\left\lfloor\frac{L}{2\epsilon}\right\rfloor+1\right)^n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated class of L-Lipschitz objectives on the n-dimensional unit box, the analytical complexity of the source-defined uniform-grid method is at most (floor(L divided by 2 epsilon) plus 1) raised to the nth power.

\forall x,y\in B_n,\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty
\mathcal G\text{ is the source-defined uniform-grid method under the stated }\epsilon\text{-accuracy criterion}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-oracle lower bound on an infinity-ball domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The function-class notation is preserved without further interpretation because Definition 3.36 is not included in the packet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $n\ge1$, $R>0$, $M>0$, and $\epsilon>0$. For every nonempty convex set $Q\subseteq B_\infty(0,R)$ and every $f\in\mathcal F_M^{0,0}(B_\infty(0,R))$, suppose each query $x\in B_\infty(0,R)$ returns only $f(x)$. A possibly randomized algorithm cannot uniformly guarantee an output $\hat x\in Q$ satisfying $f(\hat x)-\min_{y\in Q}f(y)\le\epsilon$ with at most $T$ oracle calls unless $T\ge n\ln\!\left(\frac{MR}{8\epsilon}\right)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over the stated convex problem class on the radius-R infinity ball, even a possibly randomized algorithm using only function values cannot guarantee epsilon-suboptimality unless it makes at least n log(MR/(8 epsilon)) oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: n\ge 1
\epsilon>0
\varnothing\ne Q\subseteq B_\infty(0,R)\text{ is convex}
f\in\mathcal F_M^{0,0}(B_\infty(0,R))
\text{each oracle query }x\in B_\infty(0,R)\text{ returns only }f(x)
\text{the algorithm may be randomized}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall(Q,f),\ \hat x\in Q,\ f(\hat x)-\min_{y\in Q}f(y)\le\epsilon\right]\Longrightarrow T\ge n\ln\!\left(\frac{MR}{8\epsilon}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-Square Complexity from a Square-Root Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representative sublinear rate and its induced accuracy complexity; no particular algorithm or problem geometry is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c>0\) and suppose a method's error measure satisfies \(r_k\le c/\sqrt{k}\) for every integer \(k\ge1\). For every \(\epsilon>0\), the bound guarantees \(r_k\le\epsilon\) whenever \(k\ge(c/\epsilon)^2\); consequently, \(\lceil(c/\epsilon)^2\rceil\) is an upper iteration-complexity estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the error after every positive iteration k is at most c divided by the square root of k, then accuracy epsilon is guaranteed once k is at least the square of c divided by epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
r_k\le\frac{c}{\sqrt{k}}\quad\text{for every integer }k\ge1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge\left(\frac{c}{\epsilon}\right)^2\;\Longrightarrow\;r_k\le\epsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Rate and Logarithmic Accuracy Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General geometric convergence estimate, independent of a particular method family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c>0\), \(0<q\le1\), and let \((r_k)\) be a nonnegative error sequence satisfying \(r_k\le c(1-q)^k\) for every integer \(k\ge1\). Then \(r_k\le ce^{-qk}\). For \(\epsilon>0\), any integer \(k\ge\max\{1,\,q^{-1}\ln(c/\epsilon)\}\) guarantees \(r_k\le\epsilon\); hence the dependence on the requested accuracy is logarithmic, up to integer rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric error bound with contraction parameter q is bounded by exponential decay. Solving the exponential bound for a positive target accuracy gives an iteration estimate proportional to one over q times the logarithm of c divided by epsilon, with the iteration index rounded upward.
assumptions_latex: 0<q\le1
\epsilon>0
r_k\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad r_k\le c(1-q)^k\text{ for every integer }k\ge1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_k\le ce^{-qk},\qquad k\ge\max\!\left\{1,\frac{1}{q}\ln\frac{c}{\epsilon}\right\}\;\Longrightarrow\;r_k\le\epsilon

children.title: Minimax Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Best attainable worst-case performance under a specified information model.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best worst-case query complexity among algorithms admissible under one oracle-information model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak A(\mathcal O)\) be the algorithms admissible under oracle model \(\mathcal O\), and let \(T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)\) be the query count needed by \(A\) to produce an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output with probability at least \(1-\delta\). The minimax oracle complexity is \[C^*(\mathcal F,\mathcal O,\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A(\mathcal O)}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta).\] Thus upper bounds exhibit an admissible algorithm, whereas lower bounds apply to every admissible algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimax oracle complexity minimizes, over admissible algorithms, the maximum query requirement over the problem class.
assumptions_latex: The problem class \(\mathcal F\), oracle model \(\mathcal O\), and success criterion are fixed.
All algorithms in \(\mathfrak A(\mathcal O)\) obey the same information restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A(\mathcal O)}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)\).

notation.meaning: Algorithms admissible under oracle model O.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimax oracle complexity is the infimum over algorithms of worst-case query cost

children.title: Instance-Dependent Complexity
children.top_down_role: Resource characterization using properties of individual instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query requirement retained as a function of the individual instance or its parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an oracle model and an algorithm \(A\). For an individual instance \(f\), its instance-dependent complexity is \[C_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb N: \Pr(S_f(x_t)\le\varepsilon)\ge 1-\delta\},\] where \(S_f\) is the declared error or stationarity measure. A parameterized instance-dependent bound has the form \(C_A(f,\varepsilon,\delta)\le B(\theta(f),\varepsilon,\delta)\), where \(\theta(f)\) records instance properties; no supremum over the full problem class is taken.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instance-dependent complexity measures queries for one instance, possibly bounded using its own conditioning, geometry, sparsity, or other parameters.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm, oracle model, and success measure \(S_f\) are fixed.
The probability includes every declared source of algorithmic or oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complexity remains indexed by \(f\), or by parameters \(\theta(f)\), rather than being maximized over a class.

notation.meaning: Declared instancewise error or stationarity measure.

children.title: Distribution-Relative Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity relative to a distribution over problem instances.

children.title: Distributional Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications relative to specified instance distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query complexity relative to a fixed distribution over problem instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a probability distribution on a problem class \(\mathcal F\). For algorithm \(A\), define its distributional query complexity at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) and failure level \(\delta\) by \[C_A(P,\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb N:\Pr_{f\sim P,A,\mathcal O}(S_f(x_t)\le\varepsilon)\ge 1-\delta\}.\] The probability is joint over the sampled instance and all declared algorithmic or oracle randomness. Unlike worst-case class complexity, this quantity may ignore a set of instances having \(P\)-probability at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributional complexity is the query budget achieving the target accuracy with prescribed probability when the instance is drawn from a fixed distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a fixed probability distribution on \(\mathcal F\).
The algorithm, oracle model, success measure, and randomness convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(P,\varepsilon,\delta)\) is a distribution-relative high-probability query requirement.

notation.meaning: Accuracy or stationarity measure for instance f.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distribution-relative complexity takes probability jointly over an instance distribution and execution randomness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Average-Case Complexity
children.top_down_role: Expected complexity across a distribution of instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Average-Case Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected resource consumption under a fixed instance distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a probability distribution on \(\mathcal F\), and let \(T_A(f,\varepsilon)\) be the stopping-time number of oracle calls used by algorithm \(A\) before it returns an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output on instance \(f\). The average-case query complexity is \[C_A^{\mathrm{avg}}(P,\varepsilon)=\mathbb E_{f\sim P,A,\mathcal O}[T_A(f,\varepsilon)],\] provided the expectation is well defined in \([0,+\infty]\). Finite high-probability complexity alone does not imply this expectation is finite without tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average-case complexity is the expected stopping-time query count under the instance distribution and all declared execution randomness.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a fixed distribution over instances.
\(T_A(f,\varepsilon)\) is a measurable nonnegative extended-valued stopping time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A^{\mathrm{avg}}(P,\varepsilon)=\mathbb E[T_A(f,\varepsilon)]\).

notation.meaning: Stopping-time query count on instance f.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: average-case resource use is the expectation of the instancewise stopping cost
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected stopping-cost definition fits Average-Case Complexity and correctly includes declared execution randomness. No source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Tail-Sensitive Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distribution-relative classifications sensitive to rare difficult instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Sensitive Complexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile and tail-moment resource measures that distinguish rare expensive executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the random stopping cost \(T=T_A(f,\varepsilon)\), with \(f\sim P\) and all execution randomness included, define the upper-tail complexity profile and its quantile by \[\psi(t)=\Pr(T>t),\qquad Q_{1-\delta}(T)=\inf\{t\ge0:\psi(t)\le\delta\}.\] A tail-sensitive regime reports \(Q_{1-\delta}(T)\), a bound on \(\psi(t)\), or a tail moment such as \(\mathbb E[T^p]\) for specified \(p>1\). These measures distinguish distributions with equal means but different rare-event costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail-sensitive complexity records resource quantiles, tail probabilities, or higher moments, revealing rare expensive runs hidden by an expectation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a measurable nonnegative resource cost.
The instance distribution and every source of execution randomness are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is characterized by \(\psi(t)\), \(Q_{1-\delta}(T)\), or specified moments beyond \(\mathbb E[T]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: quantiles, survival functions, and higher moments are standard tail-sensitive summaries

children.title: Nonsmooth Convex First-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: Value–subgradient and support-model complexity for general convex objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic value–subgradient oracle complexity for Lipschitz convex minimization on a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be closed and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and suppose every returned subgradient satisfies \(\lVert g\rVert_2\le G\). Assume a minimizer \(x^*\) exists and the initial point satisfies \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2\le R\). In the deterministic local value–subgradient oracle model, projected subgradient schemes attain \(f(\bar x)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon\) using \(O(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) queries, and, in sufficiently large dimension, the class requires \(\Omega(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) queries in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General Lipschitz convex minimization has optimal deterministic first-order query complexity of order squared inverse accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has subgradients bounded by \(G\) on \(X\).
A minimizer lies within Euclidean distance \(R\) of \(x_0\).
The lower bound uses a sufficiently large dimension and a local value–subgradient oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimax query complexity is \(\Theta((GR/\varepsilon)^2)\), up to universal constants.

notation.meaning: Initial distance bound to a minimizer.

review_flags: REQUEST_SOURCES: supplied locators do not identify matching nonsmooth upper- and lower-bound results
exact lower-bound dimension and oracle conventions require authoritative sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind and inverse-square rate fit the nonsmooth convex regime, but the matching lower bound depends on precise domain, oracle locality, dimension, and initialization conventions. children.title: Smooth Convex First-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: Gradient-oracle complexity under smooth convex geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic gradient-oracle complexity for Euclidean smooth convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x^*\) minimize \(f\), and suppose \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2\le R\). Accelerated first-order methods produce an iterate \(x_k\) satisfying \(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon\) after \(O(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) value-gradient queries. Under the deterministic local first-order oracle model and in sufficiently large dimension, a matching lower bound \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) holds over this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex minimization has optimal deterministic gradient-oracle complexity proportional to the square root of inverse objective accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm.
A minimizer is within distance \(R\) of the initial point.
The lower bound uses a sufficiently large dimension and a local deterministic first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimax query complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\), up to universal constants.

notation.meaning: Initial distance bound to a minimizer.

children.title: Strongly Convex First-Order Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic gradient-oracle complexity for smooth strongly convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(0<\mu\le L\), and write \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f(x^*)\). Accelerated gradient methods achieve \(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon\) using \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\) value-gradient queries when \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta_0\). In the deterministic local first-order oracle model, a matching lower bound holds, up to universal constants and standard initialization conventions, when the dimension is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth strongly convex minimization has optimal accelerated query complexity proportional to the square root of the condition number times a logarithmic accuracy factor.

The requested error satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta_0\).
The lower bound uses a sufficiently large dimension and a local deterministic first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimax query complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\) under the stated conventions.

children.title: Composite First-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: First-order complexity for objectives with explicit composite structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle complexity for minimizing a smooth-plus-proximable convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, where \(f\) is convex and differentiable and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. A composite first-order oracle call at \(x\) evaluates \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\), while a proximal call at parameter \(\lambda>0\) returns \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)\). For an algorithm \(A\), its composite complexity at accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) is the ordered pair \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{\nabla f},N_{\operatorname{prox} g})\) required to output \(x\) satisfying \(F(x)-\inf F\leq\varepsilon\). A scalar complexity is meaningful only after specifying how these two call types are weighted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite complexity counts smooth first-order calls and proximal calls needed to attain a prescribed objective gap, retaining separate counts unless a cost weighting is specified.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin} F\neq\varnothing\).
The oracle and proximal map are evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{\nabla f},N_{\operatorname{prox} g})\) with \(F(x)-\inf F\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Proximal map of the nonsmooth component.

children.title: Constrained First-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: First-order complexity under explicit feasibility constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate accounting for first-order information and feasible-set operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\), where \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex set and \(f\) is convex and differentiable. Fix a feasible-set interface \(S_C\), such as Euclidean projection or linear minimization. The constrained first-order complexity of an algorithm \(A\) at accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) is \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{\nabla f},N_{S_C})\), the worst-case numbers of gradient-oracle and feasible-set-interface calls needed to return \(x\in C\) with \(f(x)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon\). Projection and linear-minimization complexities are distinct regimes and cannot be identified without an explicit simulation or cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained complexity separately counts gradient information and the chosen feasible-set operation needed to return a feasible point with the requested objective gap.
assumptions_latex: \(f^\star=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is finite and attained.
The interface \(S_C\) and its accuracy convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{\nabla f},N_{S_C})\) and \(x\in C\), \(f(x)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Specified feasible-set oracle or subproblem interface.

children.title: Mixed-Interface Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting for first-order access combined with structured subproblem interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Interface Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued complexity for algorithms using heterogeneous oracle interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm access a problem only through interfaces \(\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_m\), whose calls may have incomparable costs. For a success predicate \(Q_\varepsilon(x)\), define its mixed-interface complexity by \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_1(\varepsilon),\ldots,N_m(\varepsilon))\), where \(N_i(\varepsilon)\) is the worst-case number of calls to \(\mathcal O_i\) before \(A\) outputs \(x\) satisfying \(Q_\varepsilon(x)\). Given positive weights \(w_i\), the induced scalar cost is \(C_{A,w}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_iN_i(\varepsilon)\). Without weights or a dominance convention, comparison uses the componentwise partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-interface complexity records one call count per oracle type; scalar comparison requires declared costs, while unweighted comparison is componentwise.
assumptions_latex: The interface family \((\mathcal O_i)_{i=1}^m\) is fixed before execution.
The success predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\) is explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_1,\ldots,N_m)\), or \(C_{A,w}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_iN_i\) under declared weights.

notation.meaning: The i-th oracle or structured interface.
Calls made to the i-th interface.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vector resource-accounting convention is coherent and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for the mixed-interface complexity model, weighted scalarization, or componentwise comparison convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex gradient-descent bound measured by gradient-norm stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable, bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Gradient descent with \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}
abla f(x_k)\) satisfies \(\min_{0\leq k<K}\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2\leq 2L(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})/K\). Consequently, to return an iterate \(x_k\) with \(\|
abla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\), it suffices to make at most \(\left\lceil 2L(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})/\varepsilon^2ightceil\) gradient-oracle calls, up to the convention for counting the initial evaluation.

children.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Expected and high-confidence complexity under local stochastic information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected and high-confidence call complexity under an unbiased, bounded-variance stochastic first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) generate iterates \((x_k)_{k\geq 0}\), let \(\mathcal F_k\) denote the history available when \(x_k\) is chosen, and let a stochastic first-order oracle return \(G(x_k,\xi_k)\). Assume \(\mathbb E[G(x_k,\xi_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=g(x_k)\), where \(g(x_k)\) is the target gradient or a specified subgradient. For a nonnegative measurable error measure \(M\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), define \(C_A^{\mathrm{exp}}(\varepsilon)=\min\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\mathbb E[M(x_N)]\leq\varepsilon\}\), when this set is nonempty. For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), define \(C_A^{\mathrm{hp}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\min\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\mathbb P(M(x_N)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\}\), when this set is nonempty. Each sampled oracle response counts as one call unless the computational model explicitly assigns a different cost to a mini-batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a specified unbiased stochastic first-order oracle, expected complexity is the least sample count attaining the requested expected error, while high-confidence complexity is the least count attaining that error with the declared success probability. Batch accounting must be specified separately.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[\|G(x_k,\xi_k)-g(x_k)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma^2\) for every queried iterate \(x_k\).
Conditional on \(\mathcal F_k\), the oracle uses fresh randomness \(\xi_k\) governed by the declared sampling model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A^{\mathrm{exp}}(\varepsilon)=\min\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\mathbb E[M(x_N)]\leq\varepsilon\}\) and \(C_A^{\mathrm{hp}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\min\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\mathbb P(M(x_N)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\}\).

notation.meaning: Algorithmic history available when the k-th query point is selected.
Random stochastic first-order response at the k-th query.
Target gradient or specified subgradient at the k-th query point.
Nonnegative measurable error or success measure.
Allowed failure probability in the high-confidence criterion.

children.title: Finite-Sum Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured in reusable component calls and dataset-normalized units.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-gradient accounting and dataset-normalized epoch complexity for finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), an incremental first-order oracle queried with \((x,i)\) returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\), or the subgradient analogue. The finite-sum oracle complexity \(N_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)\) is the number of component-oracle calls required to produce an output satisfying the declared accuracy predicate. The dataset-normalized complexity is \(N_{\mathrm{epoch}}(\varepsilon)=N_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)/n\). Repeated queries to the same component count separately, whereas reuse of stored values incurs memory and arithmetic costs but no new component-oracle call under this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum complexity counts reusable component evaluations; dividing by dataset size gives epoch-equivalent complexity, while storage and arithmetic remain separate resources.
assumptions_latex: The component index set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The oracle response and permitted storage are fixed by the computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{epoch}}(\varepsilon)=N_{\mathrm{IFO}}(\varepsilon)/n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incremental-oracle and epoch-equivalent definitions fit the finite-sum leaf, but no authoritative source is supplied for the response model, repeated-query accounting, or the separation of stored reuse from new component calls.

children.title: Coordinate Oracle Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity measured in single-coordinate derivative queries and updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). A coordinate first-order oracle queried with \((x,i)\) returns the partial derivative \(\nabla_i f(x)\), optionally together with data needed to update coordinate \(i\). For an accuracy predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\), the coordinate oracle complexity \(N_{\mathrm{coord}}(\varepsilon)\) is the worst-case or expected number of such queries, according to the declared regime, required before the algorithm outputs \(x\) satisfying \(Q_\varepsilon(x)\). One full-gradient-equivalent unit is \(d\) coordinate calls only when every coordinate query has comparable cost and no shared computation is charged twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate complexity counts individual partial-derivative queries; conversion to full-gradient equivalents requires comparable per-coordinate costs and an explicit normalization.
assumptions_latex: The coordinate system and sampling rule are fixed.
Each query exposes only the declared coordinate information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{full\text{-}equiv}}(\varepsilon)=N_{\mathrm{coord}}(\varepsilon)/d\) only under uniform comparable coordinate costs.

children.title: Block Oracle Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Block Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity measured in derivative queries or updates on prescribed orthogonal variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d,m\in\mathbb N\) and let \(\mathbb R^d=V_1\mathbin{\oplus^{\perp}}\cdots\mathbin{\oplus^{\perp}}V_m\) be a fixed orthogonal block decomposition, with orthogonal projections \(P_j\). A block first-order oracle queried with \((x,j)\in\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,m\}\) returns \(P_j\nabla f(x)\), optionally together with other block-update data fixed by the oracle specification. For \(\varepsilon>0\) and a declared accuracy predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\), the block oracle complexity \(N_{\mathrm{block}}(\varepsilon)\) is the worst-case or expected number of block queries, according to the declared regime, required to output \(x\) satisfying \(Q_\varepsilon(x)\). If \(T\) queries use block indices \(j_1,\ldots,j_T\) and \(s_j=\dim V_j\), the associated size-weighted count is \(N_{\mathrm{scalar\text{-}equiv}}=\sum_{t=1}^T s_{j_t}\). This size-weighted count and the unweighted count \(N_{\mathrm{block}}=T\) are distinct resources whenever block sizes or query costs differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block complexity counts partial-gradient queries on fixed orthogonal blocks. An unweighted block count differs from the sum of queried block dimensions when blocks have unequal sizes or costs.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable on every queried point.
The orthogonal decomposition \((V_j)_{j=1}^m\), the information returned by each query, and the worst-case or expected evaluation regime are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{block}}=T\) and \(N_{\mathrm{scalar\text{-}equiv}}=\sum_{t=1}^T s_{j_t}\) are distinct declared complexity measures.

children.title: Partial-Update Granularity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Update Granularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversions among update, coordinate-equivalent, and full-pass complexity units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(t\) updates a subset \(S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) of size \(s_t\). Three granularity measures are the update count \(N_{\mathrm{upd}}=T\), the coordinate-equivalent work \(N_{\mathrm{coord}}=\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\), and the full-pass-equivalent work \(N_{\mathrm{pass}}=d^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\). For constant granularity \(s_t=s\), these satisfy \(N_{\mathrm{coord}}=sN_{\mathrm{upd}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{pass}}=(s/d)N_{\mathrm{upd}}\). These identities normalize information volume only; they do not equate wall-clock costs when shared computation, communication, synchronization, or memory access is significant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial-update work can be reported as update count, touched coordinates, or full-pass equivalents; the conversions normalize granularity but not execution time.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\neq S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) for every update.
Each touched coordinate contributes one unit to coordinate-equivalent work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{upd}}=T\), \(N_{\mathrm{coord}}=\sum_{t=1}^T|S_t|\), and \(N_{\mathrm{pass}}=N_{\mathrm{coord}}/d\).

children.title: Zeroth-Order Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Value- and comparison-based complexity with dimension and noise dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Zeroth-Order Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query complexity using values or comparisons without derivative access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A zeroth-order value oracle queried at \(x\in\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) returns \(Y(x)=f(x)+\eta(x)\), while a comparison oracle queried at \((x,y)\) returns information about the sign of \(f(x)-f(y)\), possibly corrupted by noise. For an accuracy predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\), zeroth-order complexity is the number of value or comparison queries required to output \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(Q_\varepsilon(\widehat x)\), in expectation or with declared confidence. The oracle type, dimension \(d\), noise model, smoothness class, and admissible adaptivity are part of the complexity specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeroth-order complexity counts noisy value or comparison queries, with dimension, noise, smoothness, confidence, and adaptivity included in the model.
assumptions_latex: The query domain \(\mathcal X\) and function class are fixed.
The distributional or deterministic noise constraints are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\varepsilon)=\min\{N:Q_\varepsilon(\widehat x_N)\text{ holds under the declared success convention}\}\).

notation.meaning: Oracle noise at the query point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately identifies value and comparison models as distinct zeroth-order interfaces, but no source supports their combined taxonomy, noise conventions, success criteria, or dimension dependence. Separate or jointly authoritative locators are required.

children.title: Structured-Subproblem Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured in projection, proximal, resolvent, linear-optimization, or best-response calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Subproblem Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector accounting for projection, proximal, resolvent, linear, or best-response calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S=(S_1,\ldots,S_m)\) be specified structured-subproblem interfaces, each returning an exact or tolerance-certified solution of its declared auxiliary problem. Examples include projection, proximal, resolvent, linear-minimization, and best-response interfaces. For an algorithm \(A\), define \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{S_1},\ldots,N_{S_m})\), where \(N_{S_i}\) counts calls made before an output satisfies the accuracy predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\). If calls are inexact, the requested internal tolerances are part of each query. A scalar count is valid only after declaring unit costs or weights for the heterogeneous subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured-subproblem complexity separately counts each auxiliary solver interface, including internal tolerances; heterogeneous calls require explicit weights for scalar aggregation.
assumptions_latex: Every interface \(S_i\) has a fixed input-output specification.
The outer success predicate \(Q_\varepsilon\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(\varepsilon)=(N_{S_1},\ldots,N_{S_m})\), with scalar cost \(\sum_{i=1}^m w_iN_{S_i}\) only for declared \(w_i>0\).

notation.meaning: Number of calls to interface i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-dimensional separation-oracle feasibility lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The regularity condition on each feasible set is retained by reference because Assumption 3.2.1 is not expanded in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $n\in\mathbb N$, $R>0$, and $\epsilon\in(0,R/2)$. For the class of sets $S\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ satisfying Assumption~3.2.1 and $S\subseteq B_\infty(0,R)$, every algorithm accessing $S$ only through a separation oracle requires, in the worst case, at least $n\ln\!\left(\frac{R}{2\epsilon}\right)$ oracle calls to output either a point in $S$ or a certificate that $S\cap B_\infty(0,\epsilon)=\varnothing$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For admissible subsets of the radius-R infinity ball, any separation-oracle algorithm needs at least n log(R/(2 epsilon)) calls in the worst case to find a feasible point or certify that the set has no point in the radius-epsilon infinity ball.

0<\epsilon<R/2
S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ satisfies Assumption~3.2.1}
S\subseteq B_\infty(0,R)
\text{the algorithm accesses }S\text{ only through a separation oracle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{worst}}\ge n\ln\!\left(\frac{R}{2\epsilon}\right)

children.title: Complexity Dependence Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Navigation among qualitative complexity dependences without embedding bound statements.

children.title: Accuracy-Dependence Families
children.top_down_role: Polynomial, logarithmic, and finite-termination dependence on requested accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Dependence Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by asymptotic dependence of resource complexity on requested accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(\varepsilon)\) be a nonincreasing worst-case resource bound for tolerances \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0\). Its accuracy dependence is polynomial if \(C(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^{-p})\) for some \(p>0\); logarithmic if \(C(\varepsilon)=O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\); and finite-termination if there exists \(N_\star<\infty\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), such that \(C(\varepsilon)\leq N_\star\) throughout the stated tolerance range. Constants hidden by \(O(\cdot)\) may depend on problem parameters but not on \(\varepsilon\). A mixed bound is classified by its dominant term as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accuracy families classify complexity as polynomial, logarithmic, or uniformly finite in inverse tolerance, with hidden constants independent of the requested accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(C(\varepsilon)\) measures one fixed resource under one fixed oracle model.
All non-accuracy problem parameters are held fixed as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(\varepsilon)\in O(\varepsilon^{-p})\), \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\), or \(O(1)\) with a uniform finite-termination bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is provided, and the proposed families are not disjoint as written: a logarithmic bound is also polynomially bounded in inverse accuracy, while a uniform O(1) complexity bound requires a careful distinction from algorithmic finite termination. An authoritative taxonomy and an explicit precedence or exact-growth convention are needed.

children.title: Dimensional Dependence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications distinguished by explicit ambient-dimension dependence.

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications with explicit ambient- or effective-dimension dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies oracle bounds whose worst-case query count varies essentially with ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) be a class of optimization problems over a \(d\)-dimensional space, let \(\mathcal O\) be an oracle model, and let \(Q(d,\varepsilon)\) denote the minimax number of oracle calls required to return an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate solution. The complexity is dimension-dependent on a dimension set \(D\) if there exist \(d_1,d_2\in D\) and a fixed admissible accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(Q(d_1,\varepsilon)\ne Q(d_2,\varepsilon)\), and the dependence cannot be absorbed into constants uniform over \(D\). Polynomial, logarithmic, and threshold dependence on \(d\) all qualify.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle complexity is dimension-dependent when its minimax query bound varies essentially with dimension and that variation cannot be hidden in dimension-uniform constants.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_d\) and the oracle model \(\mathcal O\) are fixed for each compared dimension.
The accuracy criterion defining an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate solution is identical across dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(d,\varepsilon)\) has nonconstant essential dependence on \(d\).

notation.meaning: minimax oracle-query complexity in dimension d at accuracy epsilon

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. The proposed criterion combines pointwise nonconstancy with the informal condition that dependence cannot be absorbed into uniform constants; that condition is not mathematically defined and may classify incidental finite-dimensional variation as essential dependence. An authoritative oracle-complexity source is needed to fix the intended asymptotic or uniform notion.

children.title: Dimension-Free Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications without explicit dimensional scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Free Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses uniform worst-case oracle bounds over all finite ambient dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(d,\varepsilon)\) be the minimax oracle-query complexity for a family \(\{\mathcal F_d:d\in D\}\) under one fixed oracle and accuracy convention. The family has dimension-free complexity on \(D\) if there exists a function \(B(\varepsilon,\theta)\), depending only on accuracy and dimension-independent problem parameters \(\theta\), such that \(Q(d,\varepsilon)\le B(\varepsilon,\theta)\) for every \(d\in D\) and every admissible \(\varepsilon\). Constants implicit in \(B\) must also be uniform in \(d\); computational cost per query may still depend on dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity is dimension-free when one query bound, including its constants, applies uniformly to every dimension, although processing each oracle answer may remain dimension-dependent.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface and accuracy criterion are uniform over \(d\in D\).
The parameter vector \(\theta\) contains no dimension-dependent quantity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{d\in D}Q(d,\varepsilon)\le B(\varepsilon,\theta)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is mathematically coherent and correctly separates query complexity from per-query computational cost, but no source or inspectable locator supports this particular uniform-over-dimension definition and its treatment of dimension-independent parameters.

children.title: Dimensional Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where dimension-sensitive behavior changes qualitative form.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimensional Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes thresholds where finite-dimensional restrictions change an oracle-complexity law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an oracle lower-bound construction requires \(m(T)\) mutually independent directions to certify hardness through \(T\) rounds in dimension \(d\). The construction establishes its nominal lower bound only while \(d\ge m(T)\). Consequently, if the corresponding dimension-unrestricted complexity is \(T_\infty(\varepsilon)\), the threshold \(d_*(\varepsilon)=m(T_\infty(\varepsilon))\) separates two regimes: for \(d\ge d_*(\varepsilon)\) the unrestricted accuracy law can persist, whereas for \(d<d_*(\varepsilon)\) that construction no longer proves it and a finite-dimensional bound or algorithm may govern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimensional transition occurs when the dimension becomes too small to support all independent hard directions required by an unrestricted oracle lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The lower-bound construction consumes \(m(T)\) independent directions by round \(T\).
The ambient decision space has finite dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction changes validity at \(d=m(T)\), inducing an accuracy-dependent threshold \(d_*(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: number of independent directions required through T rounds
dimension threshold for the unrestricted lower-bound regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim describes a common direction-counting mechanism rather than a general property of dimensional regime transitions. The threshold formula depends on the particular lower-bound construction and requires a source specifying the construction, its dimension requirement, and the meaning of the dimension-unrestricted complexity.

children.title: Conditioning-Geometry Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity organized by smoothness, curvature, radius, width, and related geometric parameters.

children.title: Condition-Parameter Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications organized by smoothness or curvature conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Parameter Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical first-order dependence on the smooth strongly convex condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm, with \(0<\mu\le L\), minimizer \(x_*\), and condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\). Accelerated first-order methods admit an iterate satisfying \(f(x_T)-f(x_*)\le\varepsilon\) after \(T=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}\log\!\frac{f(x_0)-f(x_*)}{\varepsilon}\right)\) gradient-oracle calls. Thus, within this canonical class, the query complexity depends on conditioning through \(\sqrt{\kappa}\), up to universal constants and the logarithmic accuracy factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth strongly convex minimization, accelerated gradient methods require on the order of square-root condition number times a logarithmic accuracy factor in gradient calls.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm.
The oracle returns exact gradients and function values.
\(0<\varepsilon<f(x_0)-f(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=O\!\left(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log\!\frac{f(x_0)-f(x_*)}{\varepsilon}\right)\).

children.title: Geometric-Parameter Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications organized by radius, width, diameter, or related geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Parameter Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonsmooth first-order dependence on Lipschitz scale and feasible-set radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and suppose every returned subgradient satisfies \(\lVert g\rVert_2\le G\). If a minimizer \(x_*\in X\) obeys \(\lVert x_0-x_*\rVert_2\le R\), projected subgradient descent with an appropriate horizon-dependent stepsize returns an averaged iterate \(\bar x_T\) such that \(f(\bar x_T)-f(x_*)\le GR/\sqrt{T}\). Hence \(T=O(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) oracle calls suffice for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected subgradient complexity scales quadratically with the product of the subgradient bound and the initial radius, illustrating dependence on feasible geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has Euclidean subgradients bounded by \(G\) on \(X\).
Euclidean projection onto \(X\) is available.
A minimizer lies within distance \(R\) of \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f(x_*)\le GR/\sqrt T\), so \(T=O(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: distance bound from the initial point to a minimizer
weighted or uniform average of generated iterates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-subgradient rate is standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but the exact constant GR/sqrt(T) depends on the stepsize, indexing, and averaging convention. No citation with a theorem, section, or page locator is supplied to establish those conventions.

children.title: Conditioning–Geometry Interactions
children.top_down_role: Regimes where conditioning parameters interact with feasible-set geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning–Geometry Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses how the chosen norm jointly determines conditioning and geometric scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be a norm with dual norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_*\). If \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth relative to this norm and \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to the same norm, then \(\kappa=L/\mu\) is norm-dependent. Likewise, a feasible radius \(R=\sup_{x\in X}\lVert x-x_0\rVert\) and a gradient bound \(G=\sup_{x\in X}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_*\) depend on the primal-dual geometry. Therefore expressions such as \(GR\) or \(\sqrt{\kappa}\) must be evaluated in one compatible geometry; changing the norm can improve one parameter while worsening another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condition numbers, radii, and gradient bounds are coupled through the chosen primal-dual norm, so their complexity contributions cannot be optimized independently.
assumptions_latex: Smoothness and strong convexity are measured using the same primal norm.
Gradient magnitudes are measured in the corresponding dual norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complexity parameters \(\kappa\), \(G\), and \(R\) vary jointly with the selected geometry.

notation.meaning: dual norm associated with the selected primal norm
condition number in the selected norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the interaction leaf and correctly emphasizes compatible primal-dual geometry. However, no source is supplied, and the phrases smooth and strongly convex relative to a norm require source-aligned definitions before the joint parameter claim can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Accelerated Complexity Families
children.top_down_role: Oracle-complexity families associated with acceleration across compatible access models.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Complexity Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical accelerated rates for smooth convex and smooth strongly convex gradient-oracle models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and let \(x_*\) minimize \(f\), with \(\lVert x_0-x_*\rVert_2\le R\). An accelerated gradient method attains \(f(x_T)-f(x_*)\le O(LR^2/T^2)\), hence requires \(T=O(\!\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) gradient queries. If, additionally, \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, an accelerated method attains geometric convergence and requires \(T=O(\!\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(x_0)-f(x_*))/\varepsilon))\) queries. These are distinct compatible-access complexity families, not one bound with silently interchangeable hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration yields inverse-square iteration decay for smooth convex objectives and square-root-condition-number logarithmic complexity under additional strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns exact first-order information.
\(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth in the Euclidean norm.
For the linear-rate family only, \(f\) is also \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=O(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) in the convex case, and \(T=O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log((f(x_0)-f(x_*))/\varepsilon))\) in the strongly convex case.

notation.meaning: initial distance bound to a minimizer
