children.title: Query-Depth Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications distinguishing total queries from adaptive depth.

children.title: Parallelism Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications organized by simultaneous query capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallelism Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates total oracle calls from synchronous oracle-round depth under batch access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a \(b\)-parallel oracle model, an algorithm proceeds for \(D\) rounds and submits at most \(b\) query points in each round. Queries within round \(r\) may depend on the transcript through round \(r-1\), but not on answers produced during round \(r\). Its total query count satisfies \(Q\le bD\). Parallelism dependence is the variation of the minimax round complexity \(D_b(\varepsilon)\) with batch width \(b\), with the problem class, oracle response, success criterion, and accuracy fixed. A reduction in \(D_b\) need not imply a proportional reduction in \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel oracle complexity measures how required adaptive rounds change with batch width, separately from the total number of oracle queries.
assumptions_latex: All queries in one round are chosen before any answer from that round is observed.
The oracle and accuracy criterion remain fixed as \(b\) varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_b(\varepsilon)\) records parallel-round dependence, while \(Q\le bD_b(\varepsilon)\) records total queries.

notation.meaning: maximum number of simultaneous queries per round

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition cleanly distinguishes synchronous round depth from total query count and fits the leaf, but no source with an inspectable locator establishes the selected b-parallel oracle convention or the associated minimax quantity.

children.title: Adaptivity Dependence
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications organized by sequential feedback dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures complexity by the number of sequential transcript-dependent query stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle algorithm has adaptivity depth at most \(D\) if its queries can be partitioned into batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_D\) such that every query in \(B_r\) is a measurable function only of the algorithm's internal randomness and oracle answers to batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_{r-1}\). The adaptivity complexity \(D(\varepsilon)\) is the least such depth sufficient to produce an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output with the prescribed success probability. Fully sequential algorithms may use one query per batch; nonadaptive algorithms have one batch, regardless of its size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptivity complexity is the minimum number of sequential query stages needed when each stage may use only answers from earlier stages.
assumptions_latex: The oracle transcript and admissible randomized decision rules are specified.
Accuracy and success probability are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\varepsilon)\) equals the minimum transcript-dependent batch depth achieving the target accuracy.

notation.meaning: queries issued in adaptive stage r
minimum adaptive depth at accuracy epsilon

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed adaptivity-depth definition is plausible and locally appropriate, but its measurability and randomized-transcript conventions are model-specific. No authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Query-Depth Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes balancing total query count against adaptive depth.

knowledge_statements.title: Query-Depth Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal resource relation between total queries, batch width, and adaptive depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any synchronous oracle algorithm with batch sizes \(q_1,\ldots,q_D\), total query count \(Q=\sum_{r=1}^D q_r\), and maximum width \(b=\max_r q_r\), one has \(Q\le bD\) and \(D\ge\lceil Q/b\rceil\). Accordingly, a complexity claim for parallel oracle access should report a feasible or necessary pair \((Q,D)\), not depth alone. Increasing \(b\) can reduce the counting lower bound on \(D\), but whether the reduction is attainable depends on how much information simultaneous, nonadaptive queries reveal about the hard instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total queries, batch width, and depth satisfy a counting tradeoff, but useful parallel speedup also depends on the information revealed per batch.
assumptions_latex: Queries are grouped into \(D\) synchronous batches.
Every batch contains at most \(b\) oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\le bD\) and therefore \(D\ge\lceil Q/b\rceil\).

notation.meaning: number of oracle queries in round r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting identities Q<=bD and D>=ceil(Q/b) follow from the introduced batch sizes and are correct. The broader claim about information revealed by simultaneous queries is nontrivial and uncited, while no source defines the surrounding synchronous oracle model.

children.top_down_role: Canonical mechanisms proving limits on information obtainable from finite oracle transcripts.

children.title: Resisting-Oracle Arguments
children.top_down_role: Adaptive oracle constructions preserving unresolved hard instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Resisting-Oracle Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive lower-bound mechanism that postpones commitment to an unresolved hard instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm issue queries \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\). A resisting oracle answers sequentially while maintaining a nonempty set \(\mathcal H_t\) of admissible problem instances consistent with the transcript through round \(t\), with \(\mathcal H_t\subseteq\mathcal H_{t-1}\). The responses are selected so that, after the final query, some \(f_T\in\mathcal H_T\) satisfies the oracle model and has optimization error at the algorithm's output exceeding \(\varepsilon\). If every finite transcript produced by this strategy is jointly realizable by one admissible instance, then no algorithm using at most \(T\) queries guarantees \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy on the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resisting oracle answers adaptively while preserving at least one transcript-compatible hard instance, thereby certifying a worst-case query lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Each maintained set \(\mathcal H_t\) is nonempty.
All answers through time \(T\) are jointly realizable by an admissible instance.
The final compatible instance makes the returned point more than \(\varepsilon\)-suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case oracle complexity is strictly greater than \(T\) queries for accuracy \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: instances compatible with the transcript through time t
final admissible hard instance realizing the transcript

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle captures the deterministic resisting-oracle mechanism, but no source is supplied. As written, its scope over randomized algorithms is unclear: transcript-wise realizability by potentially different final instances does not automatically establish a fixed-instance randomized lower bound without additional minimax or distributional reasoning.

children.title: Transcript-Compatible Lower-Bound Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard-instance families compatible with the same finite transcript.

children.title: Indistinguishability Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard-instance comparisons based on identical or unresolved finite transcripts.

knowledge_statements.title: Indistinguishability Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-based lower bound from instances requiring incompatible successful outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0,f_1\) be two admissible instances and let an oracle algorithm have the same distribution of transcripts through \(T\) queries under both instances. Let \(S_i(\varepsilon)\) be the set of outputs that are \(\varepsilon\)-accurate for \(f_i\), and suppose \(S_0(\varepsilon)\cap S_1(\varepsilon)=\varnothing\). Because the output distribution is a function of the transcript and internal randomness, it is identical under \(f_0\) and \(f_1\). Hence the sum of the two success probabilities is at most one, so the algorithm fails with probability at least \(1/2\) on one instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two instances yield identical query transcripts but require disjoint accurate outputs, every algorithm must fail with probability at least one half on one instance.
assumptions_latex: Transcript distributions through \(T\) queries coincide under \(f_0\) and \(f_1\).
\(S_0(\varepsilon)\cap S_1(\varepsilon)=\varnothing\).
The output depends only on the transcript and the algorithm's internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{i\in\{0,1\}}\Pr_{f_i}\{\widehat x\in S_i(\varepsilon)\}\le 1/2\).

notation.meaning: epsilon-accurate output set for instance i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied, and the mathematical version is unreliable as stated for randomized adaptive algorithms. Equality of transcript marginal distributions alone does not ensure equality of output distributions when the output may also depend on internal randomness correlated with the transcript; the required condition should concern the joint law of the transcript and retained internal randomness, or impose an equivalent decision-rule formulation.

children.title: Interpolation Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard-instance families organized through compatibility with observed oracle data.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite first-order interpolation as a certificate for transcript compatibility and deterministic oracle lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of differentiable functions on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\mathcal T_t=\{(x_i,a_i,g_i):0\le i<t\}\) be a first-order transcript consistent with the query rule of a deterministic first-order method. If there exists \(f\in\mathcal F\) such that \(f(x_i)=a_i\) and \(\nabla f(x_i)=g_i\) for every \(0\le i<t\), then \(f\) interpolates \(\mathcal T_t\), and the method produces the recorded queries and responses through those \(t\) oracle calls when run on \(f\). If the method's transcript-determined output is not accurate for such an interpolant, then that interpolant witnesses failure within \(t\) calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a transcript follows a deterministic method's query rule and a function matches every recorded value and gradient, running the method on that function reproduces the transcript. An inaccurate transcript-determined output on such an interpolant witnesses failure within the query budget.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\) and \((a_i,g_i)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\) for every \(0\le i<t\).
The method is deterministic, each \(x_i\) is generated by its query rule from the preceding entries of \(\mathcal T_t\), and its output after \(t\) calls is determined by that transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An inaccurate interpolant in \(\mathcal F\) witnesses that the specified deterministic method cannot guarantee the target accuracy within \(t\) first-order oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Transcript of the first t query-response triples.

children.title: Transcript-Compatible Hard Families
children.top_down_role: Families of difficult instances sharing the available oracle transcript.

knowledge_statements.title: Transcript-Compatible Hard Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard instances indexed by alternatives that remain consistent with an observed oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be a deterministic oracle algorithm, let \(V\) be an index set, and let \(f_v\in\mathcal F\) for \(v\in V\). The family \(\{f_v:v\in V\}\) is transcript-compatible through round \(t\) if, for every \(v,w\in V\), running \(\mathcal A\) on \(f_v\) or \(f_w\) produces identical query-response pairs through round \(t\). It is \(\varepsilon\)-hard through round \(t\) if no common output \(\widehat x\) determined by that transcript satisfies \(f_v(\widehat x)-\inf_x f_v(x)\le\varepsilon\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard family gives identical transcripts for several instances, while no output based on that transcript is accurate for all of them.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_v\) belongs to the same oracle problem class \(\mathcal F\).
Oracle responses and the algorithm's deterministic query rule are well defined through round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transcript compatibility together with \(\varepsilon\)-hardness prevents \(\mathcal A\) from guaranteeing error at most \(\varepsilon\) in \(t\) rounds.

notation.meaning: Index set of alternative hard instances.
Output determined by the common transcript.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the transcript-compatible hard-family leaf and is internally coherent, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the chosen formulation or its lower-bound conclusion.

children.title: Direction-Revelation Lower-Bound Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard constructions restricting how quickly local information reveals new directions.

children.title: Zero-Chain Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard constructions with progressively revealed coordinate structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Chain Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate zero-chain lower-bound arguments for zero-respecting deterministic first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), define \(\operatorname{prog}(x)=\max\{j:x_j
e0\}\), with \(\operatorname{prog}(0)=0\). A differentiable function \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) is a first-order zero chain if \(\operatorname{prog}(
abla f(x))\le \operatorname{prog}(x)+1\) for every \(x\). If \(x_0=0\) and a method is zero-respecting, meaning \(\operatorname{supp}(x_{k+1})\subseteq igcup_{i=0}^{k}\operatorname{supp}(
abla f(x_i))\), then \(\operatorname{prog}(x_k)\le k\). Consequently, if every \(\varepsilon\)-accurate point \(x\) satisfies \(\operatorname{prog}(x)\ge m\), the method cannot guarantee \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy in fewer than \(m\) first-order oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order zero chain reveals at most one new coordinate per call to a zero-respecting method. Therefore, if accuracy requires reaching coordinate m, fewer than m calls cannot guarantee that accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^d\) and satisfies the stated first-order zero-chain condition.
The method starts at \(x_0=0\) and is zero-respecting.
Every \(\varepsilon\)-accurate point \(x\) satisfies \(\operatorname{prog}(x)\ge m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method cannot guarantee \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy in fewer than \(m\) first-order oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Largest index of a nonzero coordinate, with value zero at the origin.
Set of nonzero coordinate indices of x.
Minimum coordinate progress required for epsilon-accuracy.

children.title: Subspace Arguments
children.top_down_role: Hard constructions restricting oracle information to growing subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds obtained by limiting the subspace revealed through successive oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_0\subseteq S_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be subspaces such that \(x_0\in S_0\). Suppose that whenever \(x_k\in S_k\), the oracle response belongs to \(S_{k+1}\), and the method forms \(x_{k+1}\) from previously revealed vectors using operations that preserve membership in \(S_{k+1}\). Then \(x_k\in S_k\) for every \(k\). Hence, if every point with objective error at most \(\varepsilon\) lies outside \(S_t\), the method cannot achieve \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy within \(t\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each response enlarges the accessible subspace only gradually, all iterates remain trapped there until enough directions have been revealed.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm's permitted operations preserve the span of previously available vectors.
The oracle maps queries in \(S_k\) to responses in \(S_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separation of \(S_t\) from all \(\varepsilon\)-accurate points yields a lower bound exceeding \(t\) oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Subspace accessible after k revelation stages.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the Subspace Arguments leaf, but the permitted span-preserving operations and the meaning of an oracle response belonging to a subspace are model-dependent. No source establishes the stated abstraction or its query-count convention.

children.title: Direction-Revelation Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limits on how rapidly local access exposes new informative directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Revelation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query lower bound from a cap on newly revealed independent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an oracle model in which the span \(S_k\) of all vectors available after \(k\) calls satisfies \(\dim(S_{k+1})-\dim(S_k)\le r\). Assume every admissible output after \(k\) calls must lie in \(S_k\), and every point with objective error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires access to a subspace of dimension at least \(m\). Then any method in this model requires at least \(\lceil(m-\dim S_0)/r\rceil\) oracle calls to guarantee \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each call reveals at most r independent directions and accuracy needs m accessible directions, at least the stated number of calls is necessary.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle call increases the accessible span dimension by at most \(r\ge1\).
All algorithm outputs belong to the currently accessible span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case oracle complexity is at least \(\lceil(m-\dim S_0)/r\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Span accessible after k oracle calls.
Maximum number of independent directions revealed per call.
Minimum accessible dimension required for the target accuracy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the assertion that an accurate point requires access to a subspace of dimension at least m is not mathematically instantiated. A model-specific source is needed to define this requirement and validate the numerical bound.

children.title: Information-Theoretic Arguments
children.top_down_role: Statistical limits derived from the information conveyed by random responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Theoretic Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fano-type conversion of limited transcript information into optimization error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be uniform on a finite set of size \(M\ge2\), and let \(Z\) be the transcript generated by an adaptive randomized oracle interaction on instance \(f_V\). For every estimator \(\widehat V=\widehat V(Z)\), Fano's inequality gives \(\mathbb P(\widehat V\ne V)\ge1-(I(V;Z)+\log 2)/\log M\). If every point having optimization error at most \(\varepsilon\) identifies its instance index uniquely, then any algorithm returning an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate point with probability at least \(1-\delta\) must satisfy \(I(V;Z)\ge(1-\delta)\log M-\log 2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an accurate optimizer would identify one of M hidden instances, the oracle transcript must carry enough mutual information to permit that identification.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is uniform on \(M\ge2\) alternatives.
An \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output determines \(V\) uniquely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Success probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(I(V;Z)\ge(1-\delta)\log M-\log 2\).

notation.meaning: Mutual information between the hidden instance and transcript.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fano-type theorem matches the information-theoretic topic and its formula is standard, but the record supplies no source for Fano's inequality or for the optimization-to-identification reduction. The latter also needs a precise decoder or separation condition in an authoritative source.

children.title: Lower-Bound Transfer Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Limits transferred through hard distributions, deterministic–randomized principles, or other oracle problems.

children.title: Distributional Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Oracle limits obtained from hard distributions over instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed hard distribution lower-bounds deterministic algorithms and supports minimax transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a distribution on instances \(f\in\mathcal F\), and let \(L(A,f)\ge0\) denote the loss of a deterministic algorithm \(A\) after at most \(t\) oracle calls. If \(\mathbb E_{f\sim\Pi}[L(A,f)]\ge c\) for every such deterministic \(A\), then \(\Pi\) is a distributional \(t\)-query lower-bound witness of level \(c\). In particular, every deterministic \(A\) has some \(f\) in the support of \(\Pi\) for which \(L(A,f)\ge c\). Under the hypotheses of a minimax principle, the same witness also lower-bounds randomized algorithms in worst-case expected loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard input distribution forces every deterministic t-query algorithm to incur average loss c, and minimax assumptions can transfer this to randomized algorithms.
assumptions_latex: \(L(A,f)\) is nonnegative and measurable under \(f\sim\Pi\).
The randomized transfer is asserted only when the relevant minimax hypotheses hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic worst-case loss after \(t\) calls is at least \(c\), with randomized transfer subject to minimax validity.

notation.meaning: Hard probability distribution over problem instances.
Performance loss after the query budget.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional witness and deterministic averaging conclusion fit the leaf. The randomized transfer is explicitly conditional but does not state the applicable minimax hypotheses, and no source locator supports either the terminology or transfer.

children.title: Randomized Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Oracle limits for algorithms using internal randomization.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-class Yao minimax transfer from deterministic distributional hardness to randomized worst-case hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be finite, let \(\mathcal A_t\) be the deterministic algorithms using at most \(t\) oracle calls, and let \(L(A,f)\) be bounded. A randomized algorithm is a distribution \(R\) over \(\mathcal A_t\). Then
\[\inf_R\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_{A\sim R}[L(A,f)]\ge\sup_{\Pi}\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_t}\mathbb E_{f\sim\Pi}[L(A,f)].\]
Consequently, if some distribution \(\Pi\) makes every deterministic \(t\)-query algorithm incur expected loss at least \(c\), every randomized \(t\)-query algorithm has a worst-case instance with expected loss at least \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Yao's principle turns one hard distribution for all deterministic algorithms into a worst-case expected-loss lower bound for every randomized algorithm.
assumptions_latex: The instance class and relevant deterministic decision rules are finite, or a valid general minimax theorem applies.
The loss \(L\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distributional deterministic hardness at level \(c\) implies randomized worst-case expected loss at least \(c\).

notation.meaning: Loss of algorithm A on instance f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and finite-class Yao transfer fit the leaf. However, no citation is provided, and finiteness of the instance class alone does not establish finiteness of the deterministic decision-rule class; the alternative minimax conditions require a precise source.

children.title: Reduction-Based Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Oracle limits transferred from other access problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Based Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity transfer through query-preserving reductions between computational problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be oracle problems. Suppose a reduction maps every instance \(u\) of \(P\) to an instance \(R(u)\) of \(Q\), simulates each query to the \(Q\)-oracle using at most \(c\) queries to the \(P\)-oracle, and converts every \(\varepsilon_Q\)-accurate solution of \(R(u)\) into an \(\varepsilon_P\)-accurate solution of \(u\). If solving \(P\) to accuracy \(\varepsilon_P\) requires at least \(T_P(\varepsilon_P)\) oracle calls, then solving \(Q\) to accuracy \(\varepsilon_Q\) requires at least \(\lceil T_P(\varepsilon_P)/c\rceil\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution- and query-preserving reduction transfers a source problem's lower bound to the target problem, adjusted by the simulation overhead.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Q\)-oracle query is simulated using at most \(c\ge1\) queries to the \(P\)-oracle.
The solution conversion maps every \(\varepsilon_Q\)-accurate solution of \(R(u)\) to an \(\varepsilon_P\)-accurate solution of \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_Q(\varepsilon_Q)\ge\lceil T_P(\varepsilon_P)/c\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Instance reduction from problem P to problem Q.
Maximum number of P-oracle queries used to simulate one Q-oracle query.
Worst-case oracle-complexity functions for P and Q.

children.title: Transfer-Principle Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting transfer among distributional, deterministic, randomized, or reduced models.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer-Principle Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which distributional, randomized, or reduction-based lower-bound transfers cease to be valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower-bound transfer is not valid merely from hardness in a different model. Distributional hardness transfers to randomized worst-case hardness only when the randomized method is representable by mixtures of the compared deterministic rules and the required minimax interchange is justified. A reduction transfers a query lower bound only when it simulates the target oracle within the claimed cost and preserves success probability, admissible adaptivity, and accuracy. If any of these conditions fails, the source lower bound alone implies no numerical lower bound for the target oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower bounds do not transfer across models unless mixtures, minimax exchange, oracle simulation, adaptivity, success probability, and accuracy are all preserved as required.
assumptions_latex: The source and target complexity claims may use different algorithm, oracle, loss, or success conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of a required minimax or reduction-preservation condition blocks the asserted lower-bound transfer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the statement correctly warns that transfer requires model-preserving hypotheses. No citation or concrete locator supports the enumerated boundaries, so the record cannot yet be relied upon as sourced candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Oracle Complexity Optimality Landscape
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between achievable and unavoidable costs within matched information models.

children.title: Oracle-Optimal Complexity Matching
children.top_down_role: Oracle-optimality classifications at the level of access and problem families.

children.title: Upper Complexity Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Achievable oracle costs across access and problem families.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper Complexity Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case oracle-call guarantee supplied by an explicit algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class, let \(E_f(x)\ge0\) be its error criterion, and let \(A\) be an oracle algorithm. A function \(U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb N\) is an upper complexity benchmark for \(A\) if, for every \(f\in\mathcal F\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), the algorithm returns \(x\) with \(E_f(x)\le\varepsilon\) after at most \(U(\varepsilon)\) oracle calls. For randomized \(A\), the probability or expectation convention must be included in the guarantee. Hence the minimax complexity satisfies \(T^*(\varepsilon)\le U(\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper benchmark is an explicit algorithmic guarantee that every admissible instance reaches the requested accuracy within a stated number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: All instances use the same specified oracle and error criterion.
Any randomized guarantee states its expectation or success-probability convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*(\varepsilon)\le U(\varepsilon)\) for every covered accuracy \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Certified upper bound on oracle calls.
Minimax oracle complexity at accuracy epsilon.
Specified optimization error on instance f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits Upper Complexity Benchmarks, and the upper-bound implication is coherent once the problem class, oracle, error criterion, and randomized convention are fixed. No authoritative source locator is supplied for the benchmark or minimax-complexity definition.

children.title: Lower Complexity Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Unavoidable oracle costs within matched information models.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Complexity Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal worst-case oracle-call obstruction over a fixed algorithm class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class, let \(E_f(x)\ge0\) be the prescribed error, and let \(\mathfrak A\) be an algorithm class using a fixed oracle. A function \(L:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb N\) is a lower complexity benchmark if, for every \(A\in\mathfrak A\) and every covered \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(f\in\mathcal F\) for which no output produced by \(A\) before \(L(\varepsilon)\) oracle calls satisfies \(E_f(x)\le\varepsilon\). Equivalently, under the selected deterministic or randomized success convention, \(T^*(\varepsilon)\ge L(\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower benchmark says that every allowed algorithm has an instance in the problem class on which it cannot attain the target accuracy before the stated number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: The problem class \(\mathcal F\), algorithm class \(\mathfrak A\), oracle, and error criterion are fixed.
For randomized algorithms, the failure-probability or expected-error convention is specified uniformly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*(\varepsilon)\ge L(\varepsilon)\) for every covered accuracy \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Universal lower benchmark on the required number of oracle calls.
Minimax oracle complexity at accuracy epsilon under the fixed success convention.
Prescribed optimization error for instance f at output x.

children.title: Oracle-Optimality Matching
children.top_down_role: Classifications where achievable and unavoidable oracle costs coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Optimality Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax matching for a fixed problem class, oracle model, and accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal P\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), and error criterion \(\operatorname{err}\). Let \(L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be a lower bound on the worst-case number of oracle calls required to return \(x\) with \(\operatorname{err}(x;P)\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(P\in\mathcal P_\theta\). If an algorithm \(A\) satisfies \(T_A(\theta,\varepsilon)\leq C L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) throughout a stated parameter regime, for a universal constant \(C>0\), then \(A\) is oracle-optimal there. Equivalently, \(T_A(\theta,\varepsilon)=\Theta(L(\theta,\varepsilon))\) when the lower bound also applies to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm is oracle-optimal when its worst-case query upper bound matches the applicable minimax lower bound up to universal constants.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_\theta\) and \(\mathcal O\) are fixed before comparing upper and lower bounds.
The same error criterion and success convention define both bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_A(\theta,\varepsilon)=\Theta(L(\theta,\varepsilon))\) in the stated regime.

notation.meaning: Worst-case oracle calls made by algorithm A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimax oracle optimality is conventionally defined by matching upper and lower query bounds in one fixed model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching criterion is mathematically standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. The record principally defines or states a condition for oracle optimality rather than furnishing a complexity bound for a particular problem class.

children.title: Deterministic–Randomized Separations
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which algorithmic randomization changes attainable complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic–Randomized Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax query separation under identical problem, oracle, accuracy, and success conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a problem class \(\mathcal P_\theta\), let \(T_{\mathrm{det}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the least worst-case query complexity over deterministic algorithms, and let \(T_{\mathrm{rand}}(\theta,\varepsilon,\delta)\) be the least complexity over randomized algorithms succeeding with probability at least \(1-\delta\) on every instance. A deterministic–randomized separation holds along a parameter sequence when \[T_{\mathrm{rand}}(\theta,\varepsilon,\delta)=o\!\left(T_{\mathrm{det}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\right).\] An exponent separation holds when the two complexities have different polynomial exponents in a designated parameter; a constant-factor improvement alone is not an asymptotic separation under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization yields a separation when its minimax query complexity is asymptotically smaller than deterministic complexity under the same oracle and success requirements.
assumptions_latex: Randomized complexity counts the same oracle calls as deterministic complexity.
The failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\) is fixed or explicitly parameterized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{rand}}=o(T_{\mathrm{det}})\) identifies a strict asymptotic separation.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_refs.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_witnesses.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter concerns randomized coordinate-update methods but does not establish the stated minimax deterministic–randomized comparison or the little-o separation convention. A source on randomized versus deterministic oracle complexity is required.

children.title: Adaptive–Nonadaptive Separations
children.top_down_role: Complexity gaps attributable to query adaptivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive–Nonadaptive Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query-complexity gap caused solely by dependence of later queries on earlier responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle algorithm is nonadaptive if, conditional on its internal random seed, its query points \((x_1,\ldots,x_T)\) are fixed before any oracle response is observed. It is adaptive if each \(x_t\) may be measurable with respect to the seed and the transcript through round \(t-1\). For a fixed class, oracle, error target, and success convention, let \(T_{\mathrm{ad}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{nonad}}\) be the corresponding minimax query complexities. An adaptive–nonadaptive separation holds along a parameter sequence when \[T_{\mathrm{ad}}(\theta,\varepsilon)=o\!\left(T_{\mathrm{nonad}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptivity gives a separation when transcript-dependent queries require asymptotically fewer oracle calls than queries fixed in advance.
assumptions_latex: Both algorithm classes use the same oracle and output criterion.
Random seeds, when present, are sampled independently of the unknown instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{ad}}=o(T_{\mathrm{nonad}})\) defines a strict adaptivity gap.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adaptive queries are transcript-dependent while nonadaptive queries are fixed before responses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adaptive and nonadaptive query definitions are plausible and fit the container, but no source supports the transcript-measurability formulation or the selected little-o convention for a strict adaptivity separation.

children.title: Local–Global Oracle Separations
children.top_down_role: Complexity differences caused by reusable global information rather than local responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Oracle Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of pointwise local responses with reusable instance-wide information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local oracle at query \(x_t\) returns information determined only by the instance germ or prescribed first-order data at \(x_t\), whereas a global oracle response may encode an object reusable at arbitrary future points, such as a complete component operator. For fixed admissible algorithms and a common accuracy target, let \(T_{\mathrm{loc}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{glob}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) denote their minimax query complexities. A local–global oracle separation holds along a parameter sequence when \[T_{\mathrm{glob}}(\theta,\varepsilon)=o\!\left(T_{\mathrm{loc}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\right).\] The oracle outputs and the unit cost assigned to each response must be specified for this comparison to be meaningful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local–global separation occurs when reusable instance-wide responses asymptotically reduce query complexity relative to pointwise information under explicit cost conventions.
assumptions_latex: The local and global response maps are explicitly specified.
Query cost and computational work outside the oracle are accounted for consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{glob}}=o(T_{\mathrm{loc}})\) defines a strict local–global oracle gap.

notation.meaning: Minimax complexity with reusable global responses

children.title: Dimension-Accuracy Phase Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Changes in dominant information limits across dimension and accuracy ranges.

children.title: Dimension-Driven Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in dominant information limits across dimensional ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change of the active complexity term as dimension varies at fixed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a tight oracle-complexity envelope has the form \[T(d,\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\min_{j\in J} B_j(d,\varepsilon)\right),\] where each \(B_j\) is valid in the common oracle model. At fixed \(\varepsilon\), a dimension-driven regime transition between indices \(i\) and \(j\) occurs at a scale \(d_\star(\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(B_i(d_\star,\varepsilon)\asymp B_j(d_\star,\varepsilon)\), with \(B_i<B_j\) asymptotically on one side and \(B_j<B_i\) on the other. Thus the transition changes the active optimal bound, not merely its numerical value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension transition occurs where two valid complexity terms exchange dominance as dimension crosses a threshold at fixed accuracy.
assumptions_latex: All candidate bounds use the same oracle, error criterion, and success convention.
The displayed envelope is tight up to parameter-independent constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active term in \(\min_{j\in J}B_j(d,\varepsilon)\) changes at \(d\asymp d_\star(\varepsilon)\).

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization
source_refs.locator: 1.2 Dimension p. 2

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Driven Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change of the active complexity term as target accuracy varies at fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a tight oracle-complexity envelope is \[T(d,\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\min_{j\in J} B_j(d,\varepsilon)\right).\] At fixed \(d\), an accuracy-driven regime transition between terms \(B_i\) and \(B_j\) occurs at \(\varepsilon_\star(d)>0\) when \(B_i(d,\varepsilon_\star)\asymp B_j(d,\varepsilon_\star)\), and their asymptotic ordering reverses across that scale. Consequently, moderate-accuracy and high-accuracy behavior may be governed by different methods or lower bounds even though the problem dimension and oracle remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accuracy transition occurs where two tight complexity terms exchange dominance as the requested error crosses a dimension-dependent threshold.
assumptions_latex: The error parameter \(\varepsilon\) has one fixed interpretation throughout the comparison.
The candidate terms are valid under the same oracle and parameter normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active term changes at \(\varepsilon\asymp\varepsilon_\star(d)\).

children.title: Joint Parameter Phase Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Complexity boundaries determined jointly by dimension and accuracy scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Parameter Phase Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary curves partitioning the dimension–accuracy plane by active complexity laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(d,\varepsilon)=\Theta(\min_{j\in J}B_j(d,\varepsilon))\) be a tight complexity envelope. The joint phase boundary between terms \(i\) and \(j\) is \[\Gamma_{ij}=\left\{(d,\varepsilon):B_i(d,\varepsilon)\asymp B_j(d,\varepsilon)\leq B_k(d,\varepsilon)\ \text{for every }k\in J\right\}.\] Away from the union of these boundaries, each phase is a connected parameter region on which one term is asymptotically minimal. Intersections of three or more sets \(\Gamma_{ij}\) are multicritical scales where several complexity mechanisms are simultaneously active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint phase boundaries are dimension–accuracy curves where competing tight complexity terms tie and jointly dominate all remaining terms.
assumptions_latex: Every \(B_j\) is expressed in a common query-cost model.
Hidden comparison constants are uniform over the parameter region considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(\Gamma_{ij}\) partition the \((d,\varepsilon)\)-domain into regions with distinct active complexity laws.

notation.meaning: Boundary where terms i and j are jointly active

children.title: Objective Accuracy

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive objective-value accuracy for a minimization problem with attained finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper objective on a nonempty set \(C\), and assume \(f^\star=\min_{z\in C}f(z)\) is finite. A point \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) has objective accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) if \[f(x)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon.\] If the output \(X\) is random, expected objective accuracy means \(\mathbb E[f(X)-f^\star]\leq\varepsilon\), while high-probability objective accuracy means \(\mathbb P(f(X)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\); these conventions are distinct and must not be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is objective-accurate when its objective-value gap from the optimum is at most the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The minimum value \(f^\star\) is finite and attained.
The candidate point belongs to \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-gap bound under positive scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of a conditional convergence bound by the same positive factor used to scale the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $p\ge1$, $m_1,\ldots,m_p\in\mathbb N$, $P=\sum_{j=1}^p m_j$, and $f^*=\inf_x f(x)$. If, after $N\in\mathbb N$ iterations, an iterate $\hat x$ satisfies
\[
f(\hat x)-f^*\le \frac{2P C}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}
\]
for a constant $C>0$, then for $\widetilde f=f/P$ and $\widetilde f^*=f^*/P$,
\[
\widetilde f(\hat x)-\widetilde f^*\le \frac{2C}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing an objective by the positive factor P divides its optimality gap and the given convergence bound by P, removing that factor from the bound.
assumptions_latex: p\ge1
m_j\in\mathbb N\quad(j=1,\ldots,p)
P=\sum_{j=1}^p m_j
f^*=\inf_x f(x)
f(\hat x)-f^*\le \frac{2PC}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{f(\hat x)}P-\frac{f^*}P\le \frac{2C}{\sqrt{N(N+1)}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Objective Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative objective-value accuracy for minimization problems with strictly positive optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*>0\), let \(\bar x\) be feasible for a minimization problem with optimal value \(f^*\), and let \(\delta\ge 0\). The value \(f(\bar x)\) approximates \(f^*\) with relative accuracy \(\delta\) if \[f^*\le f(\bar x)\le (1+\delta)f^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimization problem whose optimal value is strictly positive, a feasible point has relative objective accuracy δ when its objective value lies between the optimum and (1+δ) times the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \bar x\text{ is feasible and }f^*\text{ is the optimal value}
\delta\ge 0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*\le f(\bar x)\le (1+\delta)f^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Linearization Accuracy Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an objective-value lower-model certificate from weighted first-order affine models of the differentiable term and the exact convex term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and set \(\bar f=f+\psi\). Given \(x_0,\ldots,x_t\in Q\), weights \(a_k\ge0\), and \(A_t:=\sum_{k=0}^t a_k>0\), define \[\ell_t:=\frac1{A_t}\min_{x\in Q}\sum_{k=0}^t a_k\left[f(x_k)+\langle\nabla f(x_k),x-x_k\rangle+\psi(x)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The accuracy certificate ell_t is the minimum over Q of the weighted average of affine first-order models of f at the sampled points, with the exact convex term psi added to every model.
assumptions_latex: Q\text{ is convex}
f:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable}
\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is convex}
x_k\in Q\quad(0\le k\le t)
a_k\ge0\quad(0\le k\le t)
A_t=\sum_{k=0}^t a_k>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_t=\frac1{A_t}\min_{x\in Q}\left\{\sum_{k=0}^t a_k\left[f(x_k)+\langle\nabla f(x_k),x-x_k\rangle+\psi(x)\right]\right\}

children.title: Solution-Set Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Quality measured geometrically relative to the solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric distance from a candidate point to the exact solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\rho)\) be a metric space and let \(S^\star\subseteq X\) be the nonempty solution set of the problem under consideration. Define \[\operatorname{dist}_\rho(x,S^\star)=\inf_{z\in S^\star}\rho(x,z).\] A point \(x\in X\) has solution-set accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) if \(\operatorname{dist}_\rho(x,S^\star)\leq\varepsilon\). In a normed space the standard convention is \(\rho(x,z)=\lVert x-z\rVert\). This target is geometric and need not be equivalent to an objective-gap target without an error bound or growth condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point has solution-set accuracy ε when its metric distance to the nonempty exact solution set is at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\rho)\) is a metric space.
The exact solution set \(S^\star\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_\rho(x,S^\star)\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Metric used to measure geometric error
Point-to-set distance induced by the metric

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order residual accuracy for smooth constrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\). Using the limiting normal cone \(N_C(x)\), define the first-order stationarity residual by \[r_{\mathrm{stat}}(x)=\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla f(x)+N_C(x)\right)\] for \(x\in C\). The point \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary if \(r_{\mathrm{stat}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\). When \(C=\mathbb R^d\), this reduces to \(\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). The chosen normal-cone convention must be stated for nonconvex \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is ε-stationary when the distance from zero to its constrained first-order residual is at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and closed.
\(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{stat}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to C at x
Euclidean distance from zero to a set S

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum normalized violation for set and functional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a feasible region in a normed space be \[F=C\cap\{x:g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,p\},\] where \(C\) is nonempty and closed. Given positive scaling constants \(s_C,s_i,t_j\), define \[r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=\max\left\{\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,C)}{s_C},\max_i\frac{[g_i(x)]_+}{s_i},\max_j\frac{|h_j(x)|}{t_j}\right\}.\] The point \(x\) has feasibility accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) if \(r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility accuracy bounds the largest normalized violation of set membership, inequality constraints, and equality constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and closed.
All scaling constants are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)\leq\varepsilon\).

children.title: Variational Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Accuracy criteria expressed through variational formulations and operator residual behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual accuracy for a constrained variational inequality in finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^d\), and fix \(\lambda>0\). Define the natural residual \[r_\lambda(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\left\lVert x-P_C\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr)\right\rVert,\qquad x\in C.\] The point \(x\) has variational accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) if \(r_\lambda(x)\leq\varepsilon\). Moreover, \(r_\lambda(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) solves the variational inequality \(\langle F(x),z-x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variational accuracy bounds the projected natural residual; zero residual is equivalent to solving the constrained variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:C\to\mathbb R^d\) is single-valued.
The stepsize satisfies \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\lambda(x)\leq\varepsilon\), with \(r_\lambda(x)=0\) equivalent to the variational inequality.

children.title: Equilibrium Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Accuracy criteria for strategic, market, or fixed-point equilibrium formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty-gap accuracy for a monotone variational equilibrium on a bounded feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(F:K\to K^*\) be continuous. Define the equilibrium, or Minty, gap at \(x\in K\) by
\[G_{\mathrm E}(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle.\]
For \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), the point \(x\) has equilibrium accuracy \(\varepsilon\) when \(G_{\mathrm E}(x)\le\varepsilon\). In particular, \(G_{\mathrm E}(x)=0\) means that \(\langle F(y),x-y\rangle\le0\) for every \(y\in K\), the Minty variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is equilibrium-accurate to tolerance ε when its worst Minty inequality violation over the feasible set is at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(F:K\to K^*\) is continuous.
\(x\in K\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is equilibrium-accurate to \(\varepsilon\iff G_{\mathrm E}(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: dual of the ambient space containing K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional Minty-gap definition for variational inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Minty-gap definition fits the terminal container and is mathematically standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. In addition, K is a subset rather than a vector space, so the operator codomain should be the dual of a declared ambient space, for example F:K→V*.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Formulation Accuracy Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of Stampacchia and Minty gap targets under monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(F:K\to K^*\). For \(x\in K\), define
\[G_{\mathrm V}(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle,\qquad G_{\mathrm E}(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle.\]
If \(F\) is monotone, meaning \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0\) for all \(x,y\in K\), then \(0\le G_{\mathrm E}(x)\le G_{\mathrm V}(x)\). Consequently, every \(\varepsilon\)-accurate variational point is \(\varepsilon\)-accurate in the equilibrium formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator, the Minty equilibrium gap never exceeds the Stampacchia variational gap, so variational accuracy implies equilibrium accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(F:K\to K^*\) is monotone.
\(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le G_{\mathrm E}(x)\le G_{\mathrm V}(x)\), hence \(G_{\mathrm V}(x)\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow G_{\mathrm E}(x)\le\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct monotonicity comparison of standard variational-inequality gaps

children.title: Lower-Bound Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-minorant certificate for a convex minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(X\subseteq E\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex with \(X\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\). Define \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). Suppose that, for some integer \(N\ge1\), exact first-order oracle records \((x_i,f_i,g_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,N\), satisfy \(x_i\in X\), \(f_i=f(x_i)\), and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\). Define
\[L:=\inf_{x\in X}\max_{1\le i\le N}\bigl\{f_i+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\bigr\}.\]
Then \(L\le p^*\), so \(L\) is a lower-bound certificate. Every computable scalar \(\widehat L\) satisfying \(\widehat L\le L\) is also a certified lower bound on \(p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite collection of exact convex-subgradient records defines affine minorants. The infimum over the feasible set of their pointwise maximum is a certified lower bound on the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(X\subseteq E\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex, with \(X\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\).
\(N\ge1\), and every oracle record is exact: \(x_i\in X\), \(f_i=f(x_i)\), and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat L\le L\le p^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap certificate combining a feasible incumbent with a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). If \(\bar x\in X\) is a feasible incumbent and \(L\) is a certified scalar satisfying \(L\le p^*\), define the incumbent gap by
\[\Delta(\bar x,L):=f(\bar x)-L.\]
Because \(p^*\le f(\bar x)\), one has \(0\le f(\bar x)-p^*\le\Delta(\bar x,L)\). Thus \(\Delta(\bar x,L)\le\varepsilon\) certifies that \(\bar x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal in absolute objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent minus a certified lower bound upper-bounds its true objective error and certifies ε-optimality when the difference is at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in X\) and \(f(\bar x)\) is finite.
\(L\le p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(\bar x,L)\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(\bar x)-p^*\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bound–Gap Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Internal validity conditions for lower-bound and incumbent-gap reports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization problem with optimal value \(p^*\), a reported triple \((\bar x,L,\Delta)\) is bound–gap consistent precisely when
\[\bar x\in X,\qquad L\le p^*\le f(\bar x),\qquad \Delta=f(\bar x)-L.\]
These relations imply \(\Delta\ge0\) and \(f(\bar x)-p^*\le\Delta\). A negative reported gap, an infeasible incumbent, or a value \(L\) not independently certified as a lower bound invalidates the associated objective-accuracy claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound-gap report is consistent only when the incumbent is feasible, the bound is valid, and the reported gap equals incumbent value minus lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is finite.
The report contains \(\bar x\), \(L\), and \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in X\), \(L\le p^*\le f(\bar x)\), and \(\Delta=f(\bar x)-L\) imply \(0\le f(\bar x)-p^*\le\Delta\).

children.title: Primal–Dual Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal–dual gap certificate for composite convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) linear, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) proper closed convex functions. For primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\), define
\[P(x):=f(x)+g(Ax),\qquad D(y):=-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y).\]
The computable gap \(G(x,y):=P(x)-D(y)\) is nonnegative by Fenchel inequalities. If strong duality gives common value \(p^*=d^*\), then \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies both \(P(x)-p^*\le\varepsilon\) and \(d^*-D(y)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strong duality, a feasible primal–dual pair with gap at most ε certifies that both objective values are within ε of optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, and \(A\) is linear.
\(P(x)\) and \(D(y)\) are finite.
Strong duality holds: \(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le P(x)-p^*\le G(x,y)\) and \(0\le d^*-D(y)\le G(x,y)\).

children.title: Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Verification through operator, fixed-point, feasibility, or stationarity residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity certificate for a monotone inclusion using a computable residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be an operator for which a candidate pair \((x,v)\) with \(v\in T(x)\) can be verified. The norm
\[r_T(x;v):=\lVert v\rVert\]
is a stationarity residual certificate. The inequality \(r_T(x;v)\le\varepsilon\) certifies the approximate inclusion \(v\in T(x)\) with \(\lVert v\rVert\le\varepsilon\); when \(\varepsilon=0\), it certifies \(0\in T(x)\). Quantitative distance-to-solution conclusions require an additional error bound or metric-subregularity constant and do not follow from a small residual alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified graph element with small dual-vector norm certifies approximate stationarity; converting residual size into distance to a solution needs an error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Membership \(v\in T(x)\) is independently verifiable.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in T(x)\) and \(\lVert v\rVert\le\varepsilon\) certify \(\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x))\le\varepsilon\); if \(\varepsilon=0\), then \(0\in T(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificate for infeasibility of nonnegative linear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), consider the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\). A vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,
\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0\]
is a directly verifiable infeasibility certificate. Indeed, any feasible \(x\) would give \(b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\), contradicting the strict inequality. Farkas' alternative states that exactly one of the primal feasibility system and the certificate system has a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative linear equations, a Farkas multiplier with nonnegative adjoint image and negative pairing with the right-hand side certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
Vector inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\Rightarrow\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Witness Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on transferring exclusion witnesses into global infeasibility claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation certificate for one point does not by itself certify that the separated feasible set is empty. Concretely, for \(C=[0,\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(z=-1\), the pair \(a=-1\), \(\beta=0\) satisfies
\[\sup_{x\in C}ax=0<az=1,\]
so it certifies \(z\notin C\), although \(C\ne\varnothing\). More generally, transferring a witness between formulations requires a proved implication from the target feasibility system to the inequalities checked by that witness; equivalence of optimal values or an approximate reformulation alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A witness excluding one point need not prove global infeasibility; witness transfer requires an exact logical implication between the relevant feasibility systems.
assumptions_latex: Certificate semantics are strict point separation.
No exact feasibility-preserving transfer map is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\notin C\) does not imply \(C=\varnothing\); transfer to infeasibility is valid only through a proved feasibility implication.

children.title: Expectation Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected solution-quality guarantee under algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a random output of an algorithm and let \(Q(X)\in[0,+\infty]\) be a measurable solution-quality loss, with expectation taken over all declared algorithmic, sampling, and oracle randomness. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the algorithm has an expectation guarantee at level \(\varepsilon\) when
\[\mathbb E[Q(X)]\le\varepsilon.\]
This statement controls average loss only: without additional distributional information it neither asserts \(Q(X)\le\varepsilon\) almost surely nor supplies a prescribed small failure probability at threshold \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation guarantee bounds the average measurable quality loss over all declared randomness, but alone gives neither pathwise nor same-threshold high-probability accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a random algorithm output.
\(Q(X)\) is measurable and nonnegative.
The probability law includes every declared source of randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Q(X)]\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected-loss interface is precise, correctly limits its conclusion to average performance, and fits the expectation-guarantee container. No source or inspectable locator is supplied, so it cannot pass source review.

children.title: High-Probability Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence solution-quality guarantee with an explicit failure budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a random algorithm output and let \(Q(X)\in[0,+\infty]\) be measurable. Given accuracy \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), a high-probability guarantee is the assertion
\[\mathbb P\{Q(X)\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\delta,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad
\mathbb P\{Q(X)>\varepsilon\}\le\delta.\]
The probability space must include every randomness source covered by the claim, and \(\delta\) must be fixed or otherwise accounted for before inspecting the same data used to construct \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability guarantee places the quality loss below ε except on an explicitly budgeted event of probability at most δ.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a random algorithm output and \(Q(X)\) is measurable.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
All randomness covered by the claim is included in \(\mathbb P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{Q(X)>\varepsilon\}\le\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-confidence probability statement and its equivalent failure-event form are correct and fit the high-probability container. The qualification concerning data-dependent confidence budgets is reasonable but also needs support; no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Almost-Sure Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise long-run validity for random optimization iterates or certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \((X_t)_{t\ge 1}\) be random iterates, and let \(S\) be the set of acceptable solutions. An almost-sure convergence guarantee is \[\mathbb P\!\left(\left\{\omega:\operatorname{dist}(X_t(\omega),S)\to 0\right\}\right)=1.\] For transcript-measurable certificates \((C_t)_{t\ge1}\), an almost-sure eventual-validity guarantee is \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigcap_{t\ge n}\{C_t\text{ is valid}\}\right)=1.\] Either statement permits exceptional sample paths only on a single probability-zero event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With probability one, the iterates approach the acceptable set, or the reported certificates become valid from some random finite time onward.
assumptions_latex: \((X_t)_{t\ge1}\) and \((C_t)_{t\ge1}\) are defined on a common probability space.
\(S\) is nonempty and distance to \(S\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(X_t,S)\to0\) almost surely, or certificate validity holds eventually almost surely.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definitions of almost-sure convergence and eventual almost-sure validity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two formulations are mathematically standard and fit the almost-sure-guarantee leaf, but the record provides no inspectable citation. A probability or stochastic-optimization source with a specific definition, theorem, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Asymptotic Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-sample validity stated without a uniform finite-time requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For transcript-measurable assertions \((A_t)_{t\ge1}\) and a target error level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), asymptotic coverage means \[\liminf_{t\to\infty}\mathbb P(A_t)\ge 1-\alpha.\] For random accuracy bounds \((R_t)_{t\ge1}\), asymptotic consistency means \(R_t\to0\) in a specified mode, such as probability or almost surely, together with eventual correctness of the implication \(R_t\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow X_t\in S_\varepsilon\). The convergence mode and limiting operation are part of the guarantee and cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic guarantee controls limiting coverage or consistency as the sample or iteration count diverges, without necessarily controlling any fixed finite time.
assumptions_latex: \(A_t\in\mathcal F_t\) for a transcript filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{t\to\infty}\mathbb P(A_t)\ge1-\alpha\), or the explicitly stated consistency limit holds.

notation.meaning: event that the time-t assertion is correct

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard asymptotic coverage and consistency interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic-coverage formula is standard, but the record combines coverage, convergence in probability, almost-sure convergence, and an informally quantified eventual-correctness implication. An authoritative source is needed to determine the intended interface and whether these variants should be separated. The generic kind "condition" is also questionable for a guarantee leaf.

children.title: Finite-Sample Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on interpreting long-run guarantees as finite-sample certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sample Validity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic or almost-sure behavior does not supply finite-time coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E_t)_{t\ge2}\) be events satisfying \(\mathbb P(E_t)=1-1/t\). Then \(\mathbb P(E_t)\to1\), so \((E_t)\) is asymptotically valid, but \(\mathbb P(E_2)=1/2\); hence no confidence level exceeding \(1/2\) is justified at time \(2\). Likewise, eventual almost-sure validity constrains only sufficiently large random times. Therefore neither asymptotic validity nor eventual almost-sure validity alone implies the finite-sample statement \[\mathbb P(E_t)\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{for every prescribed finite }t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Long-run validity alone cannot justify a stated confidence level at every finite iteration or sample size.
assumptions_latex: \((E_t)_{t\ge2}\) is any event sequence with \(\mathbb P(E_t)=1-1/t\).
The requested finite-sample level satisfies \(1-\alpha>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Asymptotic validity does not imply \(\mathbb P(E_t)\ge1-\alpha\) for every finite \(t\).

notation.meaning: event that the time-t assertion is correct

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary event sequence separates asymptotic from finite-sample validity

knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous validity over all observation times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the oracle-transcript filtration and let \(C_t\in\mathcal F_t\) assert that the current output \(X_t\) belongs to an accuracy set \(S_t\). The sequence \((C_t)_{t\ge1}\) is an anytime certificate at error level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) if \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{t=1}^{\infty}\{C_t\Rightarrow X_t\in S_t\}\right)\ge1-\alpha.\] Thus one probability statement controls every report time simultaneously, including times selected after inspecting the evolving transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anytime certificate is simultaneously correct at every time with the advertised probability, so users may inspect and act on it continuously.

children.title: Sequential Certificates
